media.author: LaurelG

questions.fun_fact: The two Ms stand for Forrest Mars and Bruce Murrie, the two men who started making them.
questions.concept: Se derrite en tu boca, no en tu mano (M&M's)

quality.notes: Smarties (1937) are also chocolate in a sugar shell, so only the 1941 date and the soldiers set M&M's apart. The hint 2 slogan is the US one.

questions.description: How much forest can you cut before the forest stops being a forest?
questions.question: Scientists warn the Amazon has a “tipping point” where it turns into dry savanna. About how much of the forest would have to be lost?
hints: It is a smaller share than most people would guess.
Close to a fifth of the forest is already gone.
It is more than a fifth but less than a third.

media.credit: Alexander Gerst · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Alexander Gerst

questions.fun_fact: The Amazon makes about half of its own rain, so cutting trees can make the rest of the forest drier.

quality.notes: Lovejoy & Nobre gave 20–25%, so '25%' is a fair choice, but it is an estimate scientists still debate. The topic is sobering more than fun. 'About half of its own rain' is a commonly quoted but rough figure.

revision.reason: Replaced the wrong answer 'About 40%' with 'About 50%', because a 40% tipping point was published in 2016 and so could also count as correct.

questions.description: A bent piece of metal that looks like it has been smiling for centuries.
questions.question: Look at this U-shaped piece of metal. What is it used for?
wrong_answers: Holding a cart wheel in place
hints: It is nailed onto something.
It belongs to a big animal you can ride.
The animal it is made for says “neigh”.

media.note: A clear photo of a single metal horseshoe, not attached to a horse.
media.credit: North Lincolnshire Museum, Martin Foreman, 2014-02-06 16:23:04 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: North Lincolnshire Museum, Martin Foreman, 2014-02-06 16:23:04

questions.fun_fact: Fixing a horseshoe doesn't hurt the horse, because the outer part of its hoof has no feeling, just like your fingernails.

quality.notes: A simple object-recognition question with little surprise. Most people recognise a horseshoe from its shape. Shares the object with q-1600 (horseshoe luck) but asks a different fact. A clear horseshoe photo is easy to find on Commons.

revision.reason: Replaced the description, which hinted at hooves by saying the object is stepped on, with a neutral funny line.

previous.description: A piece of metal that spends its whole life being stepped on.

questions.description: Round, white and friendly hippo lookalikes from the far north.
questions.question: It's late autumn in Moominvalley, and the Moomins fill their tummies with pine needles. What do they do next, all winter long?
hints: They don't leave Moominvalley at all.
The full tummies have to last them through the long, cold months.
They wake up again when the snow melts.

media.credit: yrjö jyske · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: yrjö jyske

questions.fun_fact: The Moomins were created by Finnish artist Tove Jansson, and their first book came out in 1945.

quality.notes: The Moomins are well known in Finland, Japan and parts of Europe but much less elsewhere. Players can still work it out from 'fill their tummies' plus winter, which points to hibernation, and hint 2 makes it close to obvious.

questions.description: A story of swords, roses and very tall wigs.
questions.question: A 1970s manga and anime follows Oscar, a woman raised as a man, who commands Marie Antoinette's royal guard. Which palace is in its title?
hints: The story takes place before and during the French Revolution.
The palace is famous for its Hall of Mirrors.
It lies just outside Paris and was built up by Louis XIV.

media.credit: After Jean-Baptiste André Gautier-Dagoty · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: After Jean-Baptiste André Gautier-Dagoty

questions.fun_fact: The all-female Takarazuka Revue in Japan has performed a stage musical of this story since 1974.

quality.notes: Marie Antoinette's royal guard points strongly to Versailles even for players who don't know the manga, so it is easier than 10. A portrait of Marie Antoinette may show a palace interior, but that is low risk. Asks a different fact from q-2131 (Versailles from a photo).

questions.description: Some artists quit their club so dramatically that they built a whole new clubhouse with a golden hairdo.
questions.question: This exhibition hall with a dome of golden leaves was built by the city's Secession art group. In which city is it?
hints: The city is the capital of a country in central Europe.
Gustav Klimt helped found the group that built this hall in 1898.
The city is famous for waltzes, Mozart and the old Habsburg emperors.

media.note: Exterior photo of the Secession Building with its golden laurel-leaf dome; no visible city name or signs naming the city.
media.credit: Slyronit · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Slyronit

questions.fun_fact: Locals nicknamed the golden dome “the cabbage” because of its round, leafy look.

quality.notes: The description is long and wordy for a one-liner intro. 'Secession' in the question points to Vienna for anyone who knows the term, but Munich and Prague had Secession groups too, so the options stay fair. Photos of the building are easy to find and have no city name on them (the facade shows only a motto).

questions.description: Wonder Woman's family tree has some very famous branches on Mount Olympus.
questions.question: I'm a Greek goddess the Romans called Venus. In the first Wonder Woman comics, I protected the Amazons and brought baby Diana to life. Who am I?
hints: I'm one of the gods who live on Mount Olympus.
Diana's mother shaped her from clay, and I gave her life.
I'm the goddess of love and beauty.

media.credit: Carole Raddato from FRANKFURT, Germany · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Carole Raddato from FRANKFURT, Germany

questions.fun_fact: Wonder Woman's creator, William Moulton Marston, also helped develop an early lie detector test.

quality.notes: Golden Age origin is right: Hippolyta shaped Diana from clay and Aphrodite gave her life. The Venus clue is fair, but anyone who knows the Roman names gets it at once. The Venus planet questions share only the name, not the fact. A Greek temple image would be safe as illustrative, so decorative isn't really needed.

questions.description: A villain who leaves more homework than a math teacher.
questions.question: The Riddler wears green with question marks and leaves puzzles at his crimes. In which city does he cause trouble?
hints: It's a dark, rainy city.
Superman lives somewhere else.
The Joker and the Penguin live there too.
questions.fun_fact: The Riddler first appeared in a Batman comic in 1948.

quality.notes: Riddler's debut was Detective Comics #140 in 1948, which is correct. Hint 2 is weak because it only rules out Metropolis. It is close to the Batman question, but that one asks a different fact.

review.feedback: No suitable picture found for this question.

previous.feedback: The text is fine, but no media candidate fits. None of the pictures shows a green question mark or anything to do with the Riddler. A new search can't be run, so the media slot needs a fresh search, for example "question mark sign" or "city skyline night rain". No suitable picture found for this question.

revision.reason: New illustrative image search, because none of the old candidates fit.

questions.description: Finally a reward for getting old that isn't a creaky knee.
questions.question: In 1889, this became the first country with a national pension for retired workers. Which one?
hints: It's a country in Europe.
In 1889 it was a young country, unified less than 20 years earlier.
Its capital is Berlin.

media.credit: Ding Kezhong · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ding Kezhong

questions.fun_fact: Bismarck's pension started at age 70, at a time when few workers lived that long.

quality.notes: Bismarck's 1889 old-age insurance with a starting age of 70 is correct. Hint 2, which names Bismarck, already gives the answer to many adults. Most players will reason their way to it rather than know it, so it is probably closer to 11.

revision.reason: Replaced hint 2, which named Bismarck and gave the answer away, with a vaguer hint that names no person.

hints: It's a country in Europe.
Bismarck had united it only about 20 years earlier.
Its capital is Berlin.

questions.description: A boss who handed out shorter days and fatter paychecks, which sounds made up but isn't.
questions.question: In 1914, this industrialist gave his factory workers an 8-hour day and doubled their pay. Who is he?
hints: He was American and ran a huge factory in Detroit.
He made the assembly line famous.
His company built the Model T.

media.note: A clear portrait photo of Henry Ford, without any caption or name visible.
media.credit: Fred Hartsook · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Fred Hartsook

questions.fun_fact: Ford's “five-dollar day” in 1914 was so famous that thousands of people lined up outside his factory looking for jobs.

quality.notes: The five-dollar day and the 8-hour day in 1914 are correct. The essential portrait isn't really needed, since the text already answers the question, but Commons has many clear Ford portraits. Hint 3 names the Model T, which links to q-0215, but that question asks a different fact.

questions.description: The worst boss in cartoon history, and he has had a very long time to practice.
questions.question: I own the nuclear power plant in Springfield, so Homer Simpson's paycheck comes from me. Who am I?
hints: He is the richest man in town.
He taps his fingertips together when he plots something.
His assistant is the loyal Smithers.

media.credit: Vsatinet · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Vsatinet

questions.fun_fact: Mr. Burns is said to be over 100 years old in the show, yet he still runs the plant.

quality.notes: The Simpsons is shown worldwide, but it is still a US show and less familiar to young kids in some regions. It is close to the Springfield question q-0409 in topic only.

questions.description: Your bananas have probably traveled more than you have.
questions.question: Goods bought from another country arrive at the port and go through customs. What is this kind of trade called?
hints: Countries do it with things they can't make or grow enough of themselves.
The money leaves the country, while the goods arrive.
Its opposite is selling goods to other countries, called “export”.

media.credit: Petar Milošević · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Petar Milošević

questions.fun_fact: Most goods that countries buy from abroad arrive by ship in big metal containers.

quality.notes: This is a dry definition question that feels like a school test. Hint 3 rules out Export by naming it. Tariff and Subsidy are not kinds of trade, so they are weaker distractors.

questions.description: What goes up must come down, and here it comes down very fast.
questions.question: Home prices rise far above their real value because buyers expect them to keep rising, then they crash. What do economists call this?
hints: Japan had one around 1990, and the US one burst before 2008.
Its name compares it to something that is mostly empty inside.
Children blow the same thing with soap.

media.credit: Андрей Романенко · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Андрей Романенко

questions.fun_fact: When the US housing market crashed in 2007 and 2008, it helped start a worldwide financial crisis.

quality.notes: The term is widely known from the news, so adults get it more easily than teens. Hints 2 and 3 strongly point to the answer.

questions.description: Haircuts, bus rides and doctors: things you buy but can't put in your pocket.
questions.question: Economists group jobs like banking, tourism and cutting hair into one sector of the economy. What is it called?
hints: Services don't grow or build things, they help people.
Teachers, nurses and shop workers belong to it too.
Its name comes from the Latin word for “third”.

media.credit: Nenad Stojkovic · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Nenad Stojkovic

questions.fun_fact: In many rich countries, more than 7 out of 10 workers have jobs in services.

quality.notes: This is a school-test definition. Some models put banking in a quaternary sector, and a barber can work in the informal sector, so the answer is slightly fuzzy. The description hints at services. The answer_kind axis says 'number', which doesn't match a sector name.

revision.reason: Replaced hint 2, which numbered the sectors and so ruled out the wrong options, with more examples of jobs in the sector.

hints: Services don't grow or build things, they help people.
Farming and mining come first, factories come second.
Its name comes from the Latin word for “third”.

questions.description: The shortest and most stressful job interview in the world.
questions.question: A famous job-interview challenge for salespeople goes “Sell me this…” what?
hints: It's a small, everyday object.
You'd find one on almost any office desk.
You can use it to sign a contract.

media.credit: Office of U.S. Deputy Commerce Secretary · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Office of U.S. Deputy Commerce Secretary

questions.fun_fact: The challenge became famous worldwide through a 2013 Hollywood film about a real stockbroker named Jordan Belfort.

quality.notes: Accurate: the line was made famous by The Wolf of Wall Street. Hint 2 (office desk) fits Stapler and Phone too, so it's fine. Hint 3 nearly gives it away, which is allowed. Adults who saw the film get it easily, so about 10–11 is right.

questions.description: A bridge in the Scottish Highlands that has never once had a traffic jam.
questions.question: This curved concrete bridge in Scotland was built for one kind of traffic. Which one?
hints: The bridge is very narrow, with no room for sidewalks.
Its traffic runs on a timetable.
In the Harry Potter films, the Hogwarts Express crosses it.

media.note: Photo of the Glenfinnan Viaduct with its curved row of arches, with no train on it.
media.credit: Christian David · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Christian David

questions.fun_fact: The Glenfinnan Viaduct, finished in 1901, was one of the first big bridges made of concrete.

quality.notes: Difficulty 3 is too low. With no train in the photo, a 9-year-old has to reason from the bridge's shape or recognise it from Harry Potter. That's more like 5. Commons has many photos of the Glenfinnan Viaduct, but most show the Jacobite steam train. The essential photo must be checked so it has no train, though rails may still show.

questions.description: A Welsh bridge with a lot of nerve and not much railing.
questions.question: Engineers Thomas Telford and William Jessop finished this bridge in Wales in 1805, on these tall stone pillars. What does it carry?
hints: The traffic on it moves very slowly.
Its top is a long iron trough.
It is a kind of aqueduct.

media.note: Photo of the tall stone pillars of the Pontcysyllte Aqueduct seen from the valley below; no boats or water trough visible.
media.credit: Dave Croker · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Dave Croker

questions.fun_fact: The Pontcysyllte Aqueduct is about 38 m (126 ft) high, and boats still cross it today.

quality.notes: The facts check out: Telford and Jessop, 1805, about 38 m. The question is a bit long and dry, and the engineers' names add little. The 'not much railing' description hints at the famous open edge of the trough. Many photos of the pillars also show the water trough or boats, so the photo needs care.

questions.description: A bridge that has watched about 1,400 years of people cross it.
questions.question: China's Zhaozhou Bridge, built around 605, still stands. Besides its one big stone arch, what special feature is it famous for?
questions.answer: Four small arches in its sides
wrong_answers: Hollow wooden beams in its deck
A roof covering its whole deck
Stone pillars standing in the river
hints: The extra parts make the bridge lighter.
They also let floodwater pass through.
Look at the “shoulders” above the big arch.

media.credit: Huangdan2060 · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Huangdan2060

questions.fun_fact: Europe built its first bridges with such open side arches many centuries after the Zhaozhou Bridge.

quality.notes: Accurate: it has open spandrels, two small arches at each end. The bridge is also famous for its flat, shallow arch, but that isn't an option, so the answer stays clear. Fairly dry and technical. The description is plain, not funny. The decorative query could find the Zhaozhou Bridge itself, which is fine since the image is blurred.

questions.description: The stuff of log bridges, pencils and kitchen tables.
questions.question: Wool comes from a sheep. Wood comes from a…
hints: It grows in a forest.
It has leaves and branches.
Squirrels climb it.

media.credit: Lori from New York, NY, United States · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Lori from New York, NY, United States

questions.fun_fact: The Chapel Bridge in Lucerne, Switzerland, was first built in the 1300s and is one of Europe's oldest covered wooden bridges.

quality.notes: A simple analogy that works for a 1. It's not very fun, and the bridge theme only appears in the fun fact. The description describes wood, which the question already names, and it isn't really funny. The MrBeast tree question shares the answer but asks a different fact.

questions.description: A sports store with a name that sounds like ten times the workout.
questions.question: The sports store Decathlon takes its name from Greek. “Deca” means “ten”. What does “athlon” mean?
hints: The same Greek root is in the word “athlete”.
In the Olympic decathlon, athletes run, jump and throw over two days.
Athletes take part in one of these to win a prize.

media.credit: Pierre-Yves Beaudouin · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Pierre-Yves Beaudouin

questions.fun_fact: Decathlon opened its first store in 1976 near Lille, in northern France.

quality.notes: Greek athlos/athlon does mean contest. 'Day' is a weak distractor, and 'Runner' is wrongly drawn towards by hint 1. It's a fairly dry word-root question. Teens may find it harder than 7.

questions.description: A car that never cared much whether there was a road.
questions.question: The first Land Rover, from 1948, was mainly made for which group of people?
hints: Its designer got the idea while working on his own land.
It could pull a plow and drive across fields.
Think of tractors, barns and muddy fields.

media.credit: DeFacto · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: DeFacto

questions.fun_fact: The first Land Rover design was reportedly drawn in the sand on a beach in Wales.

quality.notes: Hint 2 uses the UK spelling 'plough'; it should be 'plow'. The farm-use origin is correct: Maurice Wilks and his farm on Anglesey. The sand-drawing story is legend, but it's flagged as 'reportedly'. 'Desert explorers' is a tempting distractor, and arguably early Land Rovers served explorers too, but the main target was farmers. Rated 7, but I'd put it nearer 9.

revision.reason: Changed the British spelling 'plough' to the US spelling 'plow' in hint 2.

hints: Its designer got the idea while working on his own land.
It could pull a plough and drive across fields.
Think of tractors, barns and muddy fields.

questions.description: Three of these would make a chocolate lover happy, one would leave them confused.
questions.question: Which of these candies has no chocolate in it?
hints: It comes in many bright colors.
Its flavors are fruits like strawberry and orange.
Its slogan is “Taste the rainbow”.

media.credit: LaurelG · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: LaurelG

questions.fun_fact: Skittles were first sold in the United Kingdom in 1974, before they came to the United States.

quality.notes: Facts check out: Skittles went on sale in the UK in 1974, before the US in 1979. The candy brands lean US/UK. Kit Kat, Snickers and M&M's are sold worldwide, but Skittles is less known in some markets. A 'colorful candy jar' image could easily show Skittles or M&M's. The idea is pleasant but plain.

questions.description: Love is a chase, especially when one of you is a ninja.
questions.question: Pucca chases him all over the village to kiss him, he's a ninja who wants to be the best, and he always runs away. What's his name?
hints: He's from a cartoon made in South Korea.
He rarely speaks and carries a sword.
His name has four letters and starts with G.

media.credit: HarshLight · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: HarshLight

questions.fun_fact: Pucca started as a character on the internet in South Korea before getting her own TV series.

quality.notes: Hint 1 says it was 'made in South Korea'. The concept is from Korea's Vooz, but the 2006 TV series was co-produced with Jetix and Studio B (Canada), so the hint is only partly accurate. The distractors are real Pucca characters (Abyo, Tobe, Dada), which works well. Pucca was popular in the mid-2000s, mainly in Latin America, Europe and Asia, so the question rests on nostalgia.

questions.description: Old technology that once had the whole family sitting in one row every evening.
questions.question: What do people use this machine for?
hints: It usually sits in the living room.
It has a screen on the front.
Cartoons and the news come on it.

media.note: A clear photo of an old television set with a visible screen, switched off, no logos or text on screen.
media.credit: Sven Scheuermeier sveninho · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Sven Scheuermeier sveninho

questions.fun_fact: In 1926, Scottish inventor John Logie Baird showed one of the first working televisions, and the pictures were blurry and tiny.

quality.notes: This is a very easy question with essential media; a photo of a vintage TV is easy to find on Commons. A very old set may look unfamiliar to 6-year-olds, but the screen makes it clear. Not very surprising: a plain 'what is this' question.

questions.description: A hot little machine with a pointy nose and a very flat personality.
questions.question: A broom is used on the floor. In the same way, an iron is used on…
hints: It gets very hot.
It makes things smooth and flat.
Think of a wrinkled shirt.

media.credit: Lambtron · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Lambtron

questions.fun_fact: Long before electricity, people heated heavy metal irons on a stove or in a fire before using them.

quality.notes: A simple analogy that works. 'Carpets' fits loosely, since steam irons are sometimes used on carpets, but this does not seriously compete. It is a plain everyday question with little surprise.

questions.description: The quiet hero of every family dinner, at least until it starts humming.
questions.question: Clothes go in the washing machine. In the same way, dirty plates go in the…
hints: It's in the kitchen.
It uses water and soap.
It cleans cups, forks and plates for you.

media.credit: Historyofspiders · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Historyofspiders

questions.fun_fact: Josephine Cochrane patented her dishwasher in 1886 because she was tired of her fine china getting chipped when washed by hand.

quality.notes: Stacks of dirty plates are often photographed inside dishwasher racks, so the image has a slight risk of showing the answer. Home dishwashers are much less common in many regions, though children still know the word. This is the same analogy pattern as famous-inventors-2 but with a different answer, so there is no overlap of facts. Fun is limited; the fun fact helps.

questions.description: Rome's most famous bathtub, and nobody is allowed to swim in it.
questions.question: Lovers once left padlocks on the Pont des Arts bridge in Paris. What do visitors leave in Rome's Trevi Fountain?
hints: Visitors throw them over their shoulder into the water.
Legend says it means you will come back to Rome.
You could pay for an ice cream with them.

media.credit: Dietmar Rabich · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Dietmar Rabich

questions.fun_fact: More than a million euros are fished out of the Trevi Fountain every year and given to charity.

quality.notes: The facts are correct; about €1.4 million a year goes to Caritas. The setup with the padlocked bridge adds length but works as an analogy. The Trevi coin custom is known from films and travel, more by teens and adults than by young children.

questions.description: A very tall Canadian who never stops looking down on Toronto.
questions.question: I'm a concrete needle 553 m (1,815 ft) tall in Toronto, with a glass floor high above the city. What kind of tower am I?
hints: Nobody lives or works in my thin concrete shaft.
I was built because the city's tall buildings kept getting in the way.
The antenna on my top sends programs to millions of homes.

media.credit: Jchmrt · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jchmrt

questions.fun_fact: From 1975 to 2007, Toronto's CN Tower was the tallest free-standing structure in the world.

quality.notes: The facts check out: 553 m (1,815 ft), the glass floor, and the tower was built because skyscrapers blocked broadcast signals. The skyline photo will show the tower's antenna, which is a mild hint, but it is the subject of the question. Players can reason their way to the answer without knowing Toronto.

questions.description: The only kind of battle that ends with everyone laughing on the sofa.
questions.question: Kids shoot soft foam darts from colorful toy blasters. Which toy brand is famous for them?
hints: Its blasters are a favorite for battles in the backyard.
Its name has only four letters.
Its logo is often on orange and blue blasters.

media.credit: Joe Loong from Reston, USA · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Joe Loong from Reston, USA

questions.fun_fact: The very first Nerf product, in 1969, was a foam ball sold as the world's first official indoor ball.

quality.notes: The other brands obviously don't make foam darts, so anyone who knows the brands rules them out quickly. Nerf is a US brand, but it's widely sold around the world. A decorative 'foam toy darts' image may still show a Nerf logo, even blurred.

questions.description: A philosopher who'd send back a birthday cake for having too many candles.
questions.question: German thinker Arthur Schopenhauer said life swings like a pendulum between pain and boredom. Which outlook is he famous for?
hints: He lived in the 19th century and loved Indian philosophy.
His main book is called “The World as Will and Representation.”
It's the opposite of optimism.

media.credit: Thomas Wolf (Der Wolf im Wald) · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Thomas Wolf (Der Wolf im Wald)

questions.fun_fact: Schopenhauer had a series of pet poodles, and he called them Atma or Butz.

quality.notes: The decorative image (a pendulum) comes from a metaphor in the quote, which the house style rules out. It should show Schopenhauer's world instead, such as 19th-century Frankfurt. Adults who know Schopenhauer know he was a pessimist, but teens mostly won't, so this is closer to 11. Fairly dry.

revision.reason: Replaced hint 2, which defined pessimism, with the title of his main work.

hints: He lived in the 19th century and loved Indian philosophy.
His outlook expects the worst of life.
It's the opposite of optimism.

questions.description: Three words that philosophy students have argued about for 140 years.
questions.question: Friedrich Nietzsche wrote “God is dead… and we have killed him.” What did he mean?
questions.answer: Faith no longer guided how modern people lived
wrong_answers: Science had proved that God never existed
Christianity had replaced the old Greek gods
Churches would soon be closed by law
hints: Nietzsche was a 19th-century German philosopher.
He was describing a change in society, not a single event.
He worried that without belief, people had lost their shared values.

media.credit: Dietmar Rabich · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Dietmar Rabich

questions.fun_fact: The line appears in Nietzsche's book “The Gay Science” of 1882, spoken by a madman who runs into a market with a lantern in broad daylight.

quality.notes: The answer is a fair simplification of a reading that is still debated. 'God is dead' may make religious families uncomfortable during a family game night. The book title 'The Gay Science' in the fun fact may cause giggles or confusion for kids. The question is a dry interpretation exercise.

questions.description: An old philosopher's ideas, given a fresh coat of paint 600 years later.
questions.question: Plotinus, born in Egypt, taught in Rome in the 200s that everything flows from “the One”. Whose older ideas did his school revive?
hints: Plotinus's student Porphyry gathered his writings into the “Enneads”.
The older thinker lived in Athens about 600 years before Plotinus.
The older thinker wrote “The Republic” and described a famous cave.

media.author: Gary Todd from Xinzheng, China

questions.fun_fact: Porphyry says Plotinus seemed ashamed of having a body and refused to tell anyone his birthday.

quality.notes: Plato is the most famous option, and 'Plotinus' sounds a bit like 'Plato', so guessers have an edge. The real gap is about 650 years, not 600, which is close enough. Fairly dry.

questions.description: The runner-up wise man of China, and proud of it.
questions.question: I'm called China's “Second Sage” after Confucius, and I taught that people are born good. Who am I?
hints: I lived in the 300s BC.
My rival Xunzi said human nature is bad.
My Chinese name is Mengzi.

media.author: N509FZ

questions.fun_fact: A famous Chinese story says Mencius's mother moved house three times to find the best neighborhood for his education.

quality.notes: The facts are accurate and the distractors are strong. The question is hard but fair for well-read adults.

questions.description: Someone who never, ever runs out of things to say.
questions.question: I never stop talking, my best friend is a green ogre, and I married a dragon. Who am I?
hints: I'm from an animated film.
My ogre friend lives in a swamp.
My name is just what I am.

hints: It belongs to the crow family, a very clever bunch.
It is a common sight in European parks and fields.
In old stories, it is said to steal shiny things.

media.credit: Suffolk County Council, Alexander Bliss, 2018-01-19 18:16:00 · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Suffolk County Council, Alexander Bliss, 2018-01-19 18:16:00

questions.fun_fact: In a 2008 test, magpies with a colored dot on their neck kept trying to scratch it off after seeing it in a mirror.

quality.notes: Good, surprising fact, and parrot is a strong distractor. Hint 3 (stealing shiny things) nearly gives it, which is fine for hint 3.

questions.description: Nature's doorbell, except this one is telling you to leave.
questions.question: What sound does an angry goose make to tell you to stay away?
hints: It's an angry sound.
A snake makes this sound too.
It sounds like “ssss”.

media.credit: Trougnouf (Benoit Brummer) · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Trougnouf (Benoit Brummer)

questions.fun_fact: Geese are so good at raising the alarm that people have used them as guards for thousands of years.

quality.notes: Essential video: a clear clip of a goose hissing on Commons or Openverse is likely but not certain, and the clip needs sound. The fun fact repeats the answer of farm-animals-2 (geese as guards), but the question asks a different fact.

previous.feedback: The slot needs an essential video of a goose hissing, with sound, but all six candidates are still images and a new search isn't allowed. Photos 1, 2 and 4 show a goose with its beak open, which looks just like honking or calling, so they can't show hissing as the question asks. Photos 3, 5 and 6 are a caricature whose caption contains the word “hissed”. Either find a real goose-hissing clip (with sound) by hand, or rework the question to fit an illustrative image. No suitable picture found for this question.

revision.reason: Turned this from an essential video into a plain question with an illustrative goose photo, because no goose-hissing clip with sound is likely to exist in the sources.

previous.question: Watch: what is this goose doing to tell you to stay away?

media.note: A goose with neck stretched forward and beak open, hissing at the camera.

questions.description: Ancient Rome's most exclusive neighborhood: emperors only, please.
questions.question: The Roman emperors built their homes on this one of Rome's seven hills. Which hill is it?
hints: It rises between the Roman Forum and the Circus Maximus.
Augustus, the first emperor, lived there.
Its name gave us the word “palace”.

media.credit: PierreSelim · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: PierreSelim

questions.fun_fact: Legend says Romulus built the very first walls of Rome on this hill.

quality.notes: Solid. q-1569 names the Palatine as one of the seven hills, but it asks a different fact (that they are hills). Hint 3 (“palace”) almost gives it away, which is allowed for hint 3. The Prima Porta statue is a safe image.

questions.description: A brand-new dance, and the old one didn't even have to move out.
questions.question: In 2005 the All Blacks first performed a new haka, Kapa o Pango. Which older, much more famous haka do they still perform too?
hints: The older haka is about 200 years old.
It is said to have been composed by the Maori chief Te Rauparaha.
Its famous chant means “It is death! It is life!”

media.credit: Pierre André Leclercq · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Pierre André Leclercq

questions.fun_fact: Ka Mate is said to have been composed around 1820 by the Maori chief Te Rauparaha, while he hid from his enemies in a food storage pit.

quality.notes: The facts are right (Kapa o Pango 2005, Te Rauparaha, about 1820). The Pacific war-dance distractors are good for experts. Ka Mate is well known to rugby fans, so this is perhaps a 13. For non-fans it is close to a pure-memory question. The description joke is weak.

questions.description: A ball that clearly never learned how to roll in a straight line.
questions.question: Old rugby balls were made from a pig's bladder covered in leather. What shape is a rugby ball?
hints: It is easy to hold under one arm while running.
That shape is why it bounces in strange directions.
Think of what a hen lays.

media.credit: Jusben · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jusben

questions.fun_fact: The pig's bladders came in different sizes, so early rugby balls were all a little different until rubber bladders arrived in the 1860s.

quality.notes: The square and flat options are throwaways. The pig-bladder lead-in doesn't connect to the shape question, so the question reads oddly and isn't very fun. “Like an egg” in the answer is fine for this level.

questions.description: A full-back so elegant he made running backwards toward his own goal look like ballet.
questions.question: Serge Blanco, the legendary full-back who played 93 tests for France, was born in which country?
hints: He was not born in Europe.
He was born in a South American capital city.
He was born in Caracas.

media.credit: Helene Brasseur · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Helene Brasseur

questions.fun_fact: Blanco grew up in Biarritz, France, and played his whole club career for the town's team, Biarritz Olympique.

quality.notes: Correct: Blanco was born in Caracas and has 93 caps. This is niche sports trivia that you can't reason towards, so it is more of a 14 than a 13. Hint 2 (Caribbean coast) already decides it among the options. The description is about full-back play and is only mildly funny.

revision.reason: Replaced hint 2, which only Venezuela fit, with a hint that fits all four options.

hints: He was not born in Europe.
His birth country is on the Caribbean coast of South America.
He was born in Caracas.

questions.description: Players so fast the defenders mostly see the backs of their shirts.
questions.question: I wear number 11 or 14 and sprint along the edge of the field to score tries. My position has the name of a part of a bird. Which part?
hints: I am usually one of the fastest players on the team.
Soccer has a player with almost the same name, who also runs along the side.
Birds flap two of them to fly.

media.credit: Simon_sees. · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Simon_sees.

questions.fun_fact: In rugby union, wings are usually the team's top try scorers because they get the ball with open space in front of them.

quality.notes: history-17 also has “the wing” as its answer, but it asks a different fact. The name works in other languages too (ala, Flügel). The bird-part reasoning makes this reachable, though kids need a little sports knowledge.

questions.description: The most famous reunion spot in the desert, no phones needed.
questions.question: Islamic tradition says that two people found each other again on Mount Arafat, near Mecca, after a long separation. Who were they?
hints: This pair also appears in the Bible and the Torah.
In Arabic, the hill's name is linked to the word for “to recognize”.
They were the first man and the first woman, sent out of Paradise.

media.credit: Fahad Faisal · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Fahad Faisal

questions.fun_fact: Standing on the plain of Arafat on the 9th day of the month of Dhul-Hijjah is the most important part of the whole Hajj pilgrimage.

quality.notes: The tradition and the 'arafa / “to recognize” link are both right. Hint 1 (“the very beginning”) already points strongly to Adam and Eve. The fact is fairly obscure, so this is closer to 13.

revision.reason: Fixed the fun fact's date (9th of Dhul-Hijjah) and replaced hint 1, which gave the answer away, with a vague hint that fits all four pairs.

hints: Their story goes back to the very beginning, long before Islam.
In Arabic, the hill's name is linked to the word for “to recognize”.
They were the first man and the first woman, sent out of Paradise.
previous.fun_fact: Standing on the plain of Arafat on the ninth day of the Hajj is the most important part of the whole pilgrimage.

questions.description: Monks who have kept the lights on in the desert for about 1,500 years without a single day off.
questions.question: This monastery at the foot of Mount Sinai, in Egypt, has had monks since the 6th century. Which church do they belong to today?
hints: It was founded by the Byzantine emperor Justinian.
It is the same church as the monasteries of Mount Athos.
Its monks pray in the language of the New Testament.

media.credit: Berthold Werner · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Berthold Werner

questions.fun_fact: Saint Catherine's Monastery is often called the oldest Christian monastery still in use, and its library holds some of the oldest books in the world.
questions.concept: Monasterio de Santa Catalina del Sinaí

quality.notes: Hint 2 is loose. Sinai is an autonomous church under the Patriarchate of Jerusalem, and Mount Athos also has Russian, Serbian and Bulgarian monasteries, so “same church” only holds in a broad sense. Coptic is an excellent distractor. The fact is dry.

questions.description: A temple where the morning prayers come with high kicks.
questions.question: Monks at this Buddhist temple in the mountains of China became world-famous for which martial art?
hints: Films about these warrior monks made their fighting style famous around the world.
Bruce Lee and Jackie Chan made it famous in films.
A panda named Po learns it in a film series.

media.credit: Aaron Zhu · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Aaron Zhu

questions.fun_fact: The Shaolin Temple was founded about 1,500 years ago, and its monks still put on kung fu shows for visitors today.

quality.notes: Hints 1 and 2 both point to films, so they repeat each other. Tai chi is also Chinese, but it is clearly linked to Wudang, not Shaolin, so it is wrong but arguable for laypeople. The Shaolin gate may carry a Chinese name sign, which is harmless. Kung Fu Panda makes this easier, so about a 6.

questions.description: Some of the oldest garden residents in Jerusalem, and they have not moved once.
questions.question: These gnarled trees grow in the Garden of Gethsemane in Jerusalem, where Jesus prayed. What kind of trees are they?
hints: These trees can live for well over a thousand years.
The garden lies at the foot of a hill named after them.
Their fruit is pressed for oil.

media.note: Show a close-up of the twisted old trunks of the trees in the Garden of Gethsemane, without fruit and without signs.
media.credit: brionv from San Francisco, United States · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: brionv from San Francisco, United States

questions.fun_fact: The name Gethsemane comes from words meaning “oil press”, and some of its trees are thought to be about 900 years old.

quality.notes: Facts hold up: Gethsemane comes from the Aramaic for 'oil press', and a 2012 study dated some of the trees to about 900 years old. Hint 2 (the hill named after the trees) nearly gives it away, but it is a hint, so that's allowed. An olive trunk is easy to recognise in an essential photo, which makes it easier, though not trivial. Wikimedia Commons has photos of these trees. q-0571 also has olive as its answer, but it asks a different fact.

questions.description: A skinny glass gadget that has been telling the truth for 300 years.
questions.question: What is this tool used for?
hints: Doctors and nurses use it a lot.
Your parents might use it when you feel sick.
It tells you how hot or cold something is.

media.note: A clear photo of a classic glass liquid thermometer; ideally no visible °C or °F label.
media.credit: Jacek Halicki · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jacek Halicki

questions.fun_fact: Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit made the first reliable mercury thermometer in 1714.

quality.notes: A fairly dry identify-the-object question. Fahrenheit's mercury thermometer of 1714 is correct. Candidate physics-5 says 'A thermometer shows degrees' in its text, which brushes against this answer, but it asks a different fact.

questions.description: A question with good vibrations, measured very precisely.
questions.question: At a concert, loudness is to decibel as pitch is to…
hints: Pitch depends on how many times per second something vibrates.
Radio stations use this unit, often with “mega” in front.
It is named after Heinrich, a German physicist who studied radio waves.

media.credit: Lukasz Kobus, European Commission · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Lukasz Kobus, European Commission

questions.fun_fact: Humans can hear from about 20 to 20,000 hertz, and dogs can hear much higher sounds.

quality.notes: q-1483 asks how the hertz is defined. Same topic, different fact. A tuning fork image is safe.

questions.description: A shopping trip where one item plays by different rules.
questions.question: At the supermarket, three of these are usually sold by the liter (or gallon). Which one is not?
hints: Liters and gallons are used for liquids.
The odd one out is a dry powder.
It's sold in kilograms (or pounds) and used to bake bread.

media.credit: Wilfredor · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Wilfredor

questions.fun_fact: One liter of water weighs about 1 kilogram.

quality.notes: Plain and a bit dry. Juice is sometimes sold by the carton, but that doesn't really count against it. A blurred supermarket aisle as the decorative image is fine.

questions.description: Two circles, one nose, and a lot of magic.
questions.question: Which famous young wizard from books and films wears round glasses with thin dark frames?
hints: The boy goes to Hogwarts.
He plays Seeker for Gryffindor.
He has a lightning-shaped scar on his forehead.

media.credit: W. McBride · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: W. McBride

questions.fun_fact: Harry's round glasses became so famous that this style is often simply called “Harry Potter glasses”.

quality.notes: Hint 1 (Hogwarts) fits all four options, so it is weak but fair. The fun fact's claim that the style is 'often called Harry Potter glasses' is informal but holds up.

questions.description: Hands-free storage, as worn by tourists everywhere.
questions.question: Backpack is to back as … is to waist?
hints: It's a bag you don't hold in your hand.
It clips around your middle.
Many people wear it at the front, near the belly button.

media.credit: Vyacheslav Argenberg · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Vyacheslav Argenberg

questions.fun_fact: Ötzi the Iceman, who lived about 5,300 years ago, carried a small pouch on his belt.

quality.notes: 'Belt bag' is the only option that hints at the waist (belt ↔ waist), so the answer stands out. Briefcase and suitcase are weak distractors. Younger kids may not know the term 'belt bag', since 'fanny pack' and 'bum bag' are the regional names. The fun fact about Ötzi's belt pouch is correct.

questions.description: A tiny suitcase that only travels to school.
questions.question: It has a zipper, rides to school in your backpack and holds your pens. What is it?
hints: You need it in class.
Inside are things for writing and drawing.
It often holds an eraser and a sharpener too.

media.credit: Marie from Malang, East Java, Indonesia · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Marie from Malang, East Java, Indonesia

questions.fun_fact: Many children in the 1800s wrote on small slates with chalk instead of using paper and pencils.

quality.notes: Very easy and not very surprising, but fine for a level 1 question.

questions.description: The hottest spot in your house is a few thousand kilometers under the basement.
questions.question: Earth's inner core is a ball of solid iron and nickel. About how hot is it?
hints: It is far hotter than any oven or volcano lava.
It is hot enough to melt any metal at the surface; only the huge pressure keeps it solid.
It is about as hot as the surface of the Sun.

media.credit: Darla Sondrol · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Darla Sondrol

questions.fun_fact: The inner core is about as hot as the Sun's surface, around 5,000 °C (9,000 °F), yet it stays solid because of the huge pressure.

quality.notes: The 50,000 °C option is easy to rule out with hint 2. The estimate of about 5,200 °C makes 'about 5,000 °C' fair. An iron-nickel meteorite is a safe illustrative image.

revision.reason: Replaced hint 2 so it no longer gives away lava's temperature, which another pool question asks about.

hints: It is far hotter than any oven or volcano lava.
Lava comes out at roughly 1,000 °C, and the core is much hotter.
It is about as hot as the surface of the Sun.

questions.description: A dwarf planet shaped like an egg, spinning like it's late for breakfast.
questions.question: Haumea is an egg-shaped dwarf planet that spins very fast beyond Neptune. In which decade was it discovered?
hints: It was found long after Pluto.
It was found by modern telescopes and computers, not by eye.
It was found at about the same time as Eris, just before Pluto stopped being a planet.

media.credit: KPNO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA/P. Marenfeld · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: KPNO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA/P. Marenfeld

questions.fun_fact: Haumea spins once about every 4 hours, so fast that it got stretched into an egg shape.

quality.notes: Discovery was disputed (Brown team 2004, Ortiz team announced 2005), but both dates fall in the 2000s, so the answer holds. 'Dwarf planet' plus hint 3 (Eris, just before Pluto's demotion) make the answer easy to work out. The question is mostly date memorization, with some room to reason. Touches the Pluto-reclassification topic but asks a different fact.

questions.description: A planet that blushes all day, every day.
questions.question: “I coat the dust of the reddest planet in the solar system and give it its color.” What am I?
hints: You can find me on Earth very often too.
I form when a metal meets oxygen.
On Earth I appear on old nails and bikes left out in the rain.

media.credit: NASA/JPL/Cornell University, Maas Digital LLC · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: NASA/JPL/Cornell University, Maas Digital LLC

questions.fun_fact: Martian dust is so fine that it gets blown around the whole planet in giant dust storms.

quality.notes: Rated 10, but 'Mars is red because of rust' is common in kids' science shows and books, so it is more like a 7. Related to q-0051 (red planet) but asks why it is red, which is a different fact.

questions.description: A fishbowl for people, but without the water.
questions.question: It's round, it has a see-through front, and astronauts wear it on their heads. What is it?
hints: It protects the most important part of your body.
Bike riders wear one too.
It's like a bike rider's, but much bigger and with a big window.

media.credit: Bill Ingalls · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Bill Ingalls

questions.fun_fact: Space helmets have a small foam pad inside that astronauts use to pop their ears, and also to scratch an itchy nose.

quality.notes: Backpack, glove and boot are not worn on the head and aren't round with a see-through front, so they are weak even for 6-year-olds. Hint 2 ('bike riders wear one too') nearly gives it away. Fine as a level-1 question but not very fun. Decorative image is a reasonable choice, since any astronaut photo would show the helmet.

questions.description: The only job where wearing gold on your face is part of the uniform.
questions.question: Look at this astronaut's helmet. What is the thin layer of gold on the visor for?
hints: In space, there is no air to soften the Sun.
It works like a mirror.
It protects the astronaut's eyes and keeps heat out.

media.note: An astronaut in a spacesuit with the gold sun visor lowered, reflecting the surroundings.
media.credit: NASA or National Aeronautics and Space Administration · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: NASA or National Aeronautics and Space Administration

questions.fun_fact: The gold layer is so thin that you can still see through it.

quality.notes: The gold layer also reflects infrared heat (covered by hint 3), so the answer is fine. Hint 1 already points very strongly to sunlight. A NASA gold-visor photo is easy to find.

questions.description: The newspaper corner that knows your future, or says it does.
questions.question: How many star signs are there in the usual Western horoscope?
hints: There's one for each part of the year.
The Sun spends about a month in each sign.
It's a dozen.

media.credit: Chad Ajamian · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Chad Ajamian

questions.fun_fact: The Sun also passes through a 13th constellation, Ophiuchus, but horoscopes leave it out.

quality.notes: A dry counting fact. Probably a bit easier than 5, since many kids know their star sign and that there are 12. Astrology is a slightly odd fit for a stars-and-galaxies question.

revision.reason: Made hint 2 less direct and replaced the fun fact, which gave away another pool question's answer, with the Ophiuchus fact.

hints: There's one for each part of the year.
It's the same as the number of months.
It's a dozen.
previous.fun_fact: The Chinese zodiac also has 12 signs, but they're animals for whole years, not months.

questions.description: A sport so small it fits on your dining table.
questions.question: The shuttlecock is to badminton as what is to table tennis?
hints: It's the thing players hit back and forth.
It's very light: it weighs less than 3 grams.
It's round, white or orange, and bounces on the table.

media.credit: Tim Reckmann from Hamm, Deutschland · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Tim Reckmann from Hamm, Deutschland

questions.fun_fact: A table tennis ball weighs only 2.7 grams, yet top players can smash it at over 100 km/h (62 mph).

quality.notes: The answer is the only plastic, light-sounding option, and 'leather' and 'wooden' are easy to rule out. Descriptive answers make an analogy feel clumsy; 'a ping-pong ball' would be more natural, but then the options would be trivial. The analogy itself is not very surprising.

questions.description: Gymnastics equipment where letting go is part of the plan.
questions.question: In women's gymnastics, on which apparatus do gymnasts swing and fly between two rails?
hints: The men have a cousin of this apparatus.
The men's version has two rails at the same height.
One rail is clearly higher than the other.

media.credit: Trevor Cokley (U.S. Air Force) · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Trevor Cokley (U.S. Air Force)

questions.fun_fact: In 1976, Nadia Comăneci scored the first perfect 10 in Olympic gymnastics on this apparatus, and the scoreboard showed “1.00” because it couldn't display a 10.

quality.notes: Hint 2 describes the parallel bars and so rules out the strongest distractor early. 'Two rails' fits the parallel bars too, but 'women's gymnastics' settles it. The Comăneci fun fact is accurate and great.

questions.description: Black, twisty, and loved by exactly half of every family.
questions.question: I'm a chewy black candy, and my name comes from old Greek words for the plant part I'm made from. What does my name mean?
hints: My plant grows wild in southern Europe and Asia.
The first part of my old name is related to the word “glucose”.
Farmers have to dig into the soil to get me out.

media.credit: JohnJPJr · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: JohnJPJr

questions.fun_fact: The main sweet substance in licorice is up to 50 times sweeter than sugar.

quality.notes: Black licorice candy is common in Northern Europe, the UK and the US, but much less familiar in Latin America and parts of Asia, so players there may not recognize it from the riddle. The etymology needs reasoning (glyc- = sweet), so it is harder than 8. 'Bitter bark' is easy to rule out for a sweet candy.

questions.description: A swimming style for people who skipped every single lesson.
questions.question: I'm the first way many kids swim: head up, paddling with arms and legs under the water. Which animal am I named after?
hints: The animal is a popular pet.
It loves to fetch sticks, even from a lake.
It barks.

media.credit: Wpcpey · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Wpcpey

questions.fun_fact: Most dogs can do the doggy paddle without ever being taught.

quality.notes: Hint 2 (fetching sticks) almost gives the answer, which is fine at difficulty 2. The fun fact says most dogs paddle without being taught: the paddle is instinctive, but some breeds swim badly, so it's slightly too broad. The doggy-paddle name works in Spanish and German too. An illustrative image would have been safe, so the decorative role isn't needed.

questions.description: Pond vocabulary class is now in session.
questions.question: What is a duckling?
hints: You might see one in spring.
It follows its mother in a line.
It hatches from an egg.

media.credit: Claude Monet · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Claude Monet

questions.fun_fact: Ducklings can swim just a few hours after they hatch.

quality.notes: This is a dry word-meaning question that reads like a vocabulary drill. It also leans on an English word, though most languages have a matching diminutive. Hint 3 (“hatches from an egg”) rules out the egg option. The wrong answers are weak because they are all “a duck's ___”. The description is bland.

questions.description: The only swimming style where you never see where you're going.
questions.question: In an outdoor pool, freestyle is to seeing the pool floor as backstroke is to seeing…?
hints: You lie face up.
Indoors, you'd see the ceiling.
Outdoors you might spot clouds and birds.

media.credit: Airman 1st Class Cheyenne Morigeau · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Airman 1st Class Cheyenne Morigeau

questions.fun_fact: Backstroke swimmers count their strokes from the flags above the pool so they don't bump their heads on the wall.

quality.notes: The analogy is clumsy to read aloud. “The swimmer next to you” is a weak option, and kids could argue for “your own feet”. The answer is easy to reason out but not very satisfying. The illustrative lane-rope image shows a wrong option, though that doesn't really mislead.

revision.reason: Replaced the wrong answer “Your own feet” with “The tiles under you”, which is clearly wrong for a swimmer lying face up.

questions.description: Your arms are doing all the walking for once.
questions.question: A step is to walking as a … is to swimming?
hints: It's one single movement, not a whole length of the pool.
You do it with your arms.
Each pull of your arm through the water counts as one.

media.credit: JD Lasica from Pleasanton, CA, US · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: JD Lasica from Pleasanton, CA, US

questions.fun_fact: Top freestyle sprinters can make about one arm stroke every half second.

quality.notes: A dry vocabulary analogy. Hint 2 (“with your arms”) is debatable, since strokes also involve the legs. The fun-fact stroke rate is roughly right but not exact. “Stroke” as swimming jargon is probably a bit harder for kids than difficulty 5.

questions.description: The oldest soap trick: everyone cries at your funeral, and then you walk in.
questions.question: My author sent me over a Swiss waterfall in 1893. Readers protested, and in 1903 I came back: I had faked my death. Who am I?
hints: I'm famous for solving mysteries.
I live in London at 221B Baker Street.
My loyal friend is Dr. Watson.

media.credit: Dominicus Johannes Bergsma. · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Dominicus Johannes Bergsma.

questions.fun_fact: The story of his return, “The Adventure of the Empty House”, explains that he hid for three years while the world thought he was gone.

quality.notes: A strong riddle, and the facts are right (Reichenbach in 1893, the Empty House in 1903). Hint 1 narrows the options to Holmes or Poirot. The query “Swiss Alps waterfall” might return Reichenbach Falls with a Sherlock plaque. The other Holmes questions in the candidates ask different facts. Many adults know the waterfall death, so this feels more like a 10 than an 11.

questions.description: The loudest thing in town, and somehow nobody ever complained.
questions.question: Long before everyone had a watch, what did church bells like this one tell the whole town?
wrong_answers: What prices were at the market
hints: Today your phone tells you this.
They often rang once for every hour.
Think of a clock.

media.note: A clear photo of a big bronze church bell hanging in a bell tower.
media.credit: Mariosgt · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Mariosgt

questions.fun_fact: Big Ben in London is not the name of the clock tower but of its biggest bell.

quality.notes: The wrong answers (weather, market prices, river depth) are silly, so “what time it was” stands out at once. Bells also called people to services and warned of fires, but the time is the best answer among these options. The Big Ben fun fact is nice and true.

questions.description: The first big churches didn't start from scratch; they flipped through Rome's old building catalog.
questions.question: When Christianity became legal in Rome, the first large churches copied the shape of which kind of Roman building?
hints: Roman temples were too small inside for big crowds.
These long halls were used for courts and business.
Romans called them basilicas.

media.credit: Nhartmannphotos · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Nhartmannphotos

questions.fun_fact: That's why so many churches today are still called basilicas, a name first used for Roman public halls.

quality.notes: The fact is true (basilica plan). The answer is phrased as a description (“public meeting halls”), which makes it look different from the other options. The “building catalog” description is weak. An illustrative image (Roman forum) is safe, so the decorative role isn't needed. It's a standard art-history fact, closer to 13 than 14.

questions.description: A racket that forgot its strings and got holes instead.
questions.question: Look at this racket: solid, full of holes, no strings. It's used in a doubles sport played on a court with glass walls. Which sport?

quality.notes: The fun fact is broadly right: the joker came from euchre in the US. There it was the top trump, not a wild card, but the question says “in many games”. Hint 1 only repeats what the image shows. No real overlap with the Batman Joker question q-2025.

questions.description: A puzzle that fills Sunday mornings one little box at a time.
questions.question: What do you write in the white squares of this puzzle?
hints: The clues for this puzzle are little questions.
The answers run across and down.
Together they spell out words.

media.note: A clear photo or scan of an empty crossword grid with white and black squares and small clue numbers; no letters filled in.

media.author: Barbara (WVS)

questions.fun_fact: The first crossword puzzle was published in a New York newspaper on December 21, 1913, and it was shaped like a diamond.

quality.notes: Easy and a little dry. Young kids may not know crosswords, so 2 is slightly low. The fun fact (Arthur Wynne, New York World, December 21, 1913, diamond shape) is correct.

questions.description: The day a computer sat down at an ancient board and didn't blink.
questions.question: In 2016, the program AlphaGo became the first to beat top Go player Lee Sedol, winning 4–1 in his home country's capital. Which city?
hints: Lee Sedol is one of the greatest Go players of his generation.
The city hosted the Summer Olympics in 1988.
It's the capital of South Korea.

media.credit: Dietmar Rabich · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Dietmar Rabich

questions.fun_fact: AlphaGo's “Move 37” in the second game was so unusual that experts first thought it was a mistake.

quality.notes: Players can reason from the name Lee Sedol, which is good. London (where DeepMind is based) is a clever distractor. Saying “first to beat” Lee Sedol is fine, though AlphaGo had already beaten Fan Hui.

revision.reason: Replaced hint 2, which identified South Korea via K-pop, with the 1988 Summer Olympics.

hints: Lee Sedol is one of the greatest Go players of his generation.
The country is in East Asia, famous for K-pop.
It's the capital of South Korea.

questions.description: The smallest soldiers on the board, and the first to march.
questions.question: Look at this chess set ready to play. How many pawns does each player have?
hints: Pawns are the smallest pieces.
They fill the whole second row in front of each player.
It's the same as the number of legs on a spider.

media.note: A clear photo of a chessboard with all pieces in the starting position, both rows of pawns visible.
media.credit: MichaelMaggs · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: MichaelMaggs

questions.fun_fact: A pawn that reaches the far side of the board can turn into a queen, so a game could in theory have nine queens per side.

quality.notes: Players can simply count the pawns in the essential photo, which is fine but makes it easy. The nine-queens fun fact is correct.

questions.description: Two halves of one walnut, and they don't share the chores equally.
questions.question: Look at this brain. In most people, its left half does most of the work for which skill?
hints: You are using this skill right now.
Damage to this side can make it hard to find the right words.
It's all about words and sentences.

media.note: A clear photo or model of a human brain seen from above, showing its two halves, with no labels.
media.credit: Jensflorian · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jensflorian

questions.fun_fact: Two famous language areas, Broca's area and Wernicke's area, are named after 19th-century doctors who found them in the left half of the brain.

quality.notes: Language sits on the left side in most people, but not all, and the question hedges for that. The answer is longer and worded differently from the short distractors. The essential photo adds no real information, so an illustrative image would be enough. The question reads like a school test. Young teens rarely know about the brain's two halves, so it's probably harder than 7.

questions.description: The feeling that makes grown-ups jump onto chairs when a mouse walks by.
questions.question: I make your heart pound and your hands sweat when you see a big spider. In which part of your body do I start?
hints: It's not the part that pounds.
It's the boss of your whole body.
It sits inside your skull.

media.credit: Michael Gäbler · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Michael Gäbler

questions.fun_fact: A small almond-shaped part deep in the brain, the amygdala, can spot danger and start the fear reaction before you even realize what you saw.

quality.notes: Saying fear “starts” in one organ simplifies things, but the brain is a fair answer for kids. The chair-and-mouse joke in the description is a bit dated.

questions.description: Your brain's favorite reason for you to get off the couch.
questions.question: I make you sweat and breathe hard, and afterwards your brain releases chemicals that make you feel happy. What am I?
hints: You can't do me lying still.
Sports teams do a lot of me.
Running, swimming and dancing are all kinds of me.

media.credit: 玄史生 · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: 玄史生

questions.fun_fact: Exercise sends more blood and oxygen to the brain and can even help it grow new cells in a memory area called the hippocampus.

quality.notes: “Sweat and breathe hard” makes this very easy, which is fine for its level. The description says “get off the couch”, which rules out the passive options.

questions.description: Doctors love naming worries in Greek, because it makes them sound much fancier.
questions.question: Its name comes from the Greek word for “stranger”. It means fear or dislike of people from other countries. What is it called?
hints: Its name was built from ancient Greek words.
Campaigns against racism often fight it too.
Its first part also appears in the name of the element xenon, “the stranger”.

media.credit: Ash Thawley · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ash Thawley

questions.fun_fact: The Greek word “xenos” meant both “stranger” and “guest”, and ancient Greeks had a strong duty to welcome travelers.

quality.notes: The question defines the word directly, so it's about matching a word to its meaning. It works well with three other phobias as distractors.

revision.reason: Rewrote the description and hint 1 so neither rules out any of the wrong answers.

previous.description: A fear that has nothing to do with spiders, heights or the dark.
hints: It's about people, not places or animals.
Campaigns against racism often fight it too.
Its first part also appears in the name of the element xenon, “the stranger”.

questions.description: Your body's built-in traffic light for awkward moments.
questions.question: When people feel embarrassed, which part of their body often turns red?
hints: Everyone can see it.
People sometimes hide it with their hands.
Some people put pink makeup on it.

media.credit: DanielPenfield · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: DanielPenfield

questions.fun_fact: Blushing happens because embarrassment makes the blood vessels in your face widen, letting more blood flow in.

quality.notes: The distractors (knees, elbows, feet) are too weak. Ears and neck also blush, so they can't be used as wrong answers either. The “school stage curtain” image is only loosely tied to the question. The question is easy and plain.

revision.reason: Replaced hint 2, which made cheeks the only face option, with a hint that keeps other options possible.

hints: Everyone can see it.
It's on your face.
Some people put pink makeup on it.

questions.description: Half eagle, half lion, and all horsepower.
questions.question: A prancing horse is to Ferrari as a crowned red griffin is to which car brand?
hints: The brand comes from Scandinavia.
The same company also built fighter jets.
Its name was short for Svenska Aeroplan Aktiebolaget.

media.credit: TURPIN Catherine · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: TURPIN Catherine

questions.fun_fact: Saab's griffin was borrowed from truck maker Scania, which took it from the coat of arms of the Swedish region of Skåne.

quality.notes: Correct: Saab's crowned red griffin head came from Scania and Skåne. This is niche logo knowledge, and Saab cars have been gone since about 2011, so it's a fairly dry fact. A sharp heraldic griffin image matches the clue, but it doesn't point to a brand. Hint 1 (Scandinavia) cuts the options to Volvo and Saab, which is fine.

questions.description: Bears so soft you can eat a whole family of them without anyone growling.
questions.question: Haribo's gummy bears were first made in Germany as little “dancing bears”. About how long ago was that?
hints: Your grandparents' parents could have eaten them as children.
It was a few years after the First World War.
It happened in the early 1920s.

media.credit: MichaelFrey · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: MichaelFrey

questions.fun_fact: The name Haribo comes from its founder and his hometown: HAns RIegel from BOnn.

quality.notes: Haribo was founded in 1920 and the dancing bears came in 1922, so 'about 100 years' is correct. 'About 600 years ago' is too silly to be a real option, and '250' is weak too.

questions.description: A rabbit that skipped the carrots and went straight for dessert.
questions.question: I'm a bunny who loves chocolate milk, and the company behind my cocoa powder is named after its founder. Who was he?
hints: He lived and worked in Switzerland.
In the 1860s he made a famous baby food from milk and cereal.
His last name sounds like the first part of the bunny's drink.

media.credit: stevepb · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: stevepb

questions.fun_fact: His family name means “little nest” in a German dialect, which is why the company's logo shows birds in a nest.

quality.notes: Hershey, Lindt and Mars are also named after their founders, so the answer depends only on knowing the Nesquik bunny. That's fine, but players have to make the jump from Nesquik to Nestlé. Hint 3 plays on how the names sound, which is acceptable for a final hint. Players need the founder's name, not just the brand, so it's a bit harder than 6.

questions.description: A family name that now comes with bubbles included.
questions.question: Seven brothers from Italy moved to California, built airplane propellers, then sold a pump that made bathwater bubble. Which family was it?
hints: Today their name is a word, not just a family.
You might find their invention at a spa or a hotel pool.
Their name is now used for any hot, bubbling tub.

media.credit: Pseudopanax at English Wikipedia · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Pseudopanax at English Wikipedia

questions.fun_fact: In 1956, Candido Jacuzzi made a small whirlpool pump to help his young son, who had painful arthritis.

quality.notes: 'Bathwater bubble' plus the 'bubbles' description makes it fairly easy for anyone who knows the word jacuzzi. Small detail: the pump is usually said to be from 1956 and was made for hydrotherapy. Good Italian-brand distractors.

questions.description: A candy that pops out of a tiny cartoon neck.
questions.question: Today PEZ candy comes in dispensers with cartoon heads. But in 1927, who was the Austrian peppermint candy first made for?
hints: The cartoon heads only came many years later.
It was meant to replace a bad habit.
It was sold as a fresh-breath choice instead of a cigarette.

media.credit: Hannes Grobe/Hannes Grobe (talk) · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Hannes Grobe/Hannes Grobe (talk)

questions.fun_fact: The name PEZ comes from the German word for peppermint, “Pfefferminz”: its first, middle and last letters.

quality.notes: The fun fact's 'first, middle and last letters' of Pfefferminz is the common story but only roughly fits the letters. Hint 2 (bad habit) is quite strong. Smoking comes up only as a historical fact, which is fine.

questions.description: A bird logo that has flown millions of miles and never once flapped its wings.
questions.question: I'm a German airline with a crane bird on my tail. The first half of my name means “air”. Where does the second half come from?
questions.answer: A medieval league of trading cities
wrong_answers: The crane bird in my logo
hints: Think history, not birds.
The word is many centuries older than airplanes.
Merchants of the Hanseatic League traded across the Baltic Sea.

media.credit: Richardmaackphotography · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Richardmaackphotography

questions.fun_fact: The Hanseatic League, or Hansa, linked merchant cities around the North Sea and Baltic Sea for about 400 years.

quality.notes: Good, and you can reason towards the answer. The description's 'Middle Ages' points to the medieval option a little. The Lübeck image is safe.

revision.reason: Replaced the description that pointed to the medieval option and the hint 2 that gave the answer away.

previous.description: An airline whose name flew in from the Middle Ages.
hints: Think history, not birds.
Cities like Hamburg and Lübeck were part of it.
Merchants of the Hanseatic League traded across the Baltic Sea.

questions.description: A snack that tells you to take a break, then breaks itself.
questions.question: You snap apart a classic full-size KitKat bar. How many chocolate fingers do you get?
hints: It's an even number.
There are smaller bars with fewer fingers.
Same as the legs on a dog.

media.credit: Aude · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Aude

questions.fun_fact: KitKat was first made by Rowntree's in York, England, in 1935, under the name “Rowntree's Chocolate Crisp”.

quality.notes: The bar has regional variants (Chunky, 2-finger), but the question says 'classic full-size', which covers it. Hint 3 gives the answer, which is allowed.

revision.reason: Corrected the fun fact: KitKat was made in York, but not first sold there.

previous.fun_fact: KitKat was first sold in York, England, in 1935, under the name “Rowntree's Chocolate Crisp”.

questions.description: Six wives, one husband, and a surprising amount of pop music.
questions.question: Anne Boleyn, one of Henry VIII's six wives and a star of the musical “Six”, was queen of England in which century?
hints: She was born after Columbus had already reached America.
She lived in the time of the Tudor kings and queens.
She married the king in 1533.

questions.fun_fact: Anne Boleyn grew up at Hever Castle in Kent, and today you can visit it and see her prayer books.

quality.notes: Age fit: needs Tudor history, which is mostly British school knowledge; Six the musical is fairly niche outside the English-speaking world. Hint 2 (Elizabeth I ruled until 1603) almost gives the answer away already.

revision.reason: Cut the scenario framing, replaced hint 2 with a vaguer Tudor hint, and changed hint 1 so it no longer repeats the new question.

previous.question: You're watching the musical “Six”, where Henry VIII's wives sing like pop stars. In which century was Anne Boleyn queen?
hints: Her husband married six times.
Her daughter, Elizabeth I, ruled until 1603.
She married the king in 1533.

questions.description: Kneel down as a normal person, stand up with a fancy new name.

Judi Dench is known as “___ Judi Dench”.

questions.description: A king who brought a lot of arrows to a muddy field in France.

hints: Shakespeare wrote a famous play about him.

His son, Henry VI, became king as a baby.

questions.fun_fact: English longbowmen played a huge part in the victory at Agincourt.

quality.notes: Fun: a plain who-won-the-battle history recall with little to reason towards.

questions.description: A man whose future job title is already printed on the stamps.
questions.question: This man is next in line to the British throne. Who is he?
hints: His mother was Diana.
He got married in 2011.

questions.fun_fact: William studied at the University of St Andrews in Scotland, where he met Catherine.

questions.fun_fact: He was already James VI of Scotland, so from 1603 one man wore the crowns of both England and Scotland.

questions.description: The most important royal seat isn't even comfortable.

My other name is the Stone of Destiny.

questions.fun_fact: The stone traveled back to London for Charles III's coronation in 2023 and sat inside the old Coronation Chair.

questions.description: Millions of viewers, one very long aisle, and nobody tripped on the dress.

Isaac Newton and Charles Darwin are buried inside me.

questions.fun_fact: For the wedding, rows of real trees were placed inside the church along the aisle.

questions.description: A crown that comes with the wedding ring, but not with the job.

questions.description: A family that changed its surname to match its favorite castle.

questions.description: The most famous face you've ever kept in your pocket.
questions.question: You find a coin with Elizabeth II's profile on it. Roughly how many countries have put her face on their money?

questions.fun_fact: Guinness World Records lists her as the person shown on the most different currencies.

questions.description: A zoo painted across the night sky, with a few strange guests.

previous.question: Leo means lion, Pisces means fish and Taurus means bull. What are these names?
hints: They come from star patterns in the sky.

questions.description: Love that is worth more than its weight in metal.

media.author: Petar Milošević

questions.fun_fact: After 60 years of marriage, couples celebrate a diamond anniversary.

questions.description: The only clock that waits for you to say “go!”.

questions.description: Not yesterday, but the yesterday of yesterday.

media.author: Claudio Elias

questions.fun_fact: Some languages have a single word for it, like Spanish “anteayer” and German “vorgestern”.

questions.description: The week is a merry-go-round that always comes back.
questions.question: If today is Sunday, how many days is it until the next Sunday?
hints: Count the days of one whole week.
Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday…

media.author: Ruth Sharville

questions.fun_fact: The seven-day week is thousands of years old and goes back to ancient Babylon.

questions.description: A riddle that fits in your planner.
questions.question: Monday is to the week as September is to the…
hints: Monday is one part of a week.

questions.description: They wrapped their kings up like birthday presents, and it worked for thousands of years.

questions.description: A walking tank with a built-in hammer: no one asked for the extra feature.

questions.description: An asteroid misses its appointment and a whole film happens instead.

questions.description: Small, often yellow and very important in the kitchen, yet it never cooks anything.

questions.description: Earth is a jigsaw puzzle that refuses to sit still.

questions.description: The scribbles here were drawn by the planet itself.

hints: Two kinds of waves travel through the ground at different speeds.

questions.description: A man who measured something nobody has ever seen, without leaving his desk.
