The distractors (Moho, the 660 km boundary, inner core) are excellent for experts. Paris–Cairo is about 3,200 km, so "nearly as far" is loose. No imperial units are given for the depth.

questions.description: A city famous for its hills, its fog and one very hot week in 1906.

questions.description: A blockbuster where the end of the world arrived with a calendar date attached.

questions.description: A crack in California so famous it got its own action movie.

review.feedback: This is a base question, but the analogy depends on English. In Spanish (and partly in German), a breaking group is called by the English loanword “crew”. That makes the answer the only English word among the translated options (coro, manada, flota), which gives it away. Hint 2 (“Ships and airplanes also have one”) also falls apart, because a ship's crew is “tripulación”, not “crew”. Rework it so it doesn't depend on the English word, for example by asking about breaking battles in a way that doesn't rely on the double meaning of “crew”, or retire it.

questions.description: The only army that marches with glow sticks.
questions.question: Swifties are to Taylor Swift as ARMY is to which group?
hints: The group comes from South Korea.
It has seven members.
Its fans wave purple lights.

media.credit: Andrew King · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Andrew King

questions.fun_fact: BTS fans use the phrase “I purple you” to mean “I will love you for a long time”.

quality.notes: “In a stadium, millions of fans” makes no sense, because no stadium holds millions, and that opening clause is padding. q-1661 has the same answer (BTS) but asks a different fact. Its hints repeat that one's clues (seven members, South Korea).

revision.reason: Cut the stadium clause and kept only the analogy, as the reviewer asked.

previous.question: In a stadium, millions of fans proudly call themselves ARMY. Swifties are to Taylor Swift as ARMY is to which group?

questions.description: A stage name with one letter fewer than it should have.
questions.question: If you looked at The Weeknd's passport, which name would you read?
hints: He grew up in Toronto, Canada.
His parents came from Ethiopia.
His first name is the same as Adam and Eve's second son.

media.credit: Jchmrt · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jchmrt

questions.fun_fact: He dropped the third “e” from “weekend” because a Canadian band already used that name.

quality.notes: Rated 9, but a star's legal name is fan knowledge that most teens don't have, so 11 fits better. The distractors are strong: the real names of Drake, Post Malone and Bruno Mars.

questions.description: The only dance your dentist would approve of.
questions.question: When did the floss dance, swinging your arms around your hips, go viral around the world?
hints: It spread on phones and social media.
It became an emote in Fortnite.
It's the decade just before the 2020s.

media.credit: U.S. Army USAG-RP by Mary Davis · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: U.S. Army USAG-RP by Mary Davis

questions.fun_fact: The floss became famous after a teenager known as Backpack Kid danced it on stage with Katy Perry in 2017.

quality.notes: The wrong decades are very far from the answer, so the answer is easy to guess just from “viral” and social media.

questions.description: The person everyone at the party begs for “just one more song”.
questions.question: At a party, this person picks the songs, blends one track smoothly into the next and sometimes scratches records. What is this person called?
hints: They often wear big headphones.
They stand behind turntables or a mixing desk.
The name is just two letters.

media.credit: Vyacheslav Argenberg · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Vyacheslav Argenberg

questions.fun_fact: DJ stands for “disc jockey”, a nickname first given in the 1930s to radio hosts who played records on air.

quality.notes: An easy, fairly flat question. The answer is much shorter than the other options, so it stands out. The fun fact's story about early DJs “riding” records is a loose folk explanation. q-1535 also involves a DJ but asks a different fact (when scratching was invented). A safe illustrative image could have been used instead of a decorative one.

revision.reason: Replaced the unconfirmed “jockey rides records” folk etymology with the safe 1930s radio origin.

previous.fun_fact: DJ stands for “disc jockey”, because early DJs “rode” the records like a jockey rides a horse.

questions.description: Your spine has filed a complaint about your chair.
questions.question: You sit typing at a computer for hours. Which habit is NOT good for your posture?
wrong_answers: Elbows bent at a right angle
hints: Three of these are what a good desk setup aims for.
Look at the joints closest to the keyboard.
Your hands should stay in a straight line with your forearms.

media.credit: Shixart1985 · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Shixart1985

questions.fun_fact: Keeping your wrists bent for hours can squeeze a nerve in your wrist, which is why many keyboards come with a wrist rest.

quality.notes: Solid, but it reads like a school health worksheet. Hint 2 narrows it down a lot. The fun fact's claim about wrist rests is vague but OK.

questions.description: Some scissors just see the world from the other side.
questions.question: These scissors have their blades swapped around compared with normal ones. Who are they made for?
hints: It's about which hand holds them.
About one person in ten needs them.
Normal scissors are made for the other hand.

media.note: A clear photo of a pair of left-handed scissors, ideally with the blade on top on the left side; no text labels saying “left”.
media.credit: Bin im Garten · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Bin im Garten

questions.fun_fact: With normal scissors, a left-handed person's hand pushes the blades apart, so the paper gets chewed instead of cut.

quality.notes: The description ("from the other side") hints gently. The photo alone hardly shows that the blades are swapped, but the question text carries the clue. Commons photos may have "left" printed on them, which the note already guards against.

questions.description: A fruit that someone couldn't resist tasting before the photo.
questions.question: You look at the glowing apple logo on the back of an Apple laptop. How many bites are missing from it?
hints: The apple is not whole.
Look at its right side.
Just a single bite.

media.credit: George Chernilevsky · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: George Chernilevsky

questions.fun_fact: Designer Rob Janoff said he added the bite so people would not mistake the apple for a cherry.

quality.notes: A brand-recognition question, a bit flat. Hint 3 "Just a single bite" all but states the answer. q-1957 also covers the history of the Apple logo, but it asks a different fact.

questions.description: A bowl that is terrible at keeping secrets, or water.
questions.question: Knife is to cutting as a colander, the bowl full of holes, is to…
hints: You use it after cooking pasta.
Water goes through, food stays in.
It lets the water run out.

media.credit: Mike Kniec from Manchester, UK · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Mike Kniec from Manchester, UK

questions.fun_fact: People have strained food through bowls with holes for thousands of years; clay ones were found from the Bronze Age.

quality.notes: Good analogy, and the description is funny. The fun fact's claim about Bronze Age clay strainers seems plausible but is unverified. Kids may not know the word "colander", but the question explains it.

questions.description: The most popular button in any dark room.
questions.question: I live on the wall by the door, and when you flip me the light comes on. What do I open and close?
hints: The light bulb needs something to flow to it.
Electricity can only flow in a closed loop.
It's a loop of wires.

media.credit: Santeri Viinamäki · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Santeri Viinamäki

questions.fun_fact: The common toggle light switch was patented in 1917 by William J. Newton and Morris Goldberg.

quality.notes: "A magnet" is not the same kind of thing as the other options. q-2660 is a riddle about the light switch, a close topic but a different fact. The fun fact's 1917 patent is commonly cited, but I'm not fully sure of it. Rather school-like.

questions.description: Zebra stripes that are very good at shopping.
questions.question: At the checkout, the cashier scans this. What does it tell the computer?
hints: The stripes stand for a number.
Every kind of product has its own one.
The computer looks up the item's name and price from it.

media.note: A clear photo of a standard black-and-white barcode with its numbers, printed on a product package; no other readable text.
media.credit: Schneekoala · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Schneekoala

questions.fun_fact: The first product ever scanned with a barcode at a shop was a pack of chewing gum, in Ohio in 1974.

quality.notes: q-3058 asks players to name the barcode; this one asks what it is for. Related, but a different fact. Some barcodes can carry expiry dates (GS1 DataBar), but a standard EAN/UPC does not.

questions.description: An office animal that bites, but only paper.
questions.question: I have a metal jaw. Press me down and I push a tiny bent wire through a stack of paper to hold it together. What am I?
hints: You find me on school and office desks.
My bent wires stay in the paper.
My wires are called staples.

media.credit: Michael D Beckwith · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Michael D Beckwith

questions.fun_fact: Early staplers in the 1800s held only one staple at a time, so you had to reload them after every press.

quality.notes: Easy and clean but plain. Hint 3 ("staples") nearly says the answer, which is allowed for hint 3.

questions.description: Potato chips that live in a tower, like tiny princesses.
questions.question: Pringles all have the same curved saddle shape, they sit stacked tightly, and the tube is stiff. What does this mainly stop?
hints: Think about what happens to chips in a squashed bag.
Each chip supports the one above it.
You find fewer crumbs at the bottom.

media.credit: Evan-Amos · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Evan-Amos

questions.fun_fact: Fredric Baur, who designed the Pringles tube, was so proud of it that some of his ashes were buried in one.

quality.notes: The distractors are weak: chips don't melt, and a tube doesn't stop them getting salty, so the answer is obvious by elimination. The fun fact about Fredric Baur's ashes is a great one.

questions.description: The kitchen drawer's most popular member, and always the first one to go missing.
questions.question: What do you usually eat with this?
hints: It's a food you can't pick up with your fingers.
It's often served hot in a bowl.
It's very runny.

media.note: A clear photo of a single ordinary metal spoon on a plain background, with no food.
media.credit: Akwugo · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Akwugo

questions.fun_fact: The first spoons were probably shells and pieces of wood, and the word “spoon” once meant a chip of wood.

quality.notes: Fine for the youngest players. Other spoon foods (cereal, yogurt) could argue, but soup is the clear usual answer. manners-and-customs-6 (deep plate → soup) has the same answer but asks a different fact.

revision.reason: Replaced the description, whose mention of a bowl ruled out every wrong answer.

previous.description: The hero of every bowl at lunchtime.

questions.description: Some villains come with a smile, a nice coat, and a very hidden plan.
questions.question: A “wolf in sheep's clothing” hides bad plans behind a friendly look. Which of these characters is NOT one?
wrong_answers: The wolf in Little Red Riding Hood
hints: Three of them pretend to be kind to get what they want.
One of them dresses up as a grandmother.
The odd one out loves warm hugs and has a carrot nose.

media.credit: Gerda Arendt · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Gerda Arendt

questions.fun_fact: The idea of a wolf dressed as a sheep is very old: it appears in the Bible and in fables told for many centuries.

quality.notes: A fine odd-one-out. Olaf stands out to anyone who knows Frozen, so it is a bit easier than 6. Hans's twist needs film knowledge.

questions.description: A tough guy who has been standing in the same spot for 300 years.
questions.question: I'm a tree whose hard wood built sailing ships and barrels, and in many languages a strong person is “strong as” me. What am I?
hints: I can live for hundreds of years.
Squirrels love the nuts I drop in autumn.
My nuts are called acorns.

media.credit: Fons Heijnsbroek · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Fons Heijnsbroek

questions.fun_fact: A single large oak can be home to hundreds of different kinds of insects, birds and other animals.

quality.notes: Palm is a weak distractor, since nobody builds barrels from it. The sailing-ship image is safe as illustrative, so decorative is the wrong role.

questions.description: The first travel blogger, minus the selfies and the Wi-Fi.
questions.question: I'm a Greek traveler who wrote that 100,000 men toiled 20 years on the Great Pyramid, which helped the slave myth spread. Who am I?
hints: I lived about 2,400 years ago and wrote a long book about the wars between Greeks and Persians.
My stories mix real facts with tall tales I heard on my trips.
People call me the “Father of History”.

media.credit: Ludovic Delot · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ludovic Delot

questions.fun_fact: Workers' tombs found near Giza in the 1990s show the builders were paid laborers who ate bread, beer and even beef, not slaves.

quality.notes: Herodotus never actually says the workers were slaves, so “helped the slave myth spread” is an interpretation, though a common one. Everything else is accurate.

questions.description: Egypt was busy with pyramids, and so was someone else on the other side of the planet.
questions.question: What is the name of the 5,000-year-old sacred city in Peru's Supe Valley, seen as the oldest city in the Americas?
hints: Its stepped pyramids are about as old as the pyramids of Giza.
Its people had no pottery and no writing, but they built big stone platforms and sunken round plazas.
It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2009, and its name has only five letters.

media.credit: European Space Agency · Attribution · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: European Space Agency

questions.fun_fact: Archaeologists found flutes made of pelican and condor bones in the city, so its people loved music almost 5,000 years ago.

quality.notes: Hint 3's letter count (five letters) leaves only Caral among the options. That's allowed in a final hint, but it's a mechanical shortcut. The question is a solid expert-level item.

questions.description: A royal graveyard that's slowly taking a bath.
questions.question: The pyramids at Nuri in Sudan, where the Kushite king Taharqa was buried, were built mainly of what stone?
hints: Most Nubian pyramids were built from the local rock, not stone shipped from Egypt.
It's a soft rock made of grains pressed together over time.
A beach would supply its main ingredient.

media.credit: MODIS Land Rapid Response Team, NASA GSFC · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: MODIS Land Rapid Response Team, NASA GSFC

questions.fun_fact: The Nile's rising groundwater has flooded some of the burial chambers under the Nuri pyramids, so archaeologists have to dive to explore them.

quality.notes: Correct, and the fun fact about divers exploring flooded tombs is great. But the question itself is a dry fact about stone type, and adults who know Nubian pyramids are sandstone could fairly reason to it.

questions.description: The world's heaviest home delivery, and not a single truck in sight.
questions.question: An Egyptian tomb painting shows a giant statue pulled on a sled. Why does a man pour water on the sand in front of it?
questions.answer: To make the sled slide more easily
wrong_answers: To bless the statue for the gods
To keep dust out of the workers' eyes
hints: Think about building a sandcastle at the beach.
Dry sand piles up in front of a sled, but damp sand stays firm.
In 2014, physicists showed that the right amount of water halves the force needed to pull.
questions.fun_fact: For a long time, experts thought the man was pouring water just as a ritual, until lab tests showed it really works.

quality.notes: A satisfying question you can reason through. The Djehutihotep drawing is on Commons, so the essential image is feasible. Hint 1 (sandcastle) is strong for a first hint.

review.feedback: No suitable picture found for this question.

previous.feedback: The picked picture has an unsuitable licence (pd-us-only: PD-1923, PD-US, PD-US-expired).

revision.reason: The tomb painting image is only public domain in the US, so the question now describes the painting itself and uses an illustrative statue photo instead of the essential image.

previous.question: This Egyptian tomb painting shows a giant statue on a sled. Why is the man at the front pouring water on the sand?

media.author: No idea - see source

questions.description: A pyramid that had a very bad haircut.
questions.question: You cut the top off a pyramid with a slice parallel to its base. What is the solid shape left over called?
hints: It still has a square bottom and sloping sides.
The same word is used for a cone with its tip cut off, like a lampshade.
It comes from the Latin word for “a piece cut off”.

media.credit: Rollrule · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Rollrule

questions.fun_fact: The Egyptian Moscow Papyrus, about 3,800 years old, already shows how to work out the volume of this shape.

quality.notes: Torus is an easy elimination, and the question is a vocabulary test. The term is less widely known than a 12.

questions.description: Some leftovers vanish into the soil; others outlive your grandparents' grandparents.
questions.question: You're cleaning up after a picnic. Apple core is to “biodegradable” as what is to “not biodegradable”?
hints: Worms and bacteria can't eat it.
It can be recycled, but it never rots.
It's the shiny sheet that wrapped your sandwich.

media.credit: Acabashi · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Acabashi

questions.fun_fact: Aluminum never rots, but it can be recycled again and again without losing quality.

quality.notes: The analogy works, but it is a stiff way to ask "which of these doesn't rot?", and the picnic opener adds nothing. A 9–10-year-old can answer it, so 6 rates it too high. The decorative compost image is safe, but an illustrative picnic image would work just as well.

questions.description: It protects your new TV, then refuses to leave the planet.
questions.question: This white foam is used to pack TVs and make takeout boxes. Which kind of plastic is it?
hints: It is mostly air.
Its recycling code is the number 6.
A famous brand name for it is Styrofoam.

media.note: Clear photo of white bead-foam packing blocks or pieces, with no labels or text.
media.credit: User:Acdx · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: User:Acdx

questions.fun_fact: Foam like this is about 95–98% air, so trucks carry mostly air when they haul it to be recycled.

quality.notes: Styrofoam is strictly a Dow brand of extruded foam (blue boards), not white bead foam, though in everyday talk it means the white kind. Hint 3 nearly gives the answer, which is allowed. Fun is middling: it reads like a school question on plastic types. Many adults know "polystyrene", so it is closer to 10.

questions.description: Trees drop these every fall and never clean up after themselves.
questions.question: These fell from a tree in the yard. Which kind of waste are they?
hints: They came from something alive.
Worms love to munch them.
They can turn into compost.

media.note: Clear photo of a pile of dry brown fallen leaves.
media.credit: Florian Prischl · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Florian Prischl

questions.fun_fact: In a compost pile, dry leaves are called “browns” and balance out wet kitchen scraps.

quality.notes: The wrong options are very weak: no leaf looks like plastic, glass or electronics. A 6-year-old may not know the term "organic waste", so it is closer to 2. It is a dry, obvious question with not much to enjoy.

questions.description: Three arrows chasing each other forever and never getting tired.
questions.question: What does this symbol on a package tell you?
hints: Look at the arrows going around and around.
It's about giving old things a new life.
The package can be turned into something new instead of thrown away.

media.note: The three chasing arrows recycling symbol, with no text.
media.credit: Siera Wild · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Siera Wild

questions.fun_fact: The symbol was designed in 1970 by Gary Anderson, a college student, for a contest linked to the first Earth Day.

quality.notes: Strictly, the chasing-arrows (Möbius loop) symbol means the item is recyclable or contains recycled material. "It can be eaten" is a throwaway option. The description describes the symbol the players are already looking at, which is harmless. The Gary Anderson fun fact is good.

questions.description: The shopping bag that comes back from the store with you, week after week.
questions.question: Many reusable shopping bags like this one are made from which plant?
hints: Your T-shirt is probably made of it too.
It grows in fluffy white puffs on a bush.
Jeans are made from it.

media.note: Plain, undyed cloth tote bag with no printed text.
media.credit: Runologe · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Runologe

questions.fun_fact: A cotton bag has to be reused many times, often estimated in the dozens or even hundreds, before it is greener than thin plastic bags.

quality.notes: Jute and canvas bags exist too, but "many" covers that. Lettuce and wheat are not believable fabric plants. Some studies put the reuse number in the thousands, so "dozens or even hundreds" undersells it. It shares the answer with banknotes-12 (cotton), but that question asks a different fact.

questions.description: Jaws like garden shears, and it hasn't even had its morning coffee.
questions.question: These jaws belong to the titan beetle, which can be about 17 cm (6.7 in) long. Where does it live in the wild?
hints: It lives in a tropical rainforest.
Its home is on a mainland, not on an island.
It's the same forest where jaguars and anacondas live.

media.note: A close-up photo of a titan beetle's head and big jaws; no labels or location text.
media.credit: Bernard DUPONT from FRANCE · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Bernard DUPONT from FRANCE

questions.fun_fact: Adult titan beetles are thought not to eat at all; they live off energy stored while they were larvae.

quality.notes: Rated 10, but the Amazon is the default rainforest answer even for children, so it is much easier. The Amazon stands out as the famous option. Hint 2 ('largest rainforest on Earth') practically names it. The titan beetle also lives in the Guiana Shield, which is near the Amazon, so this is mostly fine.

revision.reason: Replaced hint 2, which named the Amazon, with a mid-strength hint that only rules out the two island options.

hints: It lives in a tropical rainforest.
Its home is the largest rainforest on Earth.
It's the same forest where jaguars and anacondas live.

questions.description: Small, shiny and colorful, like candy you must never, ever lick.
questions.question: In South America, some Indigenous hunters rubbed the poison of frogs like this one on what?
hints: They used it to hunt animals in the trees.
The poison went on the tip of something small.
You blow through a long tube to shoot it.

media.note: A clear photo of a golden poison frog (Phyllobates terribilis), no text.
media.credit: Holger Krisp · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Holger Krisp

questions.fun_fact: Poison frogs raised in zoos are not toxic, because they get their poison from the ants and mites they eat in the wild.

quality.notes: Close to q-0364 (the blowgun used to shoot darts), but it asks a different fact. 'Spear handles' and 'fishing nets' are weak distractors, because poison on a handle or a net makes no sense.

questions.description: A job description that rivers would never sign off on.
questions.question: In Brazil I'm called a “garimpeiro”. My tools are a water pump and a hose, and rivers turn brown where I work. What am I?
hints: I dig into riverbanks and sift the mud.
Mercury helps me catch tiny shiny flakes.
I'm looking for a yellow metal.

media.credit: MODIS Land Rapid Response Team, NASA GSFC · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: MODIS Land Rapid Response Team, NASA GSFC

questions.fun_fact: Mercury from gold mining ends up in fish, so people living far downstream can be poisoned without ever seeing a mine.

quality.notes: Hint 2 (mercury) is very strong. This is fine.

questions.description: Spying on trees from space: the forest's least favorite paparazzi.
questions.question: Brazil's space research institute measures how much Amazon forest is cut down each year using satellite images. In which decade did it start?
hints: It began before the internet was in most homes.
It started after Landsat satellites had been taking Earth pictures for over a decade.
It began in the same decade the Berlin Wall fell.

media.credit: NASA/Goddard Space Flight Center Conceptual Image Lab · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: NASA/Goddard Space Flight Center Conceptual Image Lab

questions.fun_fact: The project, called PRODES, has tracked Amazon forest loss every year since it began, making it one of the longest records of its kind.

quality.notes: PRODES started in 1988. This is a minor date that almost nobody knows, so the question becomes guessing by elimination from the hints. It reads like a dry school test with little payoff.

questions.description: The longest commute to a reunion in the history of marriage.
questions.question: In 1769, Isabel Godin set out to cross the Andes and float down the Amazon to reach her husband, after 20 years apart. In which country today did her trip begin?
hints: Her husband had come to South America to measure the shape of the Earth.
Her hometown was Riobamba, in the Andes.
The country is named after an imaginary line around the Earth.

media.credit: Edgar Michahelles · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Edgar Michahelles

questions.fun_fact: Isabel finally saw her husband again in 1770, after a journey of thousands of kilometers.

quality.notes: The question is long (about 170 characters). The exact reunion year (1770) in the fun fact is a little uncertain, though sources generally agree on it. An illustrative image would be safe here, so decorative is a weaker choice. q-2214 has the same answer (Ecuador) but asks a different fact.

questions.description: Royalty, spiky hair and a very serious grudge against a guy named Goku.
questions.question: I'm the proud prince of the Saiyans and Goku's greatest rival. Who am I?
hints: I come from the Dragon Ball world.
Like Goku, I can turn into a Super Saiyan with golden hair.
My son is called Trunks, and my wife is Bulma.

media.credit: Opkangas · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Opkangas

questions.fun_fact: Most Saiyan names in Dragon Ball are food jokes: Kakarot (Goku's Saiyan name) comes from “carrot,” and Raditz from “radish.”

quality.notes: Dragon Ball is famous worldwide, so it is probably a bit easier than rated.

questions.description: Motorbikes, psychic powers and a city that really should have read the safety manual.
questions.question: I'm a huge city built after a mysterious explosion wiped out the old Tokyo, and teen bikers race through my streets in a 1988 anime film. What am I called?
hints: The film is a famous cyberpunk classic by Katsuhiro Otomo.
The hero, Kaneda, rides a famous red motorbike through my streets.
The film is called “Akira.”

media.credit: David Kernan · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: David Kernan

questions.fun_fact: “Akira” is set in 2019, and in the story Tokyo was chosen to host the 2020 Olympics, years before the real city really got them.

quality.notes: The question is slightly long. The fun fact wording 'real city really' is clunky.

questions.description: A tool that always knows where it's going, unlike most people on a road trip.
questions.question: Explorers found their way with a magnetic compass. Roughly which direction does its needle point?
hints: It works because the Earth is like a giant magnet.
Sailors used this direction as their starting point to work out all the others.
On most maps it is at the top.

media.credit: Samuel Walters · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Samuel Walters

questions.fun_fact: The first compasses were made in China more than 900 years ago, using a magnetic stone.

quality.notes: Solid but plain school question; hint 2 (Arctic) already nearly gives it away. q-2375 is about recognizing a compass, which is a different fact.

revision.reason: Replaced hint 2, which named the Arctic, with a vaguer hint.

hints: It works because the Earth is like a giant magnet.
It is the direction toward the Arctic.
On most maps it is at the top.

questions.description: The only bridges you pay with instead of paying to cross.
questions.question: Every euro banknote shows a bridge on its back. What are the bridges meant to stand for?
hints: The designs were chosen for the new money that arrived in 2002.
The other side shows windows and gateways, standing for openness.
It's the same idea as the saying “to build bridges”.

media.credit: Friedrich Haag · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Friedrich Haag

questions.fun_fact: The Dutch town of Spijkenisse later built real copies of all seven bridges from the euro notes.

quality.notes: Essential media: euro banknote images on Commons are limited by copyright and deletions, so a clear reverse-side image may be hard to find. People outside Europe have less exposure to euros, though they can reason it out.

previous.feedback: None of the media candidates shows a euro banknote. 1–2 are blank pages from an old atlas and 3–6 are diagrams of the reverse transcriptase protein. The question says "like this one", so it needs a clear photo of the back of a euro note with its bridge. No new search is allowed here, so the media slot needs a manual pick, for example a Commons file of the EUR 5 or EUR 10 reverse side. No suitable picture found for this question.

revision.reason: No photo of a banknote's back was found, so the question no longer points to the image (“like this one”) and the media is now an illustrative euro banknote photo.

previous.question: Every euro banknote, like this one, shows a bridge. What are the bridges meant to stand for?

media.note: The back of a euro banknote, showing its bridge design.

questions.description: Three minutes of waiting has never tasted so good.
questions.question: Cup Noodles were invented in Japan. Which of these was NOT invented in Japan?
hints: The odd one out was invented in two countries at about the same time.
It is more than 100 years old.
It got its name from US President Theodore Roosevelt.

media.credit: Quercus acuta · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

questions.fun_fact: The oldest known fishing net, found in Finland, is more than 10,000 years old and was made from willow bark.

quality.notes: The distractors (metal plates, glass beads, wooden planks) are deliberately silly. That's OK at level 1, but nobody would pick them. A fishing boat photo may show nets with their strings, which makes it easier. The question itself is fairly dry, though the fun fact (Antrea net, willow bark) is good.

questions.description: A big, toothy smile that nobody wants to see up close.
questions.question: Lion is to the savanna as great white shark is to the…
hints: Both animals are top hunters in their home.
The shark needs water to breathe.
It's big, blue and salty.

media.credit: Bernard DUPONT from FRANCE · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Bernard DUPONT from FRANCE

questions.fun_fact: A great white shark can lose thousands of teeth in its life, because new ones keep growing in rows behind the old ones.

quality.notes: A very simple analogy with little surprise. The fun comes mostly from the fun fact.

questions.description: Giant metal giraffes that never get tired of playing with building blocks.
questions.question: What are these huge cranes at a port used for?
hints: Think about what big ships carry.
Ships bring things from all over the world.
They lift containers on and off.

media.note: A photo of a container port with tall gantry cranes next to a container ship, containers visible, no readable port names.
media.credit: Downtowngal · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Downtowngal

questions.fun_fact: Most things you buy that come from another continent, from shoes to toys, traveled part of the way in a shipping container.

quality.notes: The essential photo of port cranes over a container ship basically shows the answer in action, so it's easy. 'Pulling boats out of storms' and 'Cleaning the harbor water' are weak distractors. Related to economy-and-stock-market-17 (shipping containers at a port), but it asks a different fact.

questions.description: A grocery bag that floats like a ghost and fools a hungry ocean swimmer.
questions.question: “I swim in every ocean, I love eating jellyfish, and I often mistake floating plastic bags for them.” Who am I?
hints: I have been around since the time of the dinosaurs.
I come to the beach to lay my eggs.
I carry a hard shell on my back.

media.credit: Alexander Vasenin · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Alexander Vasenin

questions.fun_fact: Leatherback sea turtles eat so many jellyfish that they can eat about three-quarters of their own weight in them in one day.

quality.notes: The plastic-bag/jellyfish confusion is well known, so the clue really points to the turtle. The fun fact (about 73% of body weight per day) matches published leatherback research.

questions.description: The program that taught the world to never fully trust a picture again.
questions.question: People say a fake picture has been “photoshopped”. In which decade did the program Photoshop first come out?
hints: It needed home computers with screens that could show photos.
At first it ran only on Apple Macintosh computers.
Version 1.0 came out the same year Germany was reunified.

media.credit: Kskhh · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Kskhh

questions.fun_fact: Photoshop was first written by two brothers, Thomas and John Knoll, before Adobe bought it.

quality.notes: Photoshop 1.0 came out in February 1990, and German reunification was October 1990, so the facts hold. Young teens will mostly guess, and the 1980s is a strong trap (it was developed in 1987–88), so it's a bit harder than 8.

questions.description: A photo taken without any camera, which sounds like cheating but isn't.
questions.question: You save a picture of exactly what your phone or computer is showing, without using any camera. What is it called?
hints: It saves something you can already see.
It copies exactly what the display is showing.
On many phones you make one by pressing two side buttons at once.

media.credit: KK IN HK · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: KK IN HK

questions.fun_fact: On many computers you can make a screenshot with a key called “Print Screen”, from a time when it really sent the screen to a printer.

quality.notes: Clean and clear. A tablet image without a screenshot on it would be safe as illustrative, so decorative is unnecessary.

questions.description: A captain who never needs a lantern because he glows all by himself.
questions.question: I'm a green ghost pirate who sails a ghost ship and loves to scare SpongeBob. My name comes from an old sailors' legend. Who am I?
hints: My ship can never reach a port.
The legend says my ship sails forever near the southern tip of Africa.
My name tells you which country I come from: the Netherlands.

media.credit: Robert Strickland Thomas · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Robert Strickland Thomas

questions.fun_fact: Sailors have told stories about a ghost ship called the Flying Dutchman for more than 200 years.

quality.notes: Davy Jones is close: in Pirates of the Caribbean he captains a ghost ship that is itself called the Flying Dutchman. 'Green ghost' and 'SpongeBob' still settle it. Hint 3 nearly gives it away, which is allowed. SpongeBob is known worldwide.

questions.description: Traffic lights for the sea, but nobody ever turns yellow.
questions.question: You're at sea at night and see only a red light on another ship. Which side of that ship are you looking at?
hints: Ships carry a red light and a green light on opposite sides.
Red marks the side ships traditionally tied up to the harbor dock.
The green light marks starboard, the right side.

media.credit: Unknown authorUnknown author or not provided · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Unknown authorUnknown author or not provided

questions.fun_fact: Planes use the same rule: a red light on the left wing tip and a green one on the right.

quality.notes: Correct: seeing only the red light means you see the port side. Fewer adults know this than the rating suggests, so 11 fits better than 10.

questions.description: Pirate payday, minus the paperwork.
questions.question: Pirates shared out stolen treasure by their own rules. Which crew member, who led the ship in battle, usually got a double share?
hints: This person had a very important job on board.
On many pirate ships, the crew voted this person into the job.
Blackbeard and Henry Morgan both had this job.

media.credit: EgorovaSvetlana · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: EgorovaSvetlana

questions.fun_fact: Many pirate crews also paid extra to anyone hurt in battle, like an early kind of insurance.

quality.notes: Hint 3 says “Captain Hook”, so it literally contains the answer word. Cook, cabin boy and lookout are weak next to captain; the obvious answer makes this easier than 5. The description is a bit flat. The lens tag “colombia” has nothing to do with the content.

revision.reason: Reworded the question so the quartermaster no longer fits, and replaced hint 3 because it contained the word “captain”.

previous.question: After a raid, pirates shared out the stolen treasure by their own rules. Who usually got a double share?
hints: This person had a very important job on board.
On many pirate ships, the crew voted this person into the job.
Blackbeard and Captain Hook both had this job.

questions.description: Proof that being stuck indoors on vacation can make you rich and famous.
questions.question: How did the idea for Robert Louis Stevenson's novel “Treasure Island” start?
questions.answer: With an island map drawn with his stepson
wrong_answers: With a real pirate's diary found in an attic
With a shipwreck he survived as a young man
With a dream he had about a talking parrot
hints: It started on a rainy vacation in Scotland.
It began with a picture, not with words.
It was something you'd use to find buried treasure.

media.credit: John Singer Sargent · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: John Singer Sargent

questions.fun_fact: Stevenson first read the chapters aloud to his family, and his father made up what was inside Billy Bones's sea chest.

quality.notes: The answer is longer and more specific than the wrong options and fits “Treasure Island” too neatly, so it stands out. The description's “game” hints a little at play with a child.

previous.feedback: Hint 2 (“A boy was involved”) gives the answer away: only the correct option mentions a child (the stepson), so it rules out all three wrong answers. The description (“rainy-day game”) also points to play with a child, and the correct option is clearly longer and more specific than the others. Hint 2 needs to be vaguer (for example about something drawn or made at home), the description shouldn't mention a game, and the options should be closer in length.

revision.reason: Hint 2 no longer points only to the child, the description no longer mentions a game, and the options are now about the same length.

previous.description: The most famous rainy-day game that ever got out of hand.
previous.answer: With a map of an island drawn with his stepson
wrong_answers: With a real pirate's diary he found
With a dream about a talking parrot
hints: It started on a rainy vacation in Scotland.
A boy was involved.
It was something you'd use to find buried treasure.

questions.description: A poem that absolutely refuses to go to bed early.
questions.question: Who wrote the poem “Do Not Go Gentle into That Good Night”, with its famous line “Rage, rage against the dying of the light”?
hints: The poet came from Wales.
The poem is recited several times in the 2014 space film “Interstellar”.
His first name is the stage surname of the singer of “Blowin' in the Wind”.

media.credit: Keshani Kaveesha · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Keshani Kaveesha

questions.fun_fact: In the film “Interstellar”, Michael Caine's character recites the poem as the astronauts set off into space.
questions.concept: Do Not Go Gentle into That Good Night

quality.notes: Most adults don't know the poet, so 13 fits better than 12. The question is a bit long. The Interstellar link makes it fun.

questions.description: The ancient world's most talented girl band needed a manager.
questions.question: In Greek mythology, how many Muses were there?
hints: Each one looked after a different art, from poetry to dance to astronomy.
They were daughters of Zeus and Mnemosyne, the goddess of memory.
It's the number of planets people learned about before Pluto was moved to the dwarf planet group.

media.credit: Ludvig14 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ludvig14

questions.fun_fact: Each Muse had her own art: Calliope looked after epic poetry, and Urania looked after the stars.

quality.notes: Teens tend to know school mythology less well than expected, so it is closer to 10 than 9. The clue tag “scenario” doesn't fit; the question is direct.

review.feedback: This repeats the fact in related draft q-3418 (“Clio, the Muse of history, had sisters who were Muses too. How many Muses were there in all?” → 9). Keep only one of the two.

questions.description: A greeting so small you could miss it if you blink.
questions.question: You cross your thumb and index finger, and K-pop stars do it for their fans. What is this gesture from South Korea called?
hints: You only need one hand to do it.
It looks a bit like snapping your fingers.
The name says which body part makes the heart.

media.credit: Immanuelle · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Immanuelle

questions.fun_fact: In South Korea the finger heart is so common that it shows up in selfies, ads and even sports celebrations.

quality.notes: The description calls it a greeting, which it isn't really, and the joke is weak. The fun fact is vague. The answer's “heart” is easy to guess from K-pop culture.

questions.description: A lullaby so powerful it works across two worlds.
questions.question: In which country is the Pixar film Coco set?
hints: Miguel's family has made shoes for generations.
People there speak Spanish.
The story happens during the Day of the Dead.

media.credit: Johnnydeezwax · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Johnnydeezwax

questions.fun_fact: “Remember Me” won the Oscar for Best Original Song in 2018.

quality.notes: The question is long (about 170 characters) with a list of plot details that adds nothing; a shorter wording would read better on TV. Many other candidates also have Mexico as the answer, but they ask different facts.

revision.reason: Shortened the question to the film and what is asked, cutting the list of plot details.

previous.question: In Coco, Miguel dreams of music, crosses a bridge of orange petals, and sings “Remember Me” to his great-grandmother. In which country is the film set?

questions.description: Sounds Italian, but it's not a pasta dish.
questions.question: What does a song performed a cappella leave out?
hints: Choirs often sing this way.
The singers make every sound themselves, even the beat.
Guitars and violins have to stay in their cases.

media.credit: Chris Olszewski · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Chris Olszewski

questions.fun_fact: “A cappella” is Italian for “in the style of the chapel”, where singers often sang without instruments.

quality.notes: Solid. The description hints that the term is Italian, which is harmless. Young teens may know it from Pitch Perfect, but 8 fits better than 7.

questions.description: A door's worst nightmare: guests with claws and no manners.
questions.question: I'm a door handle you push down, not a knob you twist. In the film “Jurassic Park”, which dinosaurs used me to open a door?
hints: They hunted in packs in the film.
They were small, fast and very clever.
Their name is often shortened to “raptors”.

media.credit: marya from San Luis Obispo, USA · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: marya from San Luis Obispo, USA

questions.fun_fact: Lever handles are easier to use than round knobs for people with weak hands, and also, it seems, for clever dinosaurs.

quality.notes: The famous kitchen and door scene, nicely tied to design. The riddle opening ('I'm a door handle') feels a bit forced but works. Dilophosaurus is a weaker distractor for kids.

questions.description: A long word for a very kind idea.
questions.question: Designers often say a product needs “accessibility”. What does that word mean?
hints: Good design thinks about every kind of person who might use it.
It's about who can use the thing, not what it's made of.
A wheelchair user should be able to get in.

media.credit: TMat928 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: TMat928

questions.fun_fact: Ramps cut into sidewalks were made for wheelchairs, but they also help strollers, suitcases and bikes every day.

quality.notes: A vocabulary-style school question with little surprise. Accessibility is broader than disabilities (usable by everyone), but the core meaning is right. Hint 1 (ramps, braille) nearly gives the answer away. The distractors are all about sustainability, so the correct option stands out thematically.

revision.reason: Replaced hint 1, which gave the answer away, with a vague hint that names no disability feature.

hints: Think of ramps, subtitles and braille.
It's about who can use the thing, not what it's made of.
A wheelchair user should be able to get in.

questions.description: A line of poetry that has saved many people from being grounded.
questions.question: The poet Alexander Pope wrote that to forgive is divine. In that famous line, what does he call human?
hints: Every person does it, no matter how clever.
Pencils have a little tool on the other end to fix it.
You do it when you get a math problem wrong.

media.credit: Shixart1985 · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Shixart1985

questions.fun_fact: The idea is older than Pope: the ancient Romans already said “errare humanum est”, “to err is human”.

quality.notes: Players can reason out the answer from the 'forgive' contrast, which is nice. The pencil-eraser hint is cute. Pope is English, but the saying travels through the Latin form. Slightly harder than 7 for young teens.

questions.description: Even giants need little siblings to keep them company.
questions.question: These three small pyramids stand right next to the Great Pyramid of Giza. What were they built for?
hints: They were part of the same building project as the big pyramid.
They were built for important women.
The royal women of Khufu's family were buried here.

media.note: Photo of the small queens' pyramids (G1-a, G1-b, G1-c) on the east side of the Great Pyramid of Giza, the small pyramids clearly in front.
media.credit: Francesco Gasparetti · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Francesco Gasparetti

questions.fun_fact: When new, each of these little pyramids was about 30 m (98 ft) tall, but most of their outer stones were later carried away.

quality.notes: Anyone who knows pyramids were tombs can reason to the answer (see q-0451, a related but different fact). Hint 2 is already strong. Commons very likely has a clear photo of the queens' pyramids, so the essential photo is OK.

questions.description: The most expensive sleeping bag in history.
questions.question: Howard Carter opened it in 1925. It held the boy king's mummy and weighs about 110 kg (243 lb). What is Tutankhamun's innermost coffin made of?
hints: It's a metal.
It never rusts, which is why it still shines after 3,300 years.
It's the same shiny yellow metal as his famous mask.

media.credit: Vyacheslav Argenberg · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Vyacheslav Argenberg

questions.fun_fact: Inside this coffin, the mummy wore the famous golden mask, which alone weighs about 10 kg (22 lb).
questions.concept: Descubrimiento de la tumba de Tutankamón

quality.notes: Facts check out: the innermost coffin is about 110 kg and was opened in 1925. Tutankhamun's gold fame makes it easy, and the 'most expensive' description nudges toward gold. The question text runs a bit long at about 150 characters. Related to the gold-mask questions, but a different fact.

questions.description: The pyramid's building site needed something you won't see in any photo of it today.
questions.question: I'm a long slope of mud and rubble that grew taller as the pyramid grew. What was I built for?
wrong_answers: Giving visitors a path to the top
hints: The workers didn't have cranes or trucks.
Pulling something heavy up a gentle slope is easier than lifting it straight up.
Workers pulled heavy loads up me with ropes.

media.credit: Bilal Detailz · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Bilal Detailz

questions.fun_fact: In 2018, archaeologists found a 4,500-year-old ramp in an Egyptian quarry, with steps and posts for ropes along both sides.

quality.notes: 'A long slope … grew as the pyramid grew' makes the purpose easy to reason out, which suits a 4. The 2018 Hatnub ramp fun fact is accurate and nice.

questions.description: In 2012, some people bought survival kits because of some very old stone carvings.
questions.question: Maya monuments like this one carve dates in a calendar some said “ran out” on December 21, 2012. What did that date really mark?
questions.answer: The end of a long calendar cycle
wrong_answers: A rare eclipse the Maya predicted
The crowning of a new Maya king
The founding of a great Maya city
hints: Think about what a calendar does, not what the movies said.
Their Long Count calendar counts days in big units, like a car's mileage counter.
A unit of about 394 years, called a b'ak'tun, simply rolled over to the next one.

media.credit: Stuardo Herrera from Guatemala, Guatemala · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Stuardo Herrera from Guatemala, Guatemala

questions.fun_fact: Maya inscriptions mention dates thousands of years after 2012, so the Maya clearly expected the world to keep going.

quality.notes: Facts check out: the 13th b'ak'tun ended, and Palenque has inscriptions with dates far in the future. The question is a bit long at about 150 characters. The answer is a little more abstract than the distractors, but not so much that it stands out.

questions.description: A machine that never says no to a snack, as long as the snack is a plastic bottle.
questions.question: At the recycling plant, I chop old plastic bottles into tiny flakes. What am I?
hints: I work before the plastic is washed and melted.
My sharp blades spin very fast.
Offices use a small version of me for secret papers.

media.credit: TOP PLASTIC · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: TOP PLASTIC

questions.fun_fact: Small flakes melt faster and more evenly, which is why plastic is chopped up before it is made into new pellets.

quality.notes: In industry the machine is often called a granulator, but "shredder" is fine. Kids won't know what a baler is. Magnet and furnace are easy to rule out once you hear "chop". The fun is modest, a fairly dry process question.

questions.description: Two big gates, one pool of water and a lot of waiting around.
questions.question: The Panama Canal has locks with huge gates at both ends. What are canal locks for?
hints: Think of a canal that crosses hills.
Water can't flow uphill, but boats still have to.
They work like a water staircase.

media.credit: ArnoldReinhold · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: ArnoldReinhold

questions.fun_fact: The Panama Canal locks lift ships about 26 m (85 ft) up to a lake in the middle of the country.

quality.notes: Accurate, and the fun fact about the 26 m lift to Gatun Lake is correct. Hint 3 ("water staircase") nearly gives it away, which is allowed. The other Panama Canal candidates ask different facts.

questions.description: The Romans called it “our sea”, which is a bold thing to say about a sea.
questions.question: You're sailing all around Mare Nostrum in Roman times. Which of these peoples would you NOT meet on its shores?
hints: First work out which sea the Romans called “our sea”.
It is the sea between Europe and Africa.
The people you would not meet lived on a cold island far to the north.

media.credit: José Luiz · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: José Luiz

questions.fun_fact: Rome is the only power in history that ruled every coast of the Mediterranean Sea at the same time.

quality.notes: Phoenicians as a separate people are a bit loose for 'Roman times', since Carthage was destroyed in 146 BC, but the coastal Punic and Phoenician cities still existed. Players need to know what 'Mare Nostrum' means, so for young teens it is closer to an 8.

questions.description: The world's most famous bedsheet, worn to work.
questions.question: I'm a long piece of white wool, wrapped around the body and over the left shoulder. Who wore me with pride?
hints: My wearers lived in a big empire around the Mediterranean.
Their capital was a city built on seven hills.
You see me in films about Julius Caesar.
questions.fun_fact: A toga could use more than 5 m (16 ft) of wool, so rich Romans often needed help from others to put it on.

quality.notes: The distractors are easy to rule out: Vikings and samurai don't fit white wool robes, so only the pharaoh is a real option. The graduation-toga candidate asks a different fact. The query might return a draped modern cloth, which is fine.

review.feedback: No suitable picture found for this question.

previous.feedback: No candidate works for the illustrative slot, and a new search isn't allowed. Candidate 1 is a Coptic textile strip with knights, 2 is a bronze buckle, 3 is a Native American man in a blanket shop, and 4–6 are an Egyptian cattle mummy, which also hints at the "Egyptian pharaoh" option. The slot needs a new search such as "white wool cloth draped" or "folded white wool fabric". No suitable picture found for this question.

revision.reason: Changed only the image query so a new search can find draped white wool cloth.

questions.description: Being called a mule is rarely a compliment, unless you're a Roman soldier.
questions.question: The soldiers of the Roman general Gaius Marius were nicknamed “Marius's mules”. Why?
hints: The nickname is about what they did on the march, not in battle.
Fewer baggage animals meant a faster army.
Each man had a heavy pack tied to a pole on his shoulder.

media.credit: The Portable Antiquities Scheme, Dr Anna Booth, 2017-11-20 12:23:41 · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: The Portable Antiquities Scheme, Dr Anna Booth, 2017-11-20 12:23:41

questions.fun_fact: A Roman legionary on the march could carry around 30 kg (66 lb), including food, tools and cooking pots.

quality.notes: A nice question players can reason out (mules carry loads). The fact is not well known, so it is slightly harder than the stated 7. Hint 2 is fairly strong.

questions.description: A name that turns up in plays, films and history exams.
questions.question: Complete the analogy: Hercules is to strength as Brutus is to…
hints: Brutus was a Roman senator.
He had been a friend of Julius Caesar.
He joined the plot against Caesar on the Ides of March.

media.credit: Ernest Joseph Bailly · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ernest Joseph Bailly

questions.fun_fact: Brutus later had a coin made with the words “EID MAR”, short for the Ides of March.

quality.notes: The description is generic and not very funny. Hints 2 and 3 practically give the answer, which is acceptable for hint 3. The EID MAR coin fact is correct.

questions.description: A man who wore a broom on his head and still got everyone's respect.
questions.question: This Roman officer wears his helmet crest from side to side, so his men could spot him. What was his rank?
hints: He led a small unit of the legion from the front.
He often carried a vine stick as a sign of his rank.
His title comes from the Latin word for 100.

media.note: Photo of a Roman reenactor dressed as a centurion with a transverse (side-to-side) helmet crest, no captions.
media.credit: Luc Viatour · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Luc Viatour

questions.fun_fact: Despite the name, a centurion usually led about 80 men, not 100.

quality.notes: Commons/Openverse very likely have centurion reenactor photos with the side-to-side crest. 'Centurion' is a familiar word from Asterix and films, so the answer stands out a bit as the best-known title, but optio, legate and tribune are good expert-level distractors.

questions.description: Seafood that switched careers and became a road sign.
questions.question: I'm a ribbed seashell. Hikers walking the Way of Saint James to Santiago de Compostela hang me on their backpacks. What am I?
hints: The trail ends in northwest Spain, near the Atlantic coast.
Painted versions of me on posts and walls show walkers which way to go.
I'm shaped like a fan, and cooks serve the animal inside me seared in butter.

media.credit: Luis Miguel Bugallo Sánchez · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Luis Miguel Bugallo Sánchez

questions.fun_fact: Medieval pilgrims are said to have used the shell as a small bowl for drinking water and getting food along the way.

quality.notes: The cathedral facade query could show carved scallop shells or pilgrims with shells, a minor risk. The 'ribbed' clue fits scallop and cockle best. The vieira and Saint James candidates ask different facts.

questions.description: A podium finish where the medals are made of prayer.
questions.question: Islam counts the Al-Aqsa Mosque as its third holiest site, and Mecca as its first. Which city is second?
hints: Its name simply means “the city”.
The Prophet Muhammad moved there from Mecca in 622.
The Prophet Muhammad is buried there, under a famous green dome.

media.credit: Godot13 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Godot13

questions.fun_fact: Before Muslims turned to face Mecca, early Muslims prayed facing Jerusalem, where Al-Aqsa stands.

quality.notes: Accurate, but a dry ranking fact that is mostly memorisation. The fun fact is worded awkwardly ("Before Muslims turned… early Muslims prayed"). The Al-Aqsa image is safe.

questions.description: Traffic jam caused by a very relaxed VIP.
questions.question: In India, many Hindus see one animal as sacred and let it wander the streets. Which animal is it?
hints: It eats grass all day.
Many families get their milk from it.
It says “moo”.

media.credit: Vyacheslav Argenberg · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Vyacheslav Argenberg

questions.fun_fact: In many parts of India, cars and buses calmly stop and wait while cows cross the road.

quality.notes: Solid. Hint 2 (milk) fits cows best, though goats and buffalo also give milk. A safe illustrative image (an Indian street scene) would work better than a decorative one.

questions.description: Gardening, druid style: wear white, climb high, and bring your fanciest cutlery.
questions.question: The Roman writer Pliny said druids climbed sacred oak trees to cut which plant with a golden sickle?
hints: It grows on the branches of other trees, not in the ground.
It has small white berries.
In the Asterix comics, the druid Getafix uses it in his magic potion.

media.credit: Ema Lee · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ema Lee

questions.fun_fact: Mistletoe that grows on oaks is quite rare, which may be why the druids saw it as so special.

quality.notes: Correct, from Pliny's Natural History. Asterix readers will recognize Getafix's routine, so it may be a bit easier than 11.

questions.description: A hike so famous you need a ticket just to get sore legs.
questions.question: Hikers walk about four days along this ancient stone path to reach which famous city in the clouds?
hints: The city was built by the Incas in the 1400s.
The ruins are in Peru, high above the Urubamba River.
Its name means “old mountain” in the Quechua language.

media.note: Photo of the stone steps or path of the Inca Trail in the Andes mountains, without the Machu Picchu ruins in view and without signs.
media.credit: Mx._Granger · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Mx._Granger

questions.fun_fact: The Incas built a road network of about 40,000 km (25,000 miles) across South America, without using the wheel.

quality.notes: Of the options, only Machu Picchu is a city high in the mountains, so 'city in the clouds' makes the others easy to rule out. Many Inca Trail photos also show the ruins, so the media is risky. The essential role is debatable: the question would work without the photo.

questions.description: A door that teaches good manners to tall people.
questions.question: You have to bow to pass through this tiny doorway. It's the main entrance of which famous church?
hints: The first church here was built in the 300s, on the orders of Emperor Constantine.
The church stands in Bethlehem.
It's built over the cave where Jesus is said to have been born.

media.note: Close-up photo of the very low stone doorway (the Door of Humility) of the Church of the Nativity, showing only the doorway and surrounding wall; no signs.

media.author: Fallaner

questions.fun_fact: The doorway, about 1.2 m (4 ft) tall, was made smaller centuries ago, likely to stop people from riding horses into the church.

quality.notes: Good. Commons very likely has a photo of the Door of Humility, and the distractors are fair.

questions.description: A mosque that went camping and decided to stay.
questions.question: This tent-shaped mosque, named after a Saudi king and designed by a Turkish architect, stands in which capital city?
hints: The mosque stands at the foot of green, forested hills.
The city was built in the 1960s as a new capital.
The country is Pakistan.

media.note: Photo of the Faisal Mosque with its tent-like roof and four pencil-thin minarets; no visible text naming the city.

questions.fun_fact: When it was finished in 1986, the Faisal Mosque was the largest mosque in the world.

quality.notes: Clever distractors: Riyadh comes from the Saudi king, Ankara from the Turkish architect. The facts are correct (Dalokay, King Faisal, largest mosque in 1986).

questions.description: A city cut like a pizza, but with walls instead of crust.
questions.question: Jerusalem's walled Old City is holy to three religions and split into four quarters: Muslim, Christian, Jewish and which?
hints: It's one of the two smallest quarters.
It's named after a people from the Caucasus, whose kingdom was the first to make Christianity its official religion.
Their country's capital is Yerevan.

media.author: Pudelek

questions.fun_fact: The whole Old City covers less than 1 square kilometer (0.4 square miles), smaller than many city parks.

questions.description: The future was promised, and people are still waiting for their delivery.
questions.question: In “Back to the Future Part II”, Marty McFly rides a hoverboard in the future. Which year does he travel to?
hints: The film came out in 1989.
Marty's own home time is the 1980s.
That year has already passed, and fans celebrated on October 21.

media.author: Michael Barera

questions.fun_fact: Director Robert Zemeckis joked in an interview that hoverboards were real but kept off the market for safety, and many fans believed him.

quality.notes: A fun and accurate fact. The DeLorean image is safe.

questions.description: The monsters are the good guys this time, and they're very proud of it.
questions.question: In “Monsters vs. Aliens”, a giant woman, a jelly blob and a bug-headed scientist team up. What inspired these monsters?
hints: The ideas are much older than the film.
In the originals, monsters were often made by radiation or lab accidents.
Films like “The Blob”, “The Fly” and “Attack of the 50 Foot Woman”.

media.credit: D J Shin · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: D J Shin

questions.fun_fact: Ginormica grows to 49 feet 11 inches (15.2 m), just short of the woman in the 1958 film “Attack of the 50 Foot Woman”.

quality.notes: The answer is longer and more specific than the distractors and stands out. “Old” in the answer and “waiting decades” in the description point the same way. The arcade-games distractor is weak. All facts check out: Ginormica (50 Foot Woman), B.O.B. (The Blob), Dr. Cockroach (The Fly), 49 ft 11 in.

revision.reason: Replaced the drive-in hint that gave the answer away, removed the time span from the description, and shortened the answer so it doesn't stand out.

previous.description: The monsters are the good guys this time, and they've been waiting decades for it.
hints: The ideas are much older than the film.
Your grandparents might have seen them at a drive-in cinema.
Films like “The Blob”, “The Fly” and “Attack of the 50 Foot Woman”.

questions.description: Every rebellion needs a logo, and this one tweets.
questions.question: I'm a bird that can copy any tune. Katniss Everdeen wears me as a gold pin, and the rebels make me their symbol. What am I?
hints: I come from “The Hunger Games”.
The Capitol never meant for me to exist.
The last book in the series is named after me.

media.credit: University of Texas at Arlington Photograph Collection · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: University of Texas at Arlington Photograph Collection

questions.fun_fact: In the books, mockingjays came from jabberjays, spy birds made by the Capitol, mating with wild mockingbirds.

quality.notes: Hint 1 repeats what the question already says by naming Katniss. Anyone who knows Katniss gets the answer straight away, which is fine at this level.

questions.description: The worst deal ever signed in Venice, and that's saying something.
questions.question: In “The Merchant of Venice”, what does the moneylender Shylock ask for if Antonio can't repay his loan?
hints: The deal is written in a contract called a bond.
It is not money at all.
It would be cut from Antonio's own body.

media.author: kallerna

questions.fun_fact: Antonio is saved because the contract allows flesh but not a single drop of blood.

quality.notes: Good distractors from the play itself (casket, ring). Most people know “pound of flesh” as an idiom, so it is more of an adult question, about 11.

questions.description: A famous book of plays with one empty chair at the table.
questions.question: Which of these Shakespeare plays was NOT included in the First Folio, the big 1623 collection of his plays?
hints: The missing play was probably written with another author.
It's about a prince of Tyre.
Its hero shares his name with a famous leader of ancient Athens.

media.credit: Martin Droeshout · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Martin Droeshout

questions.fun_fact: Without the First Folio, around 18 of Shakespeare's plays, including Macbeth and The Tempest, might have been lost forever.

questions.description: A film where the actors were barely older than the characters, for once.
questions.question: In which year did Franco Zeffirelli's film of “Romeo and Juliet”, starring the teenagers Olivia Hussey and Leonard Whiting, come out?
hints: It came out before Leonardo DiCaprio was born.
Its Italian director was also famous for staging and filming operas.
It came out a year before the first Moon landing.

media.credit: High Contrast · CC BY 3.0 de · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: High Contrast

questions.fun_fact: Laurence Olivier secretly spoke the opening lines of the film, without being named in the credits.

quality.notes: A plain release-year question: dry, and close to the 'minor date' trap, although the hints let players work it out. The facts check out: 1968, the Moon landing in 1969, Olivier's uncredited prologue. Not much payoff when the answer is revealed.

revision.reason: Replaced hint 2, whose decade clue left only one option, with a hint about the director.

hints: It came out before Leonardo DiCaprio was born.
It was the decade of the Beatles.
It came out a year before the first Moon landing.

questions.description: A knight with a belly as big as his ego, and a thirst to match.
questions.question: In how many Shakespeare plays does the fat, joking knight Sir John Falstaff appear on stage?
hints: His drinking friend is young Prince Hal.
There's a whole comedy about him, set in Windsor.
He's in both parts of “Henry IV”, and his death is only reported in “Henry V”.

media.credit: Gregorius Oosterlinck · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Gregorius Oosterlinck

questions.fun_fact: Legend says Queen Elizabeth I asked to see Falstaff in love, so Shakespeare wrote “The Merry Wives of Windsor”.

quality.notes: Counting plays is dry. Henry V could cause small doubt, but the question says “on stage” and the hint deals with it. The Elizabeth legend in the fun fact is a nice touch.

questions.description: An old London rule: when sickness spreads, everybody stays home.
questions.question: Whenever the plague spread in Shakespeare's London, the city shut these places for months. What were they?
hints: The city closed them because big crowds packed in close together there.
Ordinary people paid a penny to stand inside.
The Globe was one of them.

media.author: Alan Murray-Rust

questions.fun_fact: During the closure of 1592–1594, Shakespeare wrote the poem “Venus and Adonis”, his first published work.

quality.notes: Naming Shakespeare makes it easy to work out the answer, which is fine. The facts check out: the 1592–94 closure and Venus and Adonis (1593) as his first published work.

revision.reason: Replaced hints 1 and 2, which gave the answer away, with vaguer hints about crowds and penny standing places.

hints: Shakespeare earned his money in them.
Actors had to go on tour when they closed.
The Globe was one of them.

questions.description: A line so fair it would cut a birthday cake perfectly every time.
questions.question: “I start at the corner of an angle and split it into two exactly equal halves.” What am I called?
hints: You can draw me with a compass and a ruler.
Fold a paper angle so its two sides line up, and the crease is me.
A median aims at the middle of the opposite side; I care only about splitting the angle.

media.credit: Lucasbosch · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Lucasbosch

questions.fun_fact: In any triangle, the three angle bisectors always meet at one point, the center of the circle that fits perfectly inside.

quality.notes: Strictly speaking this is the “angle bisector”, and a perpendicular bisector also exists, but no option clashes. It is school geometry and a bit dry. The 'nature' lens doesn't fit.

questions.description: A question with a sharp point, mostly.
questions.question: Which of these is NOT shaped like a cone?
hints: Three of them have a sharp point on top.
One of them has no point at all.
This one bounces and rolls across the field.

media.author: Shixart1985

questions.fun_fact: The rubber traffic cone was invented in the 1940s by Charles Scanlon, a man who painted lines on roads in Los Angeles.

quality.notes: Very easy and fits level 1, but not much fun. The concrete-cone fun fact (Rudabaker, 1914) is often repeated but hard to verify. The description is only weakly funny.

revision.reason: Replaced the uncertain concrete-cone fun fact with a well-known one about the rubber traffic cone.

previous.fun_fact: The very first traffic cones, from the early 1900s, were made of heavy concrete!

questions.description: Two lines that walk side by side forever and never hold hands.
questions.question: What do we call two straight lines that always stay the same distance apart and never meet?
hints: Think of the two rails of a train track.
The equals sign “=” is made of two of them.
In gymnastics, there is an apparatus called the “___ bars”.

media.author: DAHall

questions.fun_fact: Railway tracks seem to meet far away on the horizon, but that is just a trick of perspective.

quality.notes: Solid. The railway-track image works with hint 1. 'Diagonal' is a fairly weak distractor.

questions.description: A circle that someone took a big bite out of.
questions.question: What is this shape called?
hints: It has two pointed tips and one curved edge.
You can see it on some flags, like Turkey's.
It is the shape of the Moon when only a thin part is lit.

media.note: A plain black silhouette of a crescent shape (crescent moon) on a white background, with no text.
