media.author: Alexander S. Peak

questions.fun_fact: The French croissant gets its name from the word for “crescent”, because of its curved shape.

quality.notes: A clear silhouette is easy to find. Hint 2 touches on the Turkish flag question (q-0626), but this asks a different fact.

questions.description: The road sign that politely says “after you”.
questions.question: In most countries, how many sides does the road sign that tells drivers to “yield” or “give way” have?
hints: It usually has a red border around a white or yellow middle.
No other common road sign has this exact shape.
It is a triangle turned upside down.

media.credit: Ewkada · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ewkada

questions.fun_fact: The upside-down triangle shape means drivers can recognize the sign even from behind or covered in snow.

quality.notes: Hint 1 ('points down') nearly says triangle already. The fun fact about recognizing the sign from behind or under snow is a common explanation, but stated loosely. A fairly plain counting question.

revision.reason: Replaced hint 1, which described the shape, with a color-only hint.

hints: It is red and white and points down.
No other common road sign has this exact shape.
It is a triangle turned upside down.

questions.description: A city built by animators who just couldn't pick one favorite.
questions.question: I'm the skyscraper city where Hiro and Baymax fly in “Big Hero 6”, and my name mixes two real cities. Which two?
hints: One of the cities is in the United States, the other in Asia.
One is famous for a big red bridge.
The other is the capital of Japan.

media.credit: Diliff · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Diliff

questions.fun_fact: In the film, the city's famous red bridge has towers shaped like Japanese torii, the gates at Shinto shrines.

quality.notes: Kids who know 'San Fransokyo' can work it out. Shares only the topic with the Baymax question (q-0335).

revision.reason: Fixed the fun fact about the bridge's torii-shaped towers, as the reviewer asked.

previous.fun_fact: In the film, the famous red bridge of the city has curved roofs like a Japanese temple gate.

questions.description: An asteroid with a name straight out of an ancient storybook.
questions.question: The asteroid Apophis, which passes Earth in 2029, is named after an Egyptian god. Ra is to the Sun as Apophis is to…
hints: In Egyptian myth, Apophis was a giant serpent.
Every night it tried to stop the Sun god's journey.
It stood for darkness and disorder.

media.credit: Vyacheslav Argenberg · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Vyacheslav Argenberg

questions.fun_fact: On April 13, 2029, Apophis will pass closer to Earth than some of our satellites, and it will safely miss us.

quality.notes: Apophis as the serpent of chaos is correct. It is a bit niche for 12, though gamers may know it. An analogy built on an abstract concept can feel arbitrary. Hint 3 nearly gives the answer, which is allowed.

questions.description: Earth and the Moon have been together for billions of years, and one of them is very set in its ways.
questions.question: “I'm the Moon, and astronomers say I'm tidally locked to Earth.” What does that mean?
questions.answer: I always show Earth the same face
wrong_answers: I stay in one spot in the sky
hints: I do spin, but slowly.
One spin takes me exactly as long as one trip around Earth.
Nobody on Earth saw my far side until 1959.

media.credit: Gregory H. Revera · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Gregory H. Revera

questions.fun_fact: Earth's pull slowed the Moon's spin over millions of years until it matched its orbit.

quality.notes: 'I cause the ocean tides' is true but is not what 'tidally locked' means. That is acceptable, though a few players may argue. Libration aside, the answer is standard.

questions.description: A crater named “heat”, on a planet that really earns the name.
questions.question: It's an impact basin about 1,550 km (960 miles) wide, it's on Mercury, and its name means “heat” in Latin. What covers its floor?
hints: The giant impact cracked the crust deep down.
Something hot rose up and filled the basin later.
It came from volcanoes.

media.credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center from Greenbelt, MD, USA · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center from Greenbelt, MD, USA

questions.fun_fact: The impact sent shock waves through Mercury that left jumbled, hilly ground on the exact opposite side of the planet.

quality.notes: Caloris Basin: the volcanic plains on its floor and the jumbled ground on the opposite side are generally accepted, but still partly interpretation. Mercury does have water ice in its polar craters, which may confuse experts, though not here. The question is long (about 150 characters) and dry, and the 'heat' clue helps a lot.

questions.description: The Moon tugs at the water twice a day, and some places barely notice.
questions.question: Three of these places are famous for huge tides. Which one has almost no tides at all?
hints: Tides need a big, open ocean to build up.
The answer is almost completely closed in by land.
It lies between Europe and Asia, south of Ukraine and north of Turkey.

media.credit: David Smith · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: David Smith

questions.fun_fact: In the Bay of Fundy in Canada, the water can rise and fall by about 16 m (52 ft), which is about as tall as a five-story building.

quality.notes: The facts are correct: the Black Sea's tides are only a few cm, while the Yellow Sea, Severn and Fundy have huge ranges. Players can reason towards it from the enclosed-sea idea.

questions.description: A space agency with a very short name and very long rockets.
questions.question: NASA sent this robot to Mars. NASA is the space agency of which country?
hints: Its space agency was founded in 1958.
This country sent the first people to walk on the Moon.
Its flag has 50 stars on it.

media.credit: semeion.photo · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: semeion.photo

questions.fun_fact: NASA has landed five rovers on Mars, starting with tiny Sojourner in 1997.

quality.notes: Factually fine; five NASA Mars rovers is correct. It's a dry question, though: many players will just know NASA is American. A Curiosity selfie may show mission decals, but rarely a flag. Hint 2 (first Moon walkers) nearly gives it away, which is acceptable for hint 2 at this level.

questions.description: Hold a finger in front of your face, close one eye, then the other: congratulations, you're doing astronomy.
questions.question: In 1838, who first measured the parallax of a star (61 Cygni) and so found the distance to a star beyond the Sun?
hints: He was a German astronomer and mathematician.
Some special mathematical functions used in physics carry his name.
He was born in Minden, Germany, and worked at Königsberg Observatory.

media.credit: Hypatia Alexandria from Santa Fe · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Hypatia Alexandria from Santa Fe

questions.fun_fact: Bessel worked out that 61 Cygni is about 10 light-years away, close to today's value of 11.4 light-years.

quality.notes: The facts are correct: Bessel, 1838, Minden, Königsberg, ~10.3 ly vs 11.4 ly. The distractors are weak for experts: Brahe, Kepler and Herschel were all dead by 1838, so anyone who knows their dates can rule them out. Struve or Henderson, who measured parallaxes around the same time, would be fairer. Dry fact recall.

questions.description: A constellation with a side job on the world map.
questions.question: Capricorn is a zodiac sign, a constellation and a line on the world map. What animal does its name mean?
hints: The name comes from Latin and mentions horns.
This animal is great at climbing steep mountains.
It has a little beard and says “maa”.

media.credit: Chad Ajamian · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Chad Ajamian

questions.fun_fact: Capricorn is usually drawn as a sea-goat: half goat, half fish.

quality.notes: Correct (capricornus = horned goat). Hint 3 (“maa”, little beard) nearly states it, which is allowed. Decorative sky works, though an illustrative image would have been possible. Fun is moderate. Kids rarely know zodiac animals, so a bit harder than 6.

review.feedback: This base question asks what the name “Capricorn” means, so it falls apart in German, where the sign is called “Steinbock” (ibex, a wild goat): the clue is already the answer. The facts and the media are fine (pick 3), but the question can't travel to every language as it stands.

questions.description: A light in the sky with a busy schedule and a famous nickname.
questions.question: The bright “morning star” is not a star at all. At what other time of day can you see it?
wrong_answers: In the middle of the afternoon
hints: At that time, it has a second nickname.
It's really the planet Venus, which always stays near the Sun in our sky.
Then people call it the “evening star”.

media.credit: Dietmar Rabich · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Dietmar Rabich

questions.fun_fact: Long ago, people thought the morning star and the evening star were two different objects.

quality.notes: Venus can sometimes be seen in daylight, so 'At noon' and 'mid-afternoon' are not strictly impossible, but 'just after sunset' is clearly the intended and best answer. Players can reason 'morning → evening' easily. Hint 2 (stays near the Sun) points strongly to twilight.

questions.description: A star whose name was passed down by Arab sky-watchers over a thousand years ago.
questions.question: The bright star Altair has a name that comes from Arabic. What does it mean?
hints: Altair's constellation is shaped like an animal.
Altair is one of the three stars of the Summer Triangle.
Its constellation is called Aquila.

media.credit: Deralpinbergsteiger · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Deralpinbergsteiger

questions.fun_fact: Altair spins so fast, about once every 9 hours, that it bulges out around its middle.

quality.notes: Correct (al-nasr al-ta'ir; rotation ~9 h). The description only repeats the Arabic origin the question already gives, so it isn't really a joke. Hint 3 (Aquila = eagle in Latin) is close to a giveaway, which is fine for hint 3. Dry word-meaning question.

questions.description: A swan in the sky that a famous scientist was happy to be wrong about.
questions.question: “I'm Cygnus X-1, a strong X-ray source in the Swan. In 1974, Stephen Hawking bet I didn't contain one of these.” What's in me?
hints: Hawking lost the bet and paid up in 1990.
It pulls gas off a giant blue star next to it.
Not even light can escape it.

media.author: Tk833

questions.fun_fact: Hawking made the bet against his own theories as an “insurance policy”: if he was wrong about black holes, at least he'd win a prize.

quality.notes: Correct: Hawking–Thorne bet in 1974, conceded 1990, blue supergiant companion. 'Pulsar' and 'neutron star' overlap (a pulsar is a neutron star), but both are wrong, so no harm. Hawking + bet points to black hole very easily, so it's easier than 10. The first-person riddle runs a little long.

questions.description: A chart where stars get sorted like students in a class photo.
questions.question: A famous chart plots stars by brightness and temperature. It's named after Ejnar Hertzsprung and which astronomer?
hints: He was an American who worked at Princeton.

His surname is also a common first name, as in a famous British philosopher called Bertrand.

media.credit: geckzilla · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: geckzilla

questions.fun_fact: Most stars, including the Sun, sit on one diagonal band of the chart called the main sequence.

quality.notes: Correct. The Hertzsprung–Russell diagram is standard in school and university astronomy, so slightly below 14. Hint 3 (Bertrand Russell) all but gives the name away, which is allowed. A dry recall question.

questions.description: Butter’s cheaper cousin had a very royal godparent.
questions.question: Margarine was invented in 1869 after a French emperor offered a prize for a cheap butter substitute. Who was he?
hints: The emperor ruled France in the middle of the 1800s.

media.credit: TorbeyCharbel · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: TorbeyCharbel

questions.fun_fact: The word “margarine” comes from the Greek word for pearl, because of its pearly shine.

questions.description: A square full of tiny squares that wanted to outdo its older, simpler relative.
questions.question: You scan a QR code on a restaurant table. Which older code was the QR code made to improve on?

It is a row of black and white lines of different widths.

media.credit: CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

questions.fun_fact: The QR code was invented in Japan in 1994 to keep track of car parts in factories.

quality.notes: Correct (Denso Wave, 1994, car parts). It shares the barcode answer with q-3058 and product-design-11, but asks a different fact. The 'scenario' clause doesn't add much. 'Morse code' lacks the article the other options have, a small form mismatch. Easy to reason, so the stated 5 is slightly high.

questions.description: Your teeth already know the answer, they're just too polite to say.
questions.question: You unwrap a typical bar of milk chocolate. About how much of it is sugar?

The rest is mostly cocoa butter, cocoa and milk.

media.author: Knud Winckelmann

questions.description: The guest of honor in a 600-year-old painting has never said a single word.
questions.question: This detail from the Ghent Altarpiece shows an animal on an altar that stands for Jesus. What do Christians call it?
hints: Look closely at the animal in the picture.

media.author: Jan van Eyck

questions.fun_fact: The Ghent Altarpiece is often called the most stolen artwork ever; one of its panels has been missing since 1934.

questions.description: The ultimate diet challenge, with a very pushy snack salesman.
questions.question: I went without food for 40 days in the desert, and the devil dared me to turn stones into bread. Who am I?
hints: I said no to every temptation.

media.credit: dan barbarian · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: dan barbarian

questions.fun_fact: Each time he answered the devil, Jesus quoted a line from the Old Testament book of Deuteronomy.

quality.notes: Strong distractors: Moses and Elijah also have 40-day fasts or journeys. The fun fact about Deuteronomy is correct. The decorative desert image is fine. The overlap candidates share the answer Jesus but ask about a different fact.

questions.description: A dad whose day job is more famous than most kings.

hints: Jesus is said to have learned the same job as a boy.

media.author: FLASHPACKER TRAVELGUIDE

questions.fun_fact: The Greek word used in the Gospels, “tekton”, can mean any builder or craftsman, working with wood or stone.

questions.description: These cards are older than poker night, and they still dress the part.
questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the four suits in a traditional Spanish or Italian deck of cards?
hints: These old suits had already reached Europe by the late 1300s.
The three real suits are things a medieval soldier, a merchant and a host at a feast would carry.
It's a red symbol often used to mean love.

media.credit: Internet Archive Book Images · No restrictions · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Internet Archive Book Images

questions.fun_fact: The Spanish deck has no queens: its face cards are a page, a knight on a horse and a king.

quality.notes: Hearts is the only French-deck symbol, so a player who knows the poker deck can spot the odd one out without knowing the Spanish deck. Spanish and Italian decks are everyday knowledge mainly in Spain, Italy and Latin America, which gives the question a regional tilt. Hint 2 nearly gives the answer away. Facts are correct (Latin suits by the 1370s; sota, caballo, rey).

revision.reason: Replaced hint 2, which pointed to the poker deck, with a vaguer clue about the real suits.

hints: These old suits had already reached Europe by the late 1300s.
The odd one out comes from the French-style deck used for poker.
It's a red symbol often used to mean love.

questions.description: An analogy all about who lives inside what.
questions.question: A room is to a house as a chess square is to a…?
hints: Think about what a room is part of.
A square is one small part of something bigger.
It has 64 of them, in black and white.

media.credit: Shixart1985 · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Shixart1985

questions.fun_fact: A chessboard has 64 squares, but if you count every square of every size on it, there are 204.

quality.notes: All four options are 'Chess ...', so only 'board' fits the part-of-whole idea and the question becomes very easy. Outside the options, a town square is part of a city too. The description is flat. The 204-squares fun fact is correct and nice.

revision.reason: Tied the square to chess in the question so the clue only fits a chessboard.

previous.question: A room is to a house as a square is to a…?

questions.fun_fact: In 1988, computer scientists proved that the first player can always win Connect Four with perfect play.

quality.notes: Accurate: Milton Bradley 1974, solved in 1988 by Allen and Allis. Othello is a good disc-based distractor. Hint 3 works across languages ('Vier gewinnt', '4 en raya').

questions.description: Keep a straight face: this question has an unbeatable hand.
questions.question: In poker, what is the best hand you can get without wild cards?
hints: It's so rare that many players never get one in their whole life.
It's made of the ten, jack, queen, king and ace.
All five cards are of the same suit, and the name sounds like a king or queen.

media.author: Jerom Gerard

questions.fun_fact: The chance of being dealt a royal flush in five cards is about 1 in 650,000.

questions.description: A drum solo that nobody bought tickets for.
questions.question: If you forget to drink water on a hot day, I may come and throb behind your forehead. What am I?
hints: I'm a kind of pain.
I sit higher up than your neck.
A glass of water and some rest often make me go away.
questions.fun_fact: The brain itself has no pain sensors: headache pain comes from the muscles, blood vessels and nerves around it.

quality.notes: 'Behind your forehead' in the question nearly gives it away, which is acceptable at level 1. Hint 2 settles it. The fun fact is true.

questions.description: A brain that simply files things in a different drawer.
questions.question: Dyslexia is common, often runs in families, and has nothing to do with intelligence. What does it mainly make harder?
hints: It shows up most at school, in a certain kind of lesson.
Its name comes from Greek words meaning “difficulty with words”.
Books can feel like a puzzle.

media.credit: Michael Coghlan from Adelaide, Australia · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Michael Coghlan from Adelaide, Australia

questions.fun_fact: Many successful people have dyslexia, and special fonts with heavier letter bottoms were designed to make reading easier for them.

quality.notes: Reads like a school or health fact rather than something surprising. Doing math is a good distractor (that would be dyscalculia). The hint about the Greek origin is correct. The fun fact is fine, though how well these fonts work is debated.

questions.description: The invisible thing everyone in the house fights about.
questions.question: Your tablet at home shows a symbol like a fan of curved lines. What does that symbol stand for?
hints: It needs no cable at all.
Guests often ask for its password.
Without it, videos at home often stop loading.

media.credit: Shixart1985 · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Shixart1985

questions.fun_fact: Wi-Fi travels by radio waves, a lot like the ones a radio uses.

quality.notes: A dry everyday question. Other signal symbols are also curved lines (the contactless-payment and broadcast icons), but the setting on a home tablet makes Wi-Fi clear. Hint 2 (the guest password) is close to giving the answer, which is acceptable for hint 2 at this level.

A new search is not allowed, so the media needs another search, for example "child using tablet" or "tablet computer on sofa", with no Wi-Fi symbol on the screen. No suitable picture found for this question.

questions.description: It leans like a bored teenager against a wall, but it still has a day job.
questions.question: The Leaning Tower of Pisa in Italy was built for the cathedral next to it. What was its job?
hints: Many churches around the world have a tower with the same job.
Its job is to be heard, not to be looked at.
It used to call people to church with a loud ding-dong.

media.credit: Lucarelli · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Lucarelli

questions.fun_fact: The tower started to lean while it was still being built, in the 1100s, because the ground under it is soft.

quality.notes: Many players can reason that a tower next to a cathedral is a bell tower, so 8 is probably too high. The wide shot of Pisa cathedral square is fine; the bells are hardly visible.

questions.description: Grab the idol and run, because the monkeys are not happy about it.
questions.question: In which year did the phone game Temple Run come out?
hints: It is played by swiping on a touchscreen.
It became a hit a few years after the first iPhone came out.
It came out in the same year as the full release of Minecraft.

media.credit: Amitabha Gupta · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Amitabha Gupta

questions.fun_fact: Temple Run was made by a tiny studio run by a married couple.

quality.notes: The release year of a phone game is a minor date that nobody can work out, which is exactly what the house style warns against. Hint 2 (“a few years after the first iPhone”) rules out 2007, and hint 3 ties it to Minecraft's release year, which few players know. A dry question. 2011 and the Minecraft fact are correct.

questions.description: A game where gravity is the boss and you are just the assistant.
questions.question: “I'm a wooden board full of walls and holes. You turn two knobs to tilt me and guide a little ball past the holes.” What am I?
hints: There are no flippers and no buttons.
If you tilt too far, the ball drops into a hole and you start again.
You have to find the path from start to finish.

media.credit: Shixart1985 · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Shixart1985

questions.fun_fact: Wooden tilting mazes have been sold for more than 75 years and are still a classic test of steady hands.

quality.notes: Children in many countries meet the tilt-maze toy less often today, and the name “labyrinth game” is not universal, so it is a bit harder than 4. A marble run is a reasonable distractor but clearly different.

questions.description: He has an identity crisis, and honestly, who can blame him?
questions.question: In Toy Story 4, Bonnie makes a toy with googly eyes and pipe-cleaner arms. What was his main part made for?
hints: He keeps saying he is trash, not a toy.
Bonnie found his main part in a trash can at kindergarten.
It's half spoon and half fork.

media.credit: Shixart1985 · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Shixart1985

questions.fun_fact: Forky is voiced by actor Tony Hale, and Toy Story 4 won the Oscar for Best Animated Feature.

quality.notes: It shares the answer text with q-2484 (chopsticks are for eating food), but the fact is different. The question wording is a little convoluted (“his main part”).

questions.description: Signing your toys: the oldest way to say “mine”.
questions.question: In the first Toy Story film, whose name is written on the sole of Woody's boot?
hints: It was written in a child's wobbly handwriting.
He is a boy with a little sister.
He grows up and goes to college in Toy Story 3.

media.credit: CactusLn · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: CactusLn

questions.fun_fact: In early plans for the film, Woody was a ventriloquist's dummy, not a cowboy doll.

quality.notes: A small risk: the “toy cowboy boot” search could return Woody merchandise with “Andy” on the sole.

questions.description: A family that hasn't aged a single day in more than 35 years.
questions.question: You're watching the longest-running cartoon series in US TV history, and the dad yells “D'oh!”. Which show is it?
hints: It first aired as a full series in 1989.
The whole family has yellow skin.
The son is called Bart.

media.credit: JIP · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: JIP

questions.fun_fact: Homer's “D'oh!” was added to the Oxford English Dictionary in 2001.

quality.notes: The record and “D'oh!” together make it very easy, and the scenario framing adds little. The “US TV history” framing is fine because the show is known worldwide. The Simpsons appears in several candidates (tv-series-1, sweets-and-chocolate-4), but they ask different facts.

questions.description: A theater full of felt, googly eyes and hands where they shouldn't be.
questions.question: Which of these characters is NOT from The Muppet Show?
hints: The Muppet Show stars puppets made by Jim Henson.
The odd one out comes from a British animation studio.
He's a clay animal who lives on a farm.

media.credit: Andre Riemann · CC BY-SA 2.5 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Andre Riemann

questions.fun_fact: Jim Henson made the first Kermit in 1955 from his mother's old coat and a ping-pong ball cut in half.

quality.notes: Facts are right, including the Kermit 1955 story. Shaun the Sheep is famous worldwide and the Muppets are less known outside the US, so kids can get it by elimination: about 6. A 'puppet theater stage' search could find a Muppet-style picture, but that wouldn't point to the odd one out.

questions.description: Some kids skip a grade; this one skipped about four.
questions.question: The Big Bang Theory got a spin-off about one of its characters as a 9-year-old genius in Texas. Who is he?
hints: In the grown-up show, he has his own fixed spot on the couch.
He knocks three times on a door and says the person's name each time.
His famous catchphrase is “Bazinga!”.

media.credit: Preply.com Images · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Preply.com Images

questions.fun_fact: Jim Parsons, who played grown-up Sheldon, was also the narrator of Young Sheldon.

quality.notes: Correct, and Jim Parsons did narrate Young Sheldon. The Big Bang Theory is a US sitcom, though it was shown worldwide. Young teens know it less than the rating assumes, so 8 is closer than 7. The title 'Young Sheldon' is well known, which makes it easy for adults.

questions.description: A genius with a very big head and very bad ideas.
questions.question: I'm a mad scientist with a big N on my forehead, and my mutant bandicoot escaped from my lab. My islands lie off which country?
hints: My bandicoot's name is Crash.
A real bandicoot is a marsupial, like many animals in that country.
It's also home to kangaroos and koalas.

media.credit: Shixart1985 · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Shixart1985

questions.fun_fact: Crash Bandicoot first came out in 1996 on the original PlayStation.

quality.notes: Correct: Neo Cortex and the Wumpa Islands off Australia. Several candidates also have Australia as the answer, but each asks a different fact. Hint 2 (marsupials) already points strongly to Australia.

questions.description: The snowy playground where gravity gets a workout twice per trick.
questions.question: In Olympic snowboarding, riders do tricks in a giant U-shaped snow channel. What is it called?
hints: Riders go up one wall, flip in the air, and land back down to reach the other wall.
Skateboarders ride the same shape, built from wood or concrete.
Cut a big tube in two along its length and you get this shape.

media.credit: Benh LIEU SONG (Flickr) · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Benh LIEU SONG (Flickr)

questions.fun_fact: Olympic halfpipe walls are about 6.7 m (22 ft) tall, and top riders fly several meters above the edge.

quality.notes: The distractors are good: real snowboard and freestyle events. 'U-shaped' plus hint 2 and hint 3 make it easy to reason out. The fact itself is a bit dry. The description is clumsy rather than funny. Decorative media is the right choice here.

questions.description: Spiritual music that can outlast a movie, with enough clapping to fill a stadium.
questions.question: Qawwali singers clap and chant for hours. Gospel is to Christianity as qawwali is to…
hints: It is most popular in Pakistan and northern India.
A performance builds slowly from calm to a joyful, trance-like peak.
The same faith gave the world the whirling dervishes.

media.credit: Niranjan Arminius · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Niranjan Arminius

questions.fun_fact: Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan, the king of qawwali, also recorded with Western stars such as Peter Gabriel.

quality.notes: Correct: qawwali is Sufi devotional music, and Nusrat recorded with Peter Gabriel. The opening sentence ('Singers clap and chant a qawwali.') is clumsy. The distractors are strong: Sikhism and Hinduism from the same region. Hint 3 (whirling dervishes) nearly gives it away, which is allowed.

revision.reason: Replaced hints 1 and 2, which pointed to Islam, and tightened the first sentence.

previous.question: Singers clap and chant a qawwali. Gospel is to Christianity as qawwali is to…
hints: Its most famous singer was Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan.
The songs, often in Urdu or Persian, praise God and holy saints.

questions.description: Four kinds of voices walk into a church, and one of them is an impostor.
questions.question: You join a classic four-part choir. Which of these is NOT one of its four parts?
hints: Usually two parts are sung by women and two by men.
One real part is named after an Italian word meaning “to hold”.
Choir music often names the four parts with the letters S, A, T and B.

media.credit: Namwanje Sauyah · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Namwanje Sauyah

questions.fun_fact: Russian church choirs have special singers called oktavists, who sing a whole octave below a normal bass.

quality.notes: Solid SATB question. Minor issue: some men's four-part choirs (TTBB) are written with a baritone part, but 'classic four-part choir' clearly means SATB. Hint 3 (SATB) nearly gives away the answer, which is allowed for hint 3. The tenor/'to hold' link comes from Latin tenere by way of Italian, so it's acceptable. Most adults can work this out, so 10–11 fits.

questions.description: Pop music where a single letter does all the heavy lifting.
questions.question: In the music style J-pop, what does the “J” stand for?
hints: The letter names where the music comes from, not a sound or a rhythm.
Its cousin K-pop uses the same naming trick.
Its biggest stars fill stadiums in Tokyo.

media.author: PinkBeachPlanet

questions.fun_fact: The name “J-pop” is often said to have been coined by the Tokyo radio station J-Wave in the late 1980s.

quality.notes: Hint 2 (anime) almost gives the answer away. The fun fact about J-Wave is hedged with 'often said', which is fine. The question is a bit dry: it just decodes a letter. 'Jungle' as a distractor works because it is a real genre.

revision.reason: Replaced hints 1 and 2, which gave the answer away, and cut the made-up music-app setting.

previous.question: You're listening to J-pop on a music app. What does the “J” stand for?
hints: It's a pop style from Asia.
Many anime theme songs belong to this style.
Its biggest stars fill stadiums in Tokyo.

questions.description: The final chapter, and it's not a quiet one.
questions.question: It is the last book of the Bible, and it tells of four horsemen and the end of the world. Which book is it?
hints: It is in the New Testament.
It is said to have been written by a man named John on the Greek island of Patmos.
Its Greek name, “Apocalypse”, is now a word for disaster.

media.credit: Digital image courtesy of the Getty's Open Content Program. · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Digital image courtesy of the Getty's Open Content Program.

questions.fun_fact: In everyday talk “apocalypse” means a giant disaster, but the Greek word just means “uncovering”.

quality.notes: The facts are correct. Young teens around the world are unlikely to know the four horsemen, so 9 fits better than 8. The 'old Bible open pages' image could show a book heading, which is a small risk. Psalms as a distractor is slightly weak because people know it as poetry.

questions.description: A phone call to the sky, with no signal needed.
questions.question: People often do it with their hands together or kneeling on a mat. They talk to God, and Christians often end it with “Amen”. What is it?
hints: You can do it alone, quietly, anywhere.
Many children do it before bed or before a meal.
Saying grace before a meal is a short way of doing it.

media.credit: Narek Avetisyan /Narek75/ · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Narek Avetisyan /Narek75/

questions.fun_fact: “Amen” is a Hebrew word meaning roughly “so be it”, and it is used by Jews, Christians and Muslims.

quality.notes: 'They talk to God' makes this very easy, which is fine for kids, so the real level is about 2. It's a fairly plain definition question. The question text is a bit long with three facts.

questions.description: Four letters, dozens of countries and a lot of very serious meetings.
questions.question: “I am NATO, born in 1949 in Washington, D.C., and today I have more than 30 member countries.” What am I?
hints: My members are countries from both sides of an ocean.
I was created as the Cold War began.
My members promise that an attack on one of them is an attack on all.

media.credit: Robert Lamb · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Robert Lamb

questions.fun_fact: NATO's headquarters is in Brussels, Belgium.

quality.notes: The facts are correct; the North Atlantic Treaty was signed in Washington on April 4, 1949. 'More than 30 members' is safe even if membership changes. The question is a fairly dry definition, and many adults know NATO is a military alliance, so about 10.

questions.description: Brains and fruit have more in common than your lunchbox lets on.
questions.question: The cortex is to the brain as which part is to an orange?
hints: Picture the brain as if it were a piece of fruit.
Think about where the cortex sits on the brain.
You remove it before eating the fruit.

media.credit: John Campbell · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: John Campbell

questions.fun_fact: The cerebral cortex is only about 2 to 4 mm thick, but its folds give it a surface about the size of a pillowcase.

quality.notes: The analogy is a bit loose: you don't remove the cortex the way you peel an orange. Still, peel is clearly the best 'outer layer' answer, and cortex literally means 'bark/rind', which makes it satisfying. The pillowcase comparison in the fun fact is a common approximation. q-0566 (epicarp/peel) asks a different fact.

revision.reason: Replaced hint 2, which gave the answer away, with an indirect hint.

hints: Picture the brain as if it were a piece of fruit.
It's the outer layer.
You remove it before eating the fruit.

questions.description: Faces have their own way of telling you how they feel.
questions.question: Sad is to cry as funny is to…
hints: It's something you do with your mouth.
Clowns try to make you do it.
Ha ha ha!

media.credit: Robert Cudmore · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Robert Cudmore

questions.fun_fact: Laughter is contagious: just hearing someone laugh makes your brain get ready to laugh too.

quality.notes: A clean level-1 analogy. The clown image hints at laughing a little, which is fine at this level.

questions.description: Faces are like books, if you know how to read them.
questions.question: Look at this child. Which feeling is the child most likely showing?
hints: It's not a happy feeling.
There are tears on the face.
Hugs often help with this one.

media.credit: David Shankbone · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: David Shankbone

questions.fun_fact: Newborn babies cry a lot, but they usually don't make real tears until they are a few weeks old.

The essential image needs a new search, e.g. "sad crying child". No suitable picture found for this question.

revision.reason: Changed only the essential image query so a new search can find a clearly sad, crying child.

media.note: A clear photo of a child (not a baby) crying with a sad face and visible tears.

questions.description: A face so famous it gets stacked, popped and crunched every day.
questions.question: I have a big mustache and a bow tie, and my smiling face is on tall tubes of stacked potato snacks. Who am I?
hints: My snacks all have the same curved shape.
My snacks come in a can, not a bag.
My last name is the name of the snack itself.

media.credit: Simon Mortimer · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Simon Mortimer

questions.fun_fact: Pringles are made from dried potato flakes pressed into a saddle shape, so they stack neatly without breaking.

quality.notes: The mascot is usually called Mr. P; Julius Pringles is the official full name, which few people know. Still, the snack description makes it clear. Colonel Sanders and Mr. Monopoly also have mustaches, but the potato tubes settle it. Kids will need to reason from the brand to the name.

questions.description: A soap that sounds like a picnic in the Mediterranean.
questions.question: Palmolive soap got its name from the palm oil and olive oil it was made with. In which decade was it first sold?
hints: It was first made by a soap company in Milwaukee, USA.
Your great-great-grandparents could have washed with it.
It came out just a couple of years before 1900.

media.credit: Ввласенко · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ввласенко

questions.fun_fact: Palmolive first came from a soap company in Milwaukee, USA, in 1898, and soon became the best-selling soap in the world.

quality.notes: A minor product launch date is pure memorisation and is hard to reason towards, which the house style discourages. Hint 1 and the fun fact repeat the same Milwaukee fact. 'Best-selling soap in the world' is a period claim and only loosely verified.

questions.description: Some names are made of words, and some are made of people.
questions.question: William Boeing started his airplane company in 1916. In which US city?
hints: The city is on the Pacific coast of the USA.
The city is famous for its many gray, rainy days.
Its famous tower is called the Space Needle.

media.credit: Julian Herzog (Website) · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Julian Herzog (Website)

questions.fun_fact: William Boeing's father came from Germany, where the family name was spelled Böing.

quality.notes: The description is about names made of people, which doesn't match a question about a city. The question is a fairly dry, US-centred fact, though Boeing is known worldwide. Hint 3 uses the Space Needle, the subject of q-1964 (also Seattle), but this question asks a different fact. The fun fact about Böing is correct.

revision.reason: Replaced hint 2, which named the state, with a vaguer clue about the rain.

hints: The city is on the Pacific coast of the USA.
It is in Washington State, not Washington, D.C.
Its famous tower is called the Space Needle.

questions.description: Three letters that deliver packages and keep a secret.
questions.question: The three letters in the name of the delivery company DHL stand for what?
hints: It started in San Francisco in 1969.
Today it belongs to the German post office, but it wasn't born in Germany.
D, H and L stand for Dalsey, Hillblom and Lynn.

media.credit: Sue elias · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Sue elias

questions.fun_fact: DHL began by flying important shipping papers between San Francisco and Honolulu.

quality.notes: 'Three famous postmen' and 'Three cargo planes' are weak distractors. Young teens are unlikely to know this, though adults may reason that companies are often named after their founders, so it is harder than 7. Hint 3 spells out the founders, which is allowed.

questions.description: A motorcycle that took one look at the sea and jumped in.
questions.question: “Jet Ski” is really a brand name of the Japanese company Kawasaki. In which decade did it start selling them?
hints: It came after the Beatles' first records.
It was after the first Moon landing in 1969.
Disco music was at its peak then.

media.credit: Rept0n1x · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Rept0n1x

questions.fun_fact: The Jet Ski was invented by Clayton Jacobson II, an American motorcycle fan who wanted to ride on water.

questions.description: Black dress, serious face, and a crown that looks a size too small.
questions.question: Who is this British queen?
hints: She became queen at just 18.
Her husband was Prince Albert.
A period of British history is named after her.

media.note: A well-known photograph or portrait of Queen Victoria as an older woman, with no name or caption visible.
media.credit: Alexander Bassano · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Alexander Bassano

questions.fun_fact: Victoria had nine children, and her grandchildren married into royal families all over Europe.

quality.notes: Recognising a face from a photo is a dry task, and many teens can't tell Victoria from Queen Alexandra or Queen Mary. Commons portraits often carry captions, so the note asking for no name or caption matters. The description's small crown is a clue for experts. Close to q-2522 (Victorian era) only through hint 3, so it is not the same fact.

questions.description: An art show that is in no hurry to come back.
questions.question: A city holds a biennial art festival, and the last one was in 2023. In which year is the next one?
hints: “Bi” means two.
It isn't twice a year, it's once every so many years.
Add two to 2023.

media.credit: Guangywatchwii · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Guangywatchwii

questions.fun_fact: The Venice Biennale, held every two years since 1895, is one of the oldest and most famous art shows in the world.

quality.notes: This is basically a vocabulary test of the word "biennial" plus some arithmetic, so it is dry. The prefix "bi-" works in Spanish and German too (bienal, Biennale), so it travels. Hint 1 makes it trivial, and hint 3 states the method.

questions.description: Grandpa trusted this thick little book more than the weather report on TV.
questions.question: Atlas is to maps as almanac is to…
hints: Farmers used to read it to know when to plant.
A new one comes out every year.
It lists dates, holidays, Moon phases and sunrise times.

previous.feedback: The question only works within its four options: “Which of these cities has no Disney theme park named after it?” fits almost every city in the world, so the clue doesn't point to Rome in the real world. The house style rules out this kind of “which of these” question. It needs to be rewritten as a positive question that points to one answer in the real world (for example, which European capital has a Disney park named after it → Paris). That would be a different question, so I left the fix empty.

revision.reason: The “which has no park” wording only worked among its four options, so I turned it into a positive real-world question: which European capital has a Disney park named after it (Paris), with new hints to match.

questions.question: Watch this male betta fish spread his fins and gill covers wide. Why does he do this?

wrong_answers: To cool down in warm water
To catch tiny bits of food
hints: Bettas come from rice paddies and ponds in Southeast Asia.
He often does it when he sees another male, or his own reflection.
Bettas are also called “fighting fish”.

media.note: Short clip of a male betta (Siamese fighting fish) flaring: fins spread and gill covers open, ideally at a mirror or another male.
media.credit: Lile044280310 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Lile044280310

questions.fun_fact: Male bettas build floating nests of bubbles to keep their eggs safe.

quality.notes: "To get ready for sleep" and "to cool down" are weak distractors, so most players can reason to the answer, which makes it easier than 6. A betta-flaring video is likely on Openverse or Commons, but less certain than a photo.

questions.description: Leg day for animals that don't have any legs.
questions.question: Watch these salmon leap up a waterfall. Where are they trying to get to?
wrong_answers: A deep lake to sleep through winter
The beach where they lay eggs
hints: They are swimming upstream, away from the sea.
They are going there to lay their eggs.
Many find it by smell, years after they left.

media.note: Short clip of salmon leaping up a waterfall or rapids during their upstream migration.
media.credit: Ron Shawley · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ron Shawley

questions.fun_fact: Salmon can find their home stream after years at sea, partly by remembering how it smells.

quality.notes: Some sockeye salmon spawn near lakes, but "to sleep through winter" keeps that option wrong. The "colombia" lens doesn't fit a base question. Salmon-leaping footage is easy to find.

questions.description: This swimmer finds its snack before the snack knows it's been found.
questions.question: Watch this shark. It can notice a tiny bit of blood in the water from far away. Which sense does it use?
hints: It uses two small holes on its snout.
It works even when the shark can't see anything.
You use your nose for it.

media.note: Short clip of a shark swimming calmly, ideally with its snout visible; no blood, no feeding or attack.
media.credit: SystemBuilder · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: SystemBuilder

questions.fun_fact: Shark nostrils are only for smelling, not breathing: sharks breathe through their gills.

quality.notes: "Notices a tiny bit of blood from far away" leans on a popular exaggeration, though it is broadly true. Taste is a sensible distractor.

questions.description: The hardest workers in your fish tank never get a thank-you.
questions.question: Look at this aquarium filter sponge. Which living things, too small to see, live in it and help keep the water clean?
hints: There can be millions of them in one small sponge.
They turn the fish's waste into less harmful stuff.
Some of them can make you sick, but these ones are the good kind.

media.credit: Ofkun · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ofkun

questions.fun_fact: That's why fish keepers rinse filter sponges in old tank water instead of tap water: chlorine can kill the helpful bacteria.

quality.notes: Snails and shrimp are well-known tank 'cleaners', so they work as distractors, but small worms and other tiny creatures really do live in filter sponges, which weakens 'tiny living things' a little. Most 11-year-olds don't know about the bacteria cycle in a filter, so difficulty 5 is too low. The photo of a sponge doesn't help much. Hint 3 nearly gives the answer. The topic is useful but a bit dry.

revision.reason: Changed “tiny living things” to “too small to see” so worms no longer fit.

previous.question: Look at this aquarium filter sponge. Which tiny living things live in it and help keep the water clean?

questions.description: Every family tree has to start somewhere, and this one starts with her.
questions.question: She came right after Chaos, gave birth to the sky god Uranus and to the mountains, and was mother of the Titans. What does her name, Gaia, mean?
hints: In Greek myths, she was there before almost anyone else.
She gave birth to the sky, so she can't be the sky.
Words like “geography” and “geology” come from her name.

media.credit: Carole Raddato from FRANKFURT, Germany · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Carole Raddato from FRANKFURT, Germany

questions.fun_fact: Scientist James Lovelock named his Gaia hypothesis after her, picturing the whole planet as one self-regulating living system.

quality.notes: The question is about 170 characters, too long to read in one breath. The three-fact family tree mostly fills space before the real question. Many players know Gaia = Earth from pop culture. Hint 3 ('geo') nearly gives it, which is allowed.

questions.description: When Mom is sad, the whole planet gets the cold shoulder.
questions.question: Demeter was the goddess of the harvest. When her daughter was taken to the underworld, she grieved and nothing grew. Which natural cycle did this myth explain?
hints: Her daughter came back for part of every year.
When the daughter returned, flowers bloomed again.
Think of winter turning into spring.

media.credit: Yann Forget · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Yann Forget

questions.fun_fact: Her daughter Persephone had to spend part of each year below because she ate a few pomegranate seeds in the underworld.

quality.notes: 'Nothing grew' points strongly to the seasons, so players can reason it out, which is good. Hint 3 is very strong but allowed.

questions.description: A warning about trash-talking a goddess in her own specialty.
questions.question: A young weaver boasted she was better than Athena, wove a flawless tapestry in their contest, and was turned into a creature that weaves forever. Which animal group is named after her?
hints: Scorpions and ticks belong to this group too.
Its members have eight legs.
The weaver's name was Arachne.

media.credit: Reem Al-Kashif · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Reem Al-Kashif

questions.fun_fact: For its weight, spider silk is stronger than steel.

quality.notes: 'Insects' is a good trap for people who think spiders are insects. Players need to know the term 'arachnids', so this is slightly harder than 7. It is close to q-3438 (Arachnophobia, fear of spiders), but that question asks a different fact.

previous.feedback: The picked picture has an unsuitable licence (pd-us-only: PD-1923, PD-US-expired).

revision.reason: The chosen picture's licence only covers the US, so I set a new media query to get a different weaving picture.

media.credit: Pierce, C.C. (Charles C.), 1861-1946 · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Pierce, C.C. (Charles C.), 1861-1946

questions.description: Some kids build sandcastles; she got a much bigger construction job.
questions.question: In the Percy Jackson books, Annabeth Chase dreams of becoming an architect. Which place is she chosen to redesign?
hints: She is a daughter of Athena, goddess of wisdom and crafts.
She gets the job after the big battle against Kronos.
It's the mountain where the Greek gods live.

media.credit: Jebulon · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jebulon

questions.fun_fact: Rick Riordan first made up the Percy Jackson stories as bedtime tales for his son.

quality.notes: Fans of the books know it. Others can reason from 'architect' and 'gods'. Hint 3 rests on q-0142's fact (the mountain of the gods) but asks something different.

questions.description: Half party animal, and the other half is a party animal too.
questions.question: I love music, wine and dancing, and I travel in a noisy band behind the god Dionysus. I look mostly human, but with animal ears and a tail. What am I?
hints: I'm often shown with a beard and a snub nose.
Unlike a centaur, I walk on just two legs.
Phil, Hercules' grumpy trainer in the Disney film, is one of us.

media.credit: Dorieo · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Dorieo

questions.fun_fact: After serious tragedies, ancient Athenians watched comic “satyr plays”, with a chorus dressed as satyrs goofing around.

quality.notes: Many people picture satyrs with goat legs (often mixed up with fauns or Pan). 'Animal ears and a tail' fits the classical look but may confuse some players. The Phil hint is fun.

questions.description: Some record holders went decades without meeting a nail clipper.
questions.question: Your fingernails are made of a tough protein called keratin. Three of these are too. Which one is NOT?
hints: Keratin things are made by the skin; the odd one out is not.
It is hard because it holds a lot of calcium.
Your skeleton is made of it.

media.credit: Nenad Stojkovic · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Nenad Stojkovic

questions.fun_fact: Rhino horns are made of keratin too, so a rhino's horn is closer to your fingernails than to a deer's antlers.

quality.notes: Players can reason that bones are inside the body. Hint 1 makes it quite easy. The question text is clean and short, despite the 'scenario' axis.

questions.description: A skyscraper that has been in more movies than most Hollywood stars.
questions.question: This is the top of a famous skyscraper that was the tallest building in the world for about 40 years. Which building is it?
hints: It was finished in 1931.
It stands in New York City.
Its name comes from a nickname of the state of New York.

media.note: Close-up of the top tiers and spire of the Empire State Building, without any sign or caption showing its name.
media.credit: Oleg Yunakov · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Oleg Yunakov

questions.fun_fact: The Empire State Building was built in just over a year, about 410 days.

quality.notes: 'Tallest for about 40 years' points to the Empire State Building for anyone who knows the record. Burj Khalifa and Petronas are easy to rule out for people who know their dates. Wikimedia Commons very likely has a clear photo of the spire. Hint 3 is strong but allowed.

questions.description: A magic cup that's pickier than a cat at dinnertime.
questions.question: You're in the Great Hall as the Goblet of Fire picks Cedric Diggory as Hogwarts champion. In the end, how many champions' names come out?
hints: The tournament is called the Triwizard Tournament.
One name came out that nobody expected.
Cedric, Fleur, Viktor… and Harry.

media.credit: Ludovic Bertron from New York City, Usa · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ludovic Bertron from New York City, Usa

questions.fun_fact: Cedric was played by Robert Pattinson, who later became Batman.

quality.notes: Hint 3 counts the four names, which is allowed for the last hint. The 'You're in the Great Hall' setup is a bit of padding.

questions.description: She can stand on her hands longer than most people can stand in line.
questions.question: B-girls battle each other in crews, judges score them, and in 2024 they competed at the Olympics for the first time. What does a b-girl do?
hints: It's one of the four elements of hip hop.
You need strong arms and a smooth floor for it.
Spins, freezes and footwork are her tools.

media.credit: Ibex73 · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ibex73

questions.fun_fact: The first Olympic gold for b-girls went to Ami from Japan at Paris 2024.

quality.notes: 'B-' and 'crews' point fairly strongly to breaking. Ami Yuasa's 2024 gold is correct. q-3435 also links crews to breakdancers, but it asks a different fact.

questions.description: A song written with a smile, a microphone and a long list of complaints.
questions.question: Rappers write one to attack a rival, the rival often answers with one of their own, and Colombia's Shakira made a famous one with Bizarrap in 2023. What is it called?
hints: It's personal: the song is aimed at someone.
Kendrick Lamar and Drake traded several of these in 2024.
Its name uses a slang word for insulting someone.

media.credit: A S M Jobaer · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: A S M Jobaer

questions.fun_fact: Kendrick Lamar's “Not Like Us”, a song aimed at Drake, won the Grammy for Song of the Year in 2025.

quality.notes: Facts check out: the Shakira/Bizarrap session was aimed at Piqué, and Not Like Us won Song of the Year in 2025. q-1536 covers the same Bizarrap session from another angle (the series' name), so it is not the same fact. 'Freestyle' and 'remix' are weaker distractors for adults.

questions.description: Your leg kicks the doctor, and legally it wasn't your fault.
questions.question: A doctor taps just below your knee, and your leg kicks before your brain gets involved. Where does the signal turn around?
hints: It is part of your nervous system.
It runs down the middle of your back.
It sits inside your backbone.

media.credit: Samir at English Wikipedia · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Samir at English Wikipedia

questions.fun_fact: Because the signal takes a shortcut, a reflex can happen in a few hundredths of a second, faster than you can decide anything.

quality.notes: The heart and the hip bone are weak distractors. 'Before your brain gets involved' points strongly at the spinal cord. q-2287 asks what the spinal cord is made of, which is a different fact.

questions.description: The day the world's biggest search page was more fun than your homework.
questions.question: In May 2010, the Google logo became the first Doodle you could play right on the search page. Which game's 30th birthday did it celebrate?
hints: It's an old arcade game from Japan.
Its name comes from a Japanese word for the sound of munching.
Its yellow, round hero eats dots in a maze while colorful ghosts chase him.

media.credit: John Snyder · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: John Snyder

questions.fun_fact: People reportedly spent millions of hours playing that Doodle, so many that some called it a big loss of work time.

quality.notes: The facts check out: the playable Pac-Man Doodle ran on May 21, 2010. Hint 2 (maze, ghosts) all but gives the answer away. Kids know Pac-Man, but the Doodle and the 2010 → 1980 reasoning make it a bit harder than 6.

revision.reason: Replaced hint 2, which gave the answer away, with the name-origin clue and made hint 3 the strongest.

hints: It's an old arcade game from Japan.
You move through a maze, chased by colorful ghosts.
The hero is yellow, round and always eating dots.

questions.description: The greeting that starts business deals and ends sports matches.
questions.question: Which hand do people in most countries use to shake hands?
hints: Both people use the same one.
Most people write with this hand.
It's the opposite of left.

media.credit: Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office

questions.fun_fact: One of the oldest pictures of a handshake is carved in stone and is almost 3,000 years old, from ancient Assyria.

quality.notes: "Whichever hand is free" is a weak, joke-like distractor. The question is very plain and fits a languages category poorly. A decorative business-meeting photo may show a handshake, which would reveal the right hand. Hint 3 nearly states the answer.

questions.description: The language behind the music that gets every wedding guest dancing.
questions.question: At many weddings in India and Pakistan, bhangra songs in Punjabi fill the dance floor. About how many people speak Punjabi?
hints: It is spoken in two big countries.
It has more speakers than Germany has people.
It's well over 100 million, but far less than a billion.

media.credit: Shamrock23 · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Shamrock23

questions.fun_fact: Punjabi is written in two different scripts: Gurmukhi in India and Shahmukhi, based on Arabic letters, in Pakistan.

quality.notes: Speaker counts vary by source: about 113–125 million native speakers, about 150 million in total. "About 130 million" is a fair middle value, and the options are far enough apart. As a bare population estimate it is a little dry.

questions.description: The very first word of every phone call.
questions.question: You say it when you meet someone, when you answer the phone and when you wave. What kind of word is “hello”?
hints: You say it at the start, not the end.
It's friendly.
“Hi” means the same thing.

media.credit: Nancy Adams · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Nancy Adams

questions.fun_fact: Thomas Edison made “hello” the way to answer the phone, while the phone's inventor, Alexander Graham Bell, wanted people to say “ahoy”!

quality.notes: Very plain and close to obvious. "A sorry" is an awkward option. The Edison "hello" / Bell "ahoy" story is widely repeated but simplified. The description ("first word of every phone call") points straight at a greeting.

questions.description: An antelope that treats every bush as a hurdle race.
questions.question: You're on safari and a frightened impala leaps away. About how far can it jump in one leap?
hints: It's farther than a human long jumper's best of about 9 m.
It's longer than a giraffe is tall.
It's about the length of two cars, nose to tail.

media.credit: Bernard DUPONT from FRANCE · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Bernard DUPONT from FRANCE

questions.fun_fact: Impalas can also jump about 3 m (10 ft) high, sailing right over other impalas.

quality.notes: Solid. Impalas leap about 10 m long and 3 m high, and all the hints are accurate.

questions.description: The farmyard's loudest choir member is warming up.
questions.question: Listen! Which farm animal makes this sound?
hints: It usually lives in a big group called a flock.
Farmers often use dogs to herd it.
It says “baa”.

media.note: A clear recording of a sheep bleating (baa), no other animals.
media.credit: earthcalling · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: earthcalling

questions.fun_fact: Sheep can recognize the faces of other sheep, and even of people, for years.

quality.notes: Clear essential audio that is easy to find on Freesound. Calling the sheep the "loudest" choir member is a bit odd, but harmless.

background.credit: David Howard · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
background.author: David Howard

revision.reason: Rewrote hints 1 and 2: the old hint 1 was useless and the old hint 2 gave the answer away.

hints: It lives on a farm.
It has a thick, woolly coat.
It says “baa”.

questions.description: A big furry giant who never says no to a snack.
questions.question: A brown bear belongs to three of these groups. Which one does it NOT belong to?
hints: Think about what brown bears eat.
They catch salmon, but they also love berries.
This group eats only plants.

media.credit: Alexander Malkhasyan · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Alexander Malkhasyan

questions.fun_fact: Before their winter sleep, brown bears can eat so much that they gain over 1 kg (2 lb) a day.

quality.notes: "Good swimmers" is less crisp as a category than the others, but brown bears do swim well. The description's "snack" hints that bears eat everything.

questions.description: Some rhinos get a haircut for their own safety, horn included.
questions.question: Some African parks cut off rhinos' horns, fit them with trackers and guard them day and night. Who are they protected from?
hints: Think about why the horn is cut off.
What they're after is the horn itself.
These people hunt animals against the law.

media.credit: Garst, Warren, 1922-2016, photographer · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Garst, Warren, 1922-2016, photographer

questions.fun_fact: A rhino's horn is made of keratin, the same stuff as your fingernails, and it slowly grows back after being cut.

quality.notes: Tourists and photographers are not plausible threats that would call for cutting off horns and guarding rhinos day and night, so Poachers stands out. The topic is close to q-3315 (poachers and ivory), but the fact asked is different.

questions.description: Time flies when you're having fun, so let's see how well you know its pieces.
questions.question: A day is to hours as an hour is to…
hints: A day is split into 24 hours.
Each hour is split into 60 smaller parts.
The long hand of a clock counts them.

media.credit: Sridhar Rao · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Sridhar Rao

questions.fun_fact: We split hours into 60 minutes thanks to the ancient Babylonians, who loved counting in sixties.

quality.notes: The analogy depends on the next unit down, so a few players might argue for "Seconds". It works, but it feels like a school drill.

questions.description: A tiny sign with a big job in every math class.
questions.question: Taking away is to minus as putting together is to…
hints: 2 apples and 3 apples make 5 apples.
It is the opposite of minus.
Its sign looks like a little cross.

media.credit: Rhetos · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Rhetos

questions.fun_fact: The + sign probably comes from the Latin word “et”, which means “and”.

quality.notes: Very simple and dry. The fun fact about "et" is a nice touch.

questions.description: Counting practice for anyone with lots of fingers and a little patience.
questions.question: How many tens make one hundred?
hints: Count by tens: 10, 20, 30…
Keep going until you reach 100.
It is the same as the number of fingers on your hands.

media.credit: Rhetos · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Rhetos

questions.fun_fact: We probably count in tens because humans have ten fingers.

quality.notes: This is a plain school arithmetic fact, so fun is low. The description's "lots of fingers" points toward 10. A base-ten blocks image may show a hundred-flat split into ten rods, which helps a little.

questions.description: Long before museums had gift shops, they had goddesses in charge of inspiration.
questions.question: The word “museum” comes from the Muses, the Greek goddesses of the arts and sciences. How many Muses were there?
hints: Each Muse had her own art, such as poetry, history, dance or astronomy.
There were fewer Muses than months in a year.
It is three times three.

media.credit: Electron08 · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Electron08

questions.fun_fact: A “museum” first meant a “place of the Muses”: the famous Museum of Alexandria in Egypt was a center of study, not a hall of exhibits.

quality.notes: Good link between the word and the myth. The Graces candidate is a different fact. Young teens may find it slightly harder than 9.

review.feedback: This asks the same fact as related q-3773 (“In Greek mythology, how many Muses were there?”) and q-3418 (Clio's sisters: how many Muses in all?). The pool should keep only one of the three. This version is arguably the best, because it links the Muses to the word “museum”, so consider dropping the other two instead.

previous.feedback: This asks the same fact (how many Muses there were, answer 9) as q-3418 and q-3773, which are already in the pool. Keep only one of the three. This one, with its link to the word "museum", is arguably the strongest, so consider dropping the other two in its favor.

questions.description: An Ice Age giant that still steals the show in museum halls.
questions.question: You stand next to a life-size mammoth model in a museum. What covered the real animal's body?
hints: Mammoths lived where it was very cold.
They needed to stay warm in the snow.
Think of a very shaggy dog.

media.credit: Shadowgate from Novara, ITALY · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Shadowgate from Novara, ITALY

questions.fun_fact: Mammoths frozen in the ground in Siberia have been found with their hair still on, after tens of thousands of years.

quality.notes: q-0303 identifies a mammoth skeleton, which is a different fact. Fine.

questions.description: The only part of the museum where touching things is welcome.
questions.question: In many museums, the exit leads you through a room selling postcards, posters and toy dinosaurs. What is it called?
hints: You need money in this room.
Parents often try to walk through it quickly.
You can buy a souvenir here.

media.credit: AndyScott · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: AndyScott

questions.fun_fact: Many museums use their gift shops to help pay for keeping their collections safe.

quality.notes: The question basically describes a gift shop, so it's very easy. Hint 2 is funny. Decorative media is reasonable here.

questions.description: An architect who loved geometry so much he gave Paris a pyramid without a pharaoh.
questions.question: Which of these museums was NOT designed by I. M. Pei, the architect of the Louvre Pyramid?
wrong_answers: Museum of Islamic Art in Doha
Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in Cleveland
hints: The odd one out is known for flowing curves, not Pei's sharp geometry.
Its architect was the first woman to win the Pritzker Prize.
It was designed by Zaha Hadid, in Italy's capital.

media.credit: Benh LIEU SONG (Flickr) · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Benh LIEU SONG (Flickr)

questions.fun_fact: I. M. Pei was already in his 80s when he designed the Museum of Islamic Art in Doha, and he was 91 when it opened in 2008.

quality.notes: Facts check out: MAXXI is by Zaha Hadid, and Pei designed the Doha, Cleveland and Luxembourg museums. Mudam is obscure, and the odd-one-out format is dry. Fair for experts.

questions.description: Proof that you can change the world before you finish your homework.
questions.question: I spoke up for every girl's right to go to school, and at 17 I became the youngest Nobel Prize winner ever. Who am I?
hints: I won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2014.
I'm from Pakistan, and I later studied at Oxford University.
My first name starts with M, and the United Nations celebrates my birthday, July 12, as a special day.

media.credit: Shaguftakarim · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Shaguftakarim

questions.fun_fact: Malala heard she had won the Nobel Peace Prize while she was sitting in a chemistry class at school.

quality.notes: Strong distractors. Hint 3's "starts with M" is a giveaway, but that is allowed in hint 3. Probably slightly harder than 6 for kids.

questions.description: A scientist who reads the diary of a cousin who's been gone for a very long time.
questions.question: Svante Pääbo won the 2022 Nobel Prize for reading Neanderthal DNA. About when did the last Neanderthals die out?
hints: Until the end, they lived at the same time as early modern humans in Europe.
It was during the last Ice Age, long before the pyramids.
The famous Lascaux cave paintings in France are less than half as old as this.

media.credit: Gary Todd · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Gary Todd

questions.fun_fact: Thanks to Pääbo, we know most people outside Africa carry about 1 to 2 percent Neanderthal DNA.

quality.notes: The facts check out (about 40,000 years; Lascaux is about 17,000 years old). '40 million years ago' is too easy to rule out. Gets close to q-1738 (Neanderthals) but asks a different fact.

questions.description: The tiny power plant in your pocket that ran out of charge right before this question.
questions.question: The lithium-ion battery inside phones won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2019. How many scientists shared that prize?
hints: One of the winners was Akira Yoshino from Japan.
Another one, John Goodenough, was 97 years old.
A Nobel Prize can never be shared by more than this many people.

media.credit: MKFI · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: MKFI

questions.fun_fact: John Goodenough was 97 when he won, the oldest Nobel Prize winner ever.

quality.notes: Counting the winners is a dry fact, and most players will just guess. Hint 3 (the three-person limit) nearly gives the answer away, which is allowed for hint 3. Goodenough is still the oldest Nobel winner, so the fun fact holds.

questions.description: The world's biggest animal eats one of the smallest, by the bucket.
questions.question: They look like tiny shrimp, swim in huge swarms, and blue whales eat tons of them every day. What are they called?
hints: They are only about as long as your finger.
Penguins and seals love eating them too, especially near Antarctica.
Their name has just one syllable and starts with K.

media.credit: AWeith · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: AWeith

questions.fun_fact: A single blue whale can swallow millions of krill in just one day.

quality.notes: Hint 3 depends on the English spelling (one syllable, starts with K). It works in German and roughly in Spanish ('kril'), but it is tied to language. Sardines don't really fit the 'tiny shrimp' clue.

questions.description: A fancy word you can drop at dinner to sound like a scientist.
questions.question: What does the word “aquaculture” mean?
wrong_answers: Growing plants in water without soil
hints: It's a job, and a very old one.
Salmon pens in Norway and oyster beds in France are examples.
“Aqua” means water, and the second part is the same as in “agriculture”.

media.credit: Ximonic (Simo Räsänen) · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ximonic (Simo Räsänen)

questions.fun_fact: People in China were raising carp in ponds more than 2,000 years ago.

quality.notes: A plain 'what does this word mean' question; it is dry. The word has close cognates in other languages, so it translates. The description is generic. Young teens probably find it harder than 6. The hydroponics distractor is good.

questions.description: A picture that spins your brain like a washing machine.
questions.question: In cartoons and films, a spinning spiral like this one is the classic tool of which kind of performer?
hints: The performer wants you to stop thinking for yourself.
Their audience often ends up acting like a chicken on stage.
They swing a watch and whisper “You are getting sleepy…”.

media.note: A plain black-and-white spiral pattern, with no person or text.
media.credit: Jahobr · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons

questions.description: A packing material that is mostly made of nothing at all.

questions.description: A red rock with a secret that only comes out when things heat up.

questions.description: Banks love paperwork almost as much as cats love cardboard boxes.

hints: It proves that you agree and that it's really you.

previous.question: At the bank, complete: a PIN is to a bank card as a ___ is to a paper form.

questions.description: A green-eyed monster gets a job in the army, and that never ends well.

hints: The city was a rich sea power in Shakespeare's time.
The city was a republic led by a ruler called the Doge.
It is the Italian city of canals and gondolas.

media.credit: Cornelis Ketel · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Cornelis Ketel

questions.fun_fact: The full title of the play is “Othello, the Moor of Venice”, and it is where jealousy is called “the green-eyed monster”.

quality.notes: Rated too low. Knowing that Othello serves Venice is adult general culture, not something a 13–16-year-old knows, so 9 is too easy. Hints 1 and 2 also fit Genoa, which had both sea power and a Doge. That's acceptable for hints, but they don't narrow much.

questions.description: A prince with big questions and a very small sense of humor.
questions.question: Which of these lines is NOT from the play in which a prince asks “To be, or not to be”?
wrong_answers: “Neither a borrower nor a lender be.”
hints: The prince in this play lives in a castle in Denmark.

It goes on: “and all the men and women merely players.”

media.author: Mojmir Churavy

questions.fun_fact: “To be, or not to be” comes from “Hamlet”, Shakespeare's longest play: performed in full, it lasts about four hours.

quality.notes: This depends on familiarity with English-language quotes. 'Brevity is the soul of wit' and the Polonius line are much less known in translation, which is a mild Anglo bias. Matching four quotes to plays is closer to 13. Calling Hamlet a prince with a 'very small sense of humor' is off, since he's famously witty. q-2162 is also about Hamlet, but it asks a different fact.

questions.description: A Danish prince, a British actor and a golden statue walk into Hollywood.

hints: During the war, Olivier had already made a color Shakespeare film, “Henry V”.

It came out the same year London hosted the Olympic Games.

quality.notes: Facts check out: Hamlet came out in 1948, Henry V in 1944 in color, and the Best Actor first is correct. The problem is that the question is really just a release year. Players can only reason towards it through the hints (after the war, London Olympics), so it comes close to the 'minor date' kind of hard question. The trivia about the film is more interesting than the year itself.

questions.description: Every superhero needs a city with enough rooftops to brood on.

hints: It's a city in North America.

media.author: Neil Theasby

quality.notes: Hint 2 (the fruit nickname, the Big Apple) already gives it away for most players. q-2691 also has Gotham, but it asks a different fact. The Gotham village image is a nice, safe choice.

revision.reason: Replaced hint 2, which pointed to the Big Apple, with a geography hint.

hints: It's a city in North America.
Its nickname as a fruit is more famous today.
It's home to the Empire State Building and Times Square.

questions.description: The floors that never get a view, and never complain about it.

Drivers go down a ramp and look for an empty space there.

media.author: Nadine Shaabana nadineshaabana

quality.notes: Underground floors also hold machinery and storage, and some hold shopping malls or metro links, so 'most often' parking is fair but not airtight. All three distractors are rooms where people live or learn, which are clearly wrong without windows, so they are weak. The question is a bit dry.

questions.description: Clark Kent's office came with a giant spinning globe, but sadly no phone booth.

That newspaper's name is close to the name of the film's newspaper.
