quality.notes: Anyone who knows the Daily Planet can guess 'Daily News' from the name alone. Apart from that this is film-location trivia, and young teens rarely know it; I'd put it closer to 12 than 10.

questions.description: The only fire your parents will let you play with.
questions.question: People often reply with this emoji under a new song or a cool photo. What do they mean?
hints: It's a compliment.
Think of the flames as energy and excitement, not danger.
They're saying it's amazing, the best.

media.note: The fire emoji (🔥) on its own, large and clear, e.g. the Noto Emoji version from Wikimedia Commons.

questions.fun_fact: The fire emoji joined the official emoji set in 2010, together with many of today's favorite emojis.

quality.notes: Young kids without phones may not know the slang meaning, so it's slightly harder than 3. The essential emoji image is easy to find.

review.feedback: No suitable picture found for this question.

previous.feedback: None of the media candidates shows the fire emoji (🔥). The question depends on this essential image, and no new search is allowed. Use a file that shows only the fire emoji, for example Commons "File:Emoji u1f525.svg" (Noto) or the Twemoji fire SVG. No suitable picture found for this question.

revision.reason: The fire emoji exists on Commons, so I made the query the exact Noto file name so the essential image can be found.

media.note: The fire emoji (🔥) on its own, large and clear, e.g. the Noto Emoji version from Wikimedia Commons.

questions.description: This face looks at you the way you look at a fresh, hot pizza.
questions.question: What feeling does this emoji usually show?
hints: It's a happy feeling.
Look closely at its eyes.
You'd send it when you see the cutest puppy ever.

media.note: The smiling face with heart-eyes emoji (😍) on its own, large and clear, e.g. the Noto Emoji version from Wikimedia Commons.

questions.fun_fact: The heart-eyes emoji became part of the official emoji set in 2010.

quality.notes: Very easy and fine for kids, but not very surprising. The fun fact is a dry date.

review.feedback: Hint 1 ("It's a happy feeling.") gives the answer away, because love is the only happy feeling among the options (anger, fear, boredom). Change it to something vague that doesn't rule out options, or swap one wrong answer for another positive feeling such as joy or surprise, as long as it is clearly wrong for the heart-eyes face. Also, the slot has no media candidates, so it needs a new search. No suitable picture found for this question.

previous.feedback: None of the six candidates works as the essential heart-eyes emoji image. Candidates 1 and 3 show nude models with body paint, which isn't family-friendly. 2 and 6 are photos of people, 4 is an anatomy engraving, and 5 is a fanged cartoon face, not the emoji. A new search isn't allowed, so the slot needs a clean emoji graphic such as the Noto or Twemoji version of U+1F60D. No suitable picture found for this question.

revision.reason: The heart-eyes emoji exists on Commons, so I made the query the exact Noto file name so the search avoids unrelated photos.

media.note: The smiling face with heart-eyes emoji (😍) on its own, large and clear, e.g. the Noto Emoji version from Wikimedia Commons.

questions.description: Your thumb's favorite workout: two quick reps on someone's vacation photo.

media.author: Japanexperterna.se

quality.notes: It depends on knowing one app, and many 6-year-olds don't use Instagram, so it's probably a bit harder than 2. It's a plain recall question.

revision.reason: Replaced the description, whose word “love” gave away the heart.

previous.description: Love at first tap... well, second tap.

questions.description: A patch so famous it went to the Moon and back.

wrong_answers: The crew's names were kept secret
There was no room left for names
The crew had not been chosen yet
hints: The decision came from the three astronauts themselves.
About 400,000 people helped make the Moon landing possible.
They wanted the patch to stand for the whole team, not just three men.

media.credit: Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: NASA Kennedy Space Center / NASA or National Aeronautics and Space Administration

questions.fun_fact: The lunar module was named “Eagle” after the bird on this patch.

quality.notes: The answer is the only noble-sounding option, and it is longer than the rest. The distractors are fairly easy to rule out, so players can reason their way to the answer.

questions.description: The only car with a parking spot 384,000 km from the nearest garage.
questions.question: On Apollo 17, a fender on this Moon car broke and it sprayed dust everywhere. What did the astronauts fix it with?

questions.fun_fact: Three Moon cars from Apollo 15, 16 and 17 are still parked on the Moon today.

questions.description: Staring at nothing for ten days has never paid off so well.

media.author: Astroval1

questions.description: When galaxies collide, nobody bothers calling the insurance company.
questions.question: When two galaxies collide, what share of their stars crash head-on into another star?
hints: Galaxies are mostly empty space.

The stars slip past each other like ghosts.

media.author: NASA, ESA, and the Hubble Heritage Team (STScI/AURA)-ESA/Hubble Collaboration

questions.fun_fact: Stars almost never hit each other, but the gas clouds do, which can spark a burst of new stars.

questions.description: Its eyes see more colors than yours do, and its temper is just as colorful.
questions.question: This colorful sea creature is a mantis shrimp. What does it use its two big front arms for?

The question names the animal, so the image works more like an illustrative one than an essential one. Clear photos of peacock mantis shrimp are easy to find on Commons.

questions.description: Named after an insect, but the legs never got the memo.

questions.description: Proof that you were great, even if no one gave you anything shiny.

questions.description: A name that sounds like a party in a fruit bowl.
questions.question: Tutti Frutti is a name for juices, ice cream flavors and even a rock song. It comes from Italian. What does it mean?
hints: Think of the mix, not one single fruit.
“Tutti” is a word you also hear in music, when the whole orchestra plays together.
Tutti means “everyone.”

media.credit: Andy Li · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Andy Li

questions.fun_fact: In 1955 Little Richard made “Tutti Frutti” a huge rock and roll hit, and its opening shout “A-wop-bop-a-loo-bop” became famous worldwide.

quality.notes: The question lives on a foreign phrase. Spanish speakers (todo/frutas) and Italian speakers find it much easier than others, so it does not travel equally to all languages. Hint 3 almost gives the answer.

review.feedback: This base question only asks what an Italian phrase means, so it depends on one language. Played in Italian it gives itself away, and in Spanish "tutti frutti" reads almost as "todas las frutas", so it doesn't travel (international angle / clue-translation case). It can't be fixed without becoming a different question, so drop it or replace it.

questions.description: A company whose mascot is a white bear, which is odd, since it comes from nowhere near the North Pole.
questions.question: Grupo Bimbo started in Mexico in 1945, has a white bear mascot and sells in more than 30 countries. It is the world's biggest maker of what?
hints: Its products are found on the breakfast table.
Its best-known product comes in soft, sliced loaves.
Think of buns, muffins and sandwiches.

media.credit: Jeses · CC BY-SA 2.5 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jeses

questions.fun_fact: Grupo Bimbo also owns famous bakery brands in other countries, such as Sara Lee and Entenmann's in the United States.

quality.notes: Bimbo is a household name in Latin America and Spain but little known in Germany and elsewhere, so this tilts the base bundle towards the Spanish-speaking world. The question is long, with three facts packed in. The description repeats the white-bear fact from the question and is not very funny.

questions.description: A round cracker with wavy edges and a name with a backstory.
questions.question: Ritz crackers came out in the United States in 1934. Their name was chosen to make people think of what?
hints: In 1934, during the Great Depression, money was short for most families.
The name was taken from a famous place.
The name comes from the Ritz, a world-famous grand hotel in Paris.

media.credit: Corn cheese · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Corn cheese

questions.fun_fact: The Ritz hotels in Paris and London were named after Swiss hotel owner César Ritz.

quality.notes: This is a US brand, and the question depends on knowing what "Ritz" suggests in English. Families outside English-speaking countries find it hard. Hint 3 ("ritzy") is English wordplay and nearly gives the answer. The description is flat.

revision.reason: Made hint 2 vaguer, and replaced hint 3, which relied on the English word “ritzy”, with one that works in any language.

hints: In 1934, during the Great Depression, money was short for most families.
The name borrows from famous grand hotels in Paris and London.
When something is “ritzy,” it is very fancy.

questions.description: A banknote so fancy most people have never touched one.

hints: It's bigger than the notes most people carry around.

questions.description: The first trick a basketball coach teaches, right after “please stop shooting from half-court.”

questions.description: Defense so close, the other team checks if you're still there in their sleep.

questions.description: Bounce, bounce, bounce... and no, it's not a kangaroo.

questions.description: Before you can win an argument, you have to go shopping for parts.

media.author: Marc-Lautenbacher

questions.description: It's free, it weighs nothing, and you can still steal one.

questions.description: It snows on your pancakes, and nobody needs a coat.

hints: It tastes exactly as sweet as what you stir into tea.

questions.description: Your vacation photos, your music and your saved game all secretly speak the same very short language.

media.author: Rob Swystun from Winnipeg, Canada

questions.description: It eats crumbs all day and still never offers to do the dishes.

media.author: Jirka Matousek from Brussels Taipei Hong Kong Singapore Prague Shenzhen

questions.description: Two identical sisters, one mansion, and a lot of confused servants.

media.author: Basile Morin

questions.fun_fact: “La usurpadora” was so popular that Televisa remade it in 2019.

quality.notes: A base question about a Latin American telenovela from 1998 leans on Spanish-world knowledge (International angle). It was a hit in some regions, but families elsewhere and young teens mostly won't know it, so 8 is too low. Hint 1 rules out Venezuela and hint 2 (Marimar) also leans on telenovela knowledge.

review.feedback: This overlaps too much with approved q-2171, which describes the Paola Bracho twin plot and asks for the title “La usurpadora”. This question names the title together with the twins Paola and Paulina, so seeing one gives the other away. On top of that, a new base question about a 1998 Latin American telenovela depends on Spanish-world TV knowledge that families elsewhere mostly don't have (International angle), and hint 2 (“Marimar”) depends on the same knowledge.

questions.description: Rags in the first episode, riches in the last, and lots of crying in between.

hints: It's named after a fairy-tale heroine.
Before her happy ending, she spends her days cleaning for her stepfamily.
She loses a glass slipper at the ball.

media.author: Kalinka261015

questions.fun_fact: Stories like Cinderella's exist in hundreds of versions around the world; one of the oldest, written down by the Greek writer Strabo, is about a girl named Rhodopis in Egypt.

questions.description: A wave you can't surf, but you can binge-watch it.

media.author: Strategia Music

"TV dramas, pop bands" points strongly to K-pop. Beijing media coining "Hanliu" around 1999 is the usual account, slightly simplified. Related to q-3073 (K-drama analogy), but a different fact.

questions.description: Tennis courts have more lines than a school notebook, and every single one of them matters.

questions.fun_fact: The service line is exactly 21 feet (6.40 m) from the net, on every tennis court in the world.

quality.notes: The description is factually wrong: the foot-fault rule is about the baseline, not the service line. The facts in the question itself are correct (21 ft = 6.40 m; baseline at 11.89 m). As a pure estimate it is rather dry.

revision.reason: Fixed the false claim in the description, and replaced hint 2, which gave away the distance through the baseline.

previous.description: A line nobody may step over while serving, no matter how excited they get.
hints: It is a little more than half the distance from the net to the baseline.

It's a bit more than three tall adults lying head to toe.

His last name starts with M.

questions.description: The only sports event where the snack is almost as famous as the players.

questions.description: Tennis shrank in the wash and moved onto the dining table.

questions.description: A sea with so many neighbors that it's never short of beach parties.

questions.description: This chubby swimmer naps on rocks and never needs shoes.

questions.fun_fact: Seals can sleep in the water, floating upright with just their nose above the surface.

questions.description: A floating city so big it has its own post office and barber shop.

questions.description: A suit with so much silver on it, it jingles before it even sings.
questions.question: Mariachi bands wear the charro suit, with silver buttons and a huge hat. Who first wore this kind of outfit in Mexico?

quality.notes: It's about Mexico, but mariachi is known worldwide, so that's acceptable. Players can reason towards the answer. “Silver miners” is a nice trap. The mariachi image is safe.

questions.description: Fluffy, famous, and secretly part of a family nobody expects.
questions.question: The Inca prized alpaca wool. Which of these animals is NOT a close relative of the alpaca?
hints: The alpaca's family is not the family you'd guess from its wool.

questions.fun_fact: Alpacas, llamas and vicuñas belong to the camel family, and the vicuña's wool is one of the most expensive in the world.

quality.notes: Llama and vicuña are clearly relatives, so it comes down to sheep or camel. That makes it easier than 9. Hint 3 nearly gives it away, which is allowed. Calling the camel a “close” relative is fair, since they're in the same family.

questions.description: Every hero needs a sidekick, even a musical one.
questions.question: Thor is to his hammer as Miguel from Coco is to his…
hints: Miguel dreams of becoming a musician.

questions.description: Trains have rooms too, just narrower and much wobblier.
questions.question: Restaurant is to dining car as hotel room is to…
hints: Think about what you do in a hotel room at night.
This car is used on long trips through the night.
It has bunk beds and pillows.

media.author: Pudelek

questions.fun_fact: On some night trains, like those across Russia, passengers sleep on board for several nights in a row.

quality.notes: Solid but plain analogy, so fun is modest. The description's “rooms” nudges toward the sleeping car, though only slightly.

questions.description: Hundreds of tons of train, and it's all standing on tiptoe.
questions.question: About how big is the spot where one steel train wheel actually touches the rail?
hints: Hard steel on hard steel barely squashes at all.
It's much smaller than a dinner plate.
It's often compared to the size of a small coin.

media.author: darkday.

questions.fun_fact: That tiny contact spot is one reason trains roll so easily: a car tire touches the road over an area many times bigger.

quality.notes: The contact patch is usually described as coin-sized, about 1–2 cm², so the answer holds as an order of magnitude. The options are spaced by powers of ten, which keeps it fair. Hint 3 nearly gives it away, which is allowed.

questions.description: The part of the train that everyone waves at.
questions.question: What is this part of a train for?
hints: It's usually at the front of the train.

Without it, the other cars could not move.

media.author: CEphoto, Uwe Aranas

questions.fun_fact: Some very long trains need several locomotives, and some even have extra ones pushing at the back.

quality.notes: Easy question that works as essential media; a locomotive photo is easy to find. It's a little dry.

questions.description: A bridge in the Alps that runs straight into a cliff and isn't sorry about it.
questions.question: In Switzerland, trains cross the curved stone Landwasser Viaduct and go straight into a tunnel in a cliff. When was it built?
hints: It was built from stone arches, not modern concrete.
It was built for a mountain railway in eastern Switzerland.
It was finished right at the start of a new century.

media.author: Kabelleger / David Gubler (http://www.bahnbilder.ch)

questions.fun_fact: The Landwasser Viaduct was built without scaffolding from the ground: workers used steel towers that rose with the stone piers.

quality.notes: Built 1901–1902, so “Around 1900” holds. The fun fact about building without ground scaffolding is roughly right: masonry rose around steel towers. The question is a bit long, and it's a date guess, so fun is moderate. Hint 1 (“stone arches”) already rules out the later options.

questions.description: The one day a year when a new boss starts work with a million people watching.
questions.question: In 1985 and again in 2025, freezing cold moved the US president's swearing-in ceremony indoors. Where was it held instead?
hints: The ceremony didn't have to travel far from its usual spot.
This building is where Congress meets.
It's a round hall right under a famous white dome.

media.author: Bert Kaufmann from Roermond, Netherlands

questions.fun_fact: In 1985 it was so cold for Ronald Reagan's swearing-in that the big parade afterwards was cancelled too.

quality.notes: US-centric base question: it needs knowledge of US inauguration customs and Washington buildings that families elsewhere don't have. Facts check out: Reagan in 1985 and Trump in 2025 were sworn in in the Rotunda, and the 1985 parade was cancelled. Hint 2 makes it easy. It's a fairly dry civics fact.

review.feedback: This base question needs US-only civics knowledge: where a US inauguration moves when it's too cold, and which buildings in Washington could host it. Families outside the US have no way to know this or work it out, so it breaks the International angle. It would fit better in a US regional bundle, or should be replaced.

questions.description: Nine people who get the last word, and they never retire unless they want to.
questions.question: Its nine members are nominated by the president, serve for life and can strike down laws that break the US Constitution. What is it?
hints: It is one of the three branches of the US government.

Its members are called justices.

media.author: Chris Potter

questions.fun_fact: Its building has a basketball court on the top floor, nicknamed “the highest court in the land.”

quality.notes: Justices are nominated by the president but also confirmed by the Senate; “serve for life” is a simplification. This is US civics in a base question, though the court is fairly well known worldwide. Hint 3 (“justices”) gives it away. A gavel image is a bit off, since the Court doesn't use one. The fun fact is good.

questions.description: The most powerful desk in the world has its own room, and this is it.
questions.question: What is this famous room in the White House called?
hints: The president signs laws and meets world leaders here.

Its name comes from its egg-like shape.

quality.notes: The facts are correct (West Wing; the Resolute desk was Queen Victoria's gift in 1880). Commons very likely has clear Oval Office photos. The curved walls in the photo hint at the name a little. US-specific, but the room is known worldwide from films.

questions.description: A giant stone raft that's been sailing west since before the dinosaurs said goodbye.
questions.question: It carries most of a continent and half of the South Atlantic floor, and the Nazca Plate dives under its western edge. Which plate is it?
hints: Its eastern edge is a ridge running down the middle of the Atlantic Ocean.

media.author: Trougnouf (Benoit Brummer)

questions.fun_fact: The Andes are still rising, because the Nazca Plate keeps sliding under South America by a few centimeters every year.

quality.notes: Plate names are school knowledge, so this is fairly dry. The African Plate also carries a continent and half the South Atlantic floor, but the Nazca clue rules it out. Decorative volcano image is fine because an Andes image would hint at the answer. Hint 3 nearly gives it away, which is allowed.

questions.description: The beach under your towel is going on a very, very slow trip.
questions.question: You're on a beach in Hawaii, which rides on the Pacific Plate. About how far does this plate move in one year?
hints: You could never feel it, but over millions of years it adds up.

questions.fun_fact: Because the plate slides over a fixed hot spot, Hawaii's volcanoes form a chain, with the oldest islands farthest to the northwest.

questions.description: Earth has a very hot heart, and no one has ever taken its temperature in person.
questions.question: About how hot is it at the very center of Earth's core?
hints: It's much hotter than melted lava.

quality.notes: Estimates for the core run about 5,000–6,000 °C, so 'about 5,000' is acceptable. Hint 1 already rules out two options. Difficulty 5 is too low: few 11-year-olds know this order of magnitude.

review.feedback: This repeats approved q-2868 ("Earth's inner core is a ball of solid iron and nickel. About how hot is it?" → About 5,000 °C): it asks the same fact with the same answer. Drop it, or swap it for a different fact about volcanoes.

questions.description: The short program: like a job interview, but on blades and with sparkles.

questions.fun_fact: Both scores are added together, so a great free skate can lift a skater from far behind to a medal.

questions.description: Four people in a speeding sled, and only one of them gets to decide where it goes.

questions.description: A race in circles where everyone leans like they're chasing the last cookie.

questions.description: A tiny village where the local hobby seems to be collecting gold medals.

media.author: Ximonic, Simo Räsänen

questions.fun_fact: Tärnaby has only a few hundred people, yet it has produced several world champions in Alpine skiing.

quality.notes: The facts check out: Stenmark won 86 World Cup races, and Pärson grew up in Tärnaby, won world titles in all five events and took slalom gold in Turin in 2006. This is real specialist trivia, so 15 fits. Fun is 3 because the village-link fact suits ski fans and will be fairly dry for most families. Distractors are fine: two are Swedish slalom skiers and one is Croatian, and an expert can still tell them apart.

questions.description: A factory where the boss literally makes money all day long.
questions.question: It is a factory with heavy presses, it stamps a country's coins, and ancient Rome's stood by the temple of Juno Moneta. What is it called?
hints: It's a place where things are made, not where they're kept.
Huge machines press designs onto blank metal discs there.
Brand-new coins come straight from it, before anyone has spent them.

media.credit: Trainholic · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Trainholic

questions.fun_fact: The words “money” and “mint” both come from Juno Moneta, because Rome's coin workshop stood next to her temple.

quality.notes: This is correct, and the Juno Moneta origin of both "money" and "mint" makes a nice fun fact. Hint 1 already rules out "treasury" and "vault", which is fine for a hint. The question works in every language: the Spanish "Casa de la Moneda" and the German "Münze" still name a place, so nothing depends on English wordplay.

questions.description: The loudest alarm clock nobody wanted to hear.
questions.question: During World War II, a wailing siren in a city sent people running to shelters. What was it warning them about?
hints: Thick walls and city gates were no help against this danger.
People hid in cellars and underground stations.
The danger came from the sky.

media.credit: CC BY-SA 2.5 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: No machine-readable author provided. Stevage assumed (based on copyright claims).

questions.fun_fact: When the danger was over, a long steady tone called the “all clear” told people it was safe to come out.

quality.notes: Distractors are 3: an enemy submarine is not a plausible threat to a city, and "spies" would never set off a siren, so a team can easily reason down to planes and tanks. Fun is 3 because it is a fairly plain school-style fact, though the "all clear" fun fact helps. Late in the war, sirens also warned of V-1 flying bombs, but "enemy planes" is still clearly the intended answer. The tone is fine because the question asks about the warning, not about suffering.

questions.description: Some words are so old they've outlived every kingdom that ever spoke them.

Some Jain monks sweep the path in front of them so they don't step on insects.

questions.fun_fact: Gandhi's birthday, October 2, is now the United Nations' International Day of Non-Violence.

With the options, most adults can work it out, so it's closer to a 12 than a 14. It's a fairly dry definition question.

revision.reason: Replaced the description and hint 2, which pointed to non-harm, with neutral versions.

previous.description: A rule so gentle it even watches where it puts its feet.
hints: The idea goes back more than 2,000 years in India.
Gandhi made it the heart of his protests.
Some Jain monks sweep the path in front of them so they don't step on insects.

questions.description: A very old master who says nothing happens by accident, not even this question.

I'm the only tortoise among the masters in “Kung Fu Panda”.

questions.fun_fact: Oogway's famous line says today is a gift, “that is why it is called the present”.

questions.description: Most birds carry this spring-loaded piece of gear under their feathers.

previous.description: Every bird carries this spring-loaded piece of gear under its feathers.

questions.description: It stands so still you'd think it was a garden ornament.

questions.description: Some body parts like to travel in pairs; one prefers to go solo.

questions.fun_fact: People can live perfectly well without their appendix, and doctors remove it in hundreds of thousands of people every year.

questions.description: The windows to the soul come in a surprisingly small range of curtains.

media.author: Jennifer Woodard Maderazo

questions.description: Your mouth's own built-in sauce, served with every meal.
questions.question: Which of these does spit NOT do?
questions.answer: Cool your body down when you're hot

hints: You make it all day long without even noticing.

media.author:
U.S. Department of Agriculture

questions.description: Un espanto que dejó la mina, pero no la mala costumbre de ensuciarlo todo.

Que lleva un tarro en la cabeza
hints: El nombre está hecho de dos palabras pegadas.

media.author: The authors are unknown, but the pictures belong to the Alliance for Responsible Mining.

previous.feedback: Verificación de datos: uncertain. I could not verify the details. A source confirms the Patetarro exists in Antioquian folklore, but it says he throws worms at crops out of revenge. I found nothing on the tarro-for-a-leg story, the abandoned mines, or the trail that dries plants.

questions.description: Un vecino del monte que se viste con todo lo que el viento tumba al suelo.

previous.feedback: The fun fact (the Hojarasquín helps lost walkers find their way) is unverified by the fact check, and I can't confirm it either. Replace it with a supported fact, e.g. that peasants describe him as a tree-like man seen as the conscience of nature. Verificación de datos: uncertain. The answer is supported: the legend says he punishes those who harm the forest and its animals. I found nothing saying he helps lost walkers find their way, so the fun fact is unverified.

revision.reason: Replaced the unverified fun fact about helping lost walkers with the reviewer's suggested fact (a tree-like man seen as the conscience of nature).

media.author: Cayambe

quality.notes: Canada stands out too clearly as the cold northern country. Hint 2 ("warm all year") is an overgeneralization, since high Andes peaks on the equator have snow. q-3329 is about the equator but asks its length, a different fact.

previous.feedback: Hint 2 ("Three of these countries are in South America or Africa") gives the answer away: anyone who knows Canada is in North America is left with only Canada, so it is as strong as hint 3. Replace it with a vague hint, for example that the equator crosses two continents' rainforests, or that it passes through only 13 countries.

revision.reason: Replaced hint 2, which gave the answer away, with a vaguer hint about the rainforests the equator crosses.

questions.description: A promise so old it was first made in ancient Greek.
questions.question: New doctors often swear it at graduation. It is named after the Greek “father of medicine” and promises to help patients and keep their secrets. What is it?

quality.notes: Facts are right: the oath does include confidentiality, it is about 2,400 years old, and “first, do no harm” is not in the original wording. Distractors (3): “The Olympic Oath” is weak because it has nothing to do with doctors. “The Socratic Oath” is mostly there as a name that sounds alike. “The Aesculapian Oath” is the only strong distractor. Fun (3): fairly standard school-style general knowledge, and the question is a bit long with its three stacked facts. Anyone who links “father of medicine” to Hippocrates gets it at once, which is fine at this level. Hint 3 nearly spells out the answer, which is allowed. A medical graduation image is fine as decorative, though an illustrative image would also have been safe. Difficulty 10–11 seems right.

quality.notes: A good reasoning question. “Most likely” softens the claim enough. The scenario works as the clue itself, so it is fine.

questions.description: A breakup so famous it gets its own scenes in the movies.
questions.question: Because she had given him no heir, Napoleon divorced his first wife in 1809. Who was she?

questions.fun_fact: Napoleon kept divorce in his 1804 Civil Code; France banned it in 1816 and only brought it back in 1884.

revision.reason: Removed the inaccurate divorce-law clause and turned it into a direct question, as the reviewer asked.

questions.description: A pizza so big that the delivery driver needed a map and a nap.

media.author: McKay Savage from London, UK

questions.fun_fact: In 2008, Ecuador became the first country to write the rights of nature, Pachamama, into its constitution.

quality.notes: Similar in kind to q-4621 (Gaia = Earth), but a different culture and a different fact. Hint 1 makes it easy. The fun fact about Ecuador's 2008 constitution is correct.

previous.feedback: Hint 2 (“She is right under your feet”) gives the answer away: of Moon, Sun, Rain and Mother Earth, only the Earth is under your feet. The question also names “Pachamama”, which literally means “Mother Earth/World” (pacha = earth/world, mama = mother). That breaks the clue-translation rule: “mama” points straight to “Mother”, especially in Spanish (“Madre Tierra”). review.feedback: This base question depends on English words. Its main clue (cocoa and coffee "beans" share the answer's name) and hint 2 ("jelly beans") don't carry over to Spanish, where you'd say "granos de café/cacao", "frijoles" and "gomitas". Without them, a pod-grown seed that can be black, red or white could also be peas or lentils. Rebuild it around a clue that works in every language, such as the Mesoamerican origin of black or pinto beans, or retire it.

previous.feedback: This question overlaps with approved q-4038, which asks for Jack's beanstalk from the same fairy tale. Its central clue (Jack trades his cow for magic beans, and a giant lives at the top of the plant) is the same Jack and the Beanstalk fact, so seeing one question gives away the other. Without the fairy tale, "grows in a pod, black, red or white" also fits lentils and peas.

questions.question: In films, one small fire sets off every sprinkler in a building. In a real skyscraper, which sprinklers spray water when a fire starts?
questions.answer: Only those heated by the fire
wrong_answers: Only those on the burning floor
All those on the floors above
hints: There is no big switch that turns them all on.
Smoke alone does not set them off.
Each one waits until it gets very hot.

media.credit: Tony Webster · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Tony Webster

questions.fun_fact: Many sprinkler heads hold a tiny glass bulb of liquid that bursts at about 68 °C (155 °F), letting the water out.

quality.notes: Good myth-busting question. The fun fact is right: red bulbs burst at 68 °C (155 °F).

questions.description: A shopping-mall ride that never makes it onto the theme-park map.
questions.question: What is shown in this picture?
hints: You find it in shopping malls and airports.
You stand still and it takes you up.
It is a staircase that moves by itself.

media.note: A silhouette photo of an escalator, ideally with people standing on it, clearly showing the moving steps and handrail.
media.credit: Magdalena Roeseler · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Magdalena Roeseler

questions.fun_fact: The steps of an escalator flatten out at the top and bottom, then go back underneath in a loop.

quality.notes: Simple identification question. A silhouette may not clearly separate escalator from ladder or slide, and Commons may not have a clear escalator silhouette. A normal photo would be safer.

questions.description: Two buildings that always dressed alike.
questions.question: This old skyline shows two famous identical towers. What were they called?
hints: They opened in the early 1970s.
Each tower had 110 floors.
They were often called the Twin Towers.

media.query: World Trade Center twin towers silhouette skyline
media.note: A silhouette of the Lower Manhattan skyline before 2001 with the two flat-topped twin towers clearly visible; no text.
media.credit: 小林 良規 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: 小林 良規

questions.fun_fact: In 1974, the French artist Philippe Petit walked on a tightrope stretched between the two towers.

quality.notes: A sensitive subject (9/11): it asks only the name, but the playful “always dressed alike” sits uneasily. The Emirates Towers are not identical, and the Rockefeller Center is not a pair of towers, so those two distractors are weak. A pre-2001 silhouette with no text may be hard to find. Hint 2 (Lower Manhattan) almost settles it.

revision.reason: Replaced hint 2, which named New York, with the 110-floor fact.

hints: They opened in the early 1970s.
They stood in Lower Manhattan, New York.
They were often called the Twin Towers.

questions.description: A moon that can't decide between day clothes and night clothes, so it wears both.
questions.question: In Arthur C. Clarke's novel “2001: A Space Odyssey”, the Star Gate waits on this moon. Which group from Greek myth is its name taken from?
hints: This moon goes around Saturn.
Its namesake was the father of Atlas and Prometheus.
The biggest moon of Saturn is named after the whole group.

media.credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/Space Science Institute/Lunar and Planetary Institute · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: NASA/JPL-Caltech/Space Science Institute/Lunar and Planetary Institute

questions.fun_fact: Iapetus has a mountain ridge running around its middle that makes it look like a giant walnut.

quality.notes: Iapetus as the Star Gate moon is correct for the novel (in the film it is Jupiter). The question is roundabout: the 2001 detail only leads to a moon, and then it asks for the myth group. Once hint 1 says Saturn, the answer can be worked out, because Saturn's moons are named after Titans. It touches Titan topics (solar-system-2, q-0955) but asks a different fact. The description about the two-tone moon is great.

questions.description: A small moon that looks like it was glued together from leftover pieces.
questions.question: Miranda, the moon of Uranus with the tallest known cliff in the solar system, was discovered in 1948 by which astronomer?
hints: He was born in the Netherlands and later worked in the United States.
A year later, he also found Nereid, a moon of Neptune.
A belt of icy worlds beyond Neptune is named after him.

media.credit: NASA/JPL · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: NASA/JPL

questions.fun_fact: Nobody saw Miranda's giant cliff, Verona Rupes, until Voyager 2 flew past in 1986, almost 40 years after the moon was found.

quality.notes: Facts are correct (Miranda 1948, Nereid 1949, Verona Rupes). Knowing who discovered something is fairly dry. The year 1948 rules out Herschel and Huygens for experts, so it comes down to Tombaugh versus Kuiper.

questions.description: Some of the oldest items astronauts left on the Moon are still being used today.
questions.question: Apollo 11, 14 and 15 left these on the Moon. Scientists still use them to measure how the Moon drifts away about 3.8 cm (1.5 in) each year. What are they?
hints: They need no power at all, so they still work after more than 50 years.
Scientists time how long the light takes to come back to Earth.
You see your own face in one every morning in the bathroom.

media.credit: ESO/J. Girard (djulik.com) · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: ESO/J. Girard (djulik.com)

questions.fun_fact: So little light makes it back that most laser shots aimed at the Apollo mirrors return not a single particle of light to the telescope.

quality.notes: Strictly speaking they are retroreflectors (corner-cube prisms), but “mirrors” is fair for a general audience. Hint 3 nearly gives the answer away, which is allowed.

questions.description: These passengers flew around the Moon before any human, and nobody asked for their autographs.
questions.question: In 1968, the Soviet probe Zond 5 flew around the Moon and back. Its main passengers were the first animals ever to make that trip. What were they?
hints: They came back hungry and a bit lighter, but healthy.
They can go a long time without food or water.
They carry their home on their back.

media.credit: NASA · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: NASA

questions.fun_fact: The two tortoises reached the Moon three months before the first humans did, on Apollo 8.

quality.notes: The surprising answer works well. Dogs and monkeys are strong distractors because the Soviets famously flew dogs. Few adults know this fact, so it may be closer to 13 than 12, though the hints let players reason towards it. The other tortoise questions in the pool ask different facts.

questions.description: Fingers that work outside the space station need a little extra help.
questions.question: What do NASA spacewalk gloves like these have built into the fingertips?
hints: Astronauts can turn them on when their hands get cold.
They use electricity from the suit's battery.
They work a bit like a heated car seat.

media.note: Clear photo of a NASA spacewalk (EVA) glove on its own.
media.credit: NASA/Michael S. Hopkins · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: NASA/Michael S. Hopkins

questions.fun_fact: The rubbery fingertips also help astronauts feel what they are holding, even through the thick glove.

quality.notes: The photo is labeled essential but isn't really needed to answer; an illustrative image would fit better. Commons very likely has clear EVA glove photos. Players can guess heaters because space is cold. Hint 3 comes very close to the answer, which is allowed.

questions.description: Years of work, a huge budget, and the whole show lasted less than a minute.
questions.question: In 1996, the first Ariane 5 rocket left the launch pad and broke apart after about 40 seconds, with no one on board. What caused it?
questions.answer: A number too big for the software
wrong_answers: A bird flying into an engine
hints: The rocket's hardware was fine; the problem was in its code.
The code had been reused from the older, slower Ariane 4.
The rocket's speed value no longer fit in the space the program had for it.

media.credit: European Space Agency · Attribution · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: European Space Agency

questions.fun_fact: Ariane 5 later became a very reliable rocket and launched the James Webb Space Telescope in 2021.

quality.notes: The distractors are clever (the Mars Climate Orbiter units mix-up, the Challenger seal), so an expert can tell them apart. The answer wording is a bit informal compared with the others. An illustrative image of an Ariane rocket would have been safe; decorative isn't needed.

questions.description: The universe's own pasta machine.
questions.question: In this animation, a star gets too close to a black hole and is stretched into a long, thin stream. Why does this happen?
questions.answer: Gravity pulls its near side much harder than its far side
wrong_answers: The black hole spins it around like a top
The star's own heat melts it into strings
The black hole's light pushes it away
hints: The Moon does something similar, much more gently, to Earth's oceans.
The same thing would happen to anything big that got that close, even a planet.
Think of a rope where one end is pulled much harder than the other.

media.note: A NASA animation of a star being stretched into a stream of gas as it passes close to a black hole.
media.credit: Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio - Caltech-IPAC/Robert Hurt, Caltech-IPAC/Keith Miller, NASA/JPL/Chelsea Gohd, Global Science and Technology, Inc./Ella Kaplan, NASA/GSFC/Mark SubbaRao

questions.fun_fact: Scientists really call this stretching “spaghettification”.

quality.notes: The answer is the only option that sounds scientific and precise, so it stands out. Hints 1 and 3 both use tides, so one is wasted. NASA tidal disruption animations are easy to find.

revision.reason: Replaced hint 2, which stated the answer, and rewrote hint 3 so it no longer repeats the tides idea.

hints: The Moon does something similar, much more gently, to Earth's oceans.
Gravity gets stronger very quickly as you get closer.
It's the same pull that makes ocean tides.

questions.description: An old paper map with no roads, only stars.
questions.question: The Dunhuang Star Chart, found in a cave in China, is the oldest complete star map known. About when was it made?
hints: It's drawn on paper.
It's from the time of China's Tang dynasty.
It was made in the 600s.

media.credit: Zhangzhugang · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Zhangzhugang

questions.fun_fact: The chart shows more than 1,300 stars and is kept today at the British Library in London.

quality.notes: The options are spread too widely: '100 years ago' doesn't fit 'oldest known', and hint 1 (paper) rules out 5,000 years. That makes it easier than 11. It's also a fairly dry date question. The dating (Tang dynasty, about 650–680 AD) is right. 'Oldest complete star map' is the usual claim, more precisely the oldest complete preserved star atlas.

questions.description: Your socks' favorite spa treatment.
questions.question: I join the washing machine near the end, in the rinse. I make towels fluffy and clothes smell fresh. What kind of product am I?
hints: I don't remove dirt.
I go in after the washing part is done.
Towels come out cuddly thanks to me.

media.credit: Petar Milošević · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Petar Milošević

questions.fun_fact: Procter & Gamble sells the same fabric softener as Downy in the Americas and as Lenor in much of Europe.

quality.notes: It's a simple household riddle and not very surprising. 'Fluffy' and the rinse step point clearly to softener. Many 11-year-olds don't know laundry products well, so 6 may be more realistic.

questions.description: The reason your jaw gets a workout at birthday parties.
questions.question: In 1922, Hans Riegel of Haribo in Germany made one of the first gummy candies, shaped like an animal that danced at fairs back then. Which animal?
hints: It's a big, furry animal.
In stories, it loves honey.
Winnie-the-Pooh is one.

media.credit: Thomas Wolf (Der Wolf im Wald) · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Thomas Wolf (Der Wolf im Wald)

questions.fun_fact: The name Haribo comes from the first two letters of HAns RIegel and BOnn, his home city.

quality.notes: Gummy bears are known worldwide, so most players get this at once. The decorative Bonn image is safe. An illustrative image would also be safe here, but decorative is acceptable.

questions.description: Ice, but with a fancy outfit and a sugar habit.
questions.question: In which country is kakigōri, shaved ice topped with sweet syrup, a favorite treat at summer festivals?
hints: The country is in Asia and is made of islands.
The ice is often topped with green tea syrup.
Its capital is Tokyo.

media.credit: CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

questions.fun_fact: People in Japan have eaten shaved ice for about 1,000 years; long ago only nobles could get ice in summer.

quality.notes: Korea (bingsu), the Philippines (halo-halo) and Taiwan all have similar shaved ice, but the Japanese name pins the answer to Japan. Players who recognise Japanese-sounding words get it at once. Hint 1 ("made of islands") also fits the Philippines. The question is fairly dry: it boils down to which country a name belongs to.

questions.description: A chocolate that skipped the most chocolatey part of the recipe.
questions.question: Which chocolate is made only from cocoa butter, sugar and milk, with none of the dark cocoa solids?
hints: It is often used to decorate cakes.
It has no brown cocoa powder in it.
It is the color of snow.

media.credit: Arjun G. Menon · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Arjun G. Menon

questions.fun_fact: Because white chocolate has no cocoa solids, some people say it isn't really chocolate at all.

quality.notes: "Mint chocolate" is a weak option because it is a flavour, not a basic type of chocolate. Hint 2 only repeats the question. The question reads like a recipe definition, so it is fairly dry.

questions.description: The sweet reward that makes finishing your vegetables totally worth it.
questions.question: What is this treat called?
hints: It melts quickly on a hot day.
You keep it in the freezer.
It is frozen juice on a stick.

media.note: A clear photo of a colorful fruit ice pop (popsicle) on a wooden stick, no brand logo.
media.credit: Pink Sherbet Photography from USA · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Pink Sherbet Photography from USA

questions.fun_fact: The story goes that the ice pop was invented in 1905 by an 11-year-old boy who left a drink with a stir stick outside on a cold night.

quality.notes: A clear stock photo of an ice pop is easy to find, so the essential image works. The fun fact is nicely hedged with "the story goes".

revision.reason: Rewrote the description so it no longer suggests that the treat melts or is frozen.

previous.description: Summer's favorite snack, always racing against the sun.

questions.description: The biggest room of the church, and it never leaves the harbor.
questions.question: The nave, the long main hall of a church, is named after the Latin word for “ship”. Who was it mainly built for?
hints: They were the largest group in any church.
In the Middle Ages, the area right around the altar was kept for others.
These people came in from the town to hear the Mass.

media.credit: Diliff · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Diliff

questions.fun_fact: In the Middle Ages, the nave often had no benches at all: people stood or brought their own stools.

quality.notes: Ordinary worshippers are the natural guess for the main hall, so players can reason their way there easily. Hint 3 nearly states the answer, which is allowed. The question feels a bit like a school lesson.

questions.description: A room on wheels that never gets to choose where it goes.
questions.question: It has wheels, it is hooked to others in a long line, and people or goods ride inside it. What is it?
hints: It cannot move by itself.
An engine pulls it along.
It rolls on rails.

media.credit: Shixart1985 · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Shixart1985

questions.fun_fact: In 2001, an iron ore train in Australia had 682 cars and stretched over 7 km (4.6 miles).

quality.notes: Bus, bicycle and taxi can't be hooked together in a long line, so the answer is trivial even at level 1. The riddle is plain. The fun fact (the 682-car BHP train of 2001) is correct.

questions.description: It toots, it chugs, and it is in no hurry at all.
questions.question: Little trains like this one drive around many towns. What are they for?
hints: People ride it on vacation.
It stops at famous sights.
Its riders take lots of photos.

media.note: Photo of a small tourist road train (engine plus open cars) in a town street, ideally with passengers, no readable city name.
media.credit: Elliott Brown from Birmingham, United Kingdom · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Elliott Brown from Birmingham, United Kingdom

questions.fun_fact: Many of these little trains aren't real trains at all: a small truck dressed up as an engine pulls them along normal streets.

quality.notes: Photos of tourist road trains are common, so the essential image is fine as long as it has no visible town name.

questions.description: A tree that's good at breakfast and bad at hiding its color.
questions.question: I have shiny green leaves and sweet-smelling white flowers. My sweet, juicy fruit gave its name to a color of the rainbow. What am I?
hints: My fruit is often squeezed into juice for breakfast.
You peel my fruit and split it into segments.
My fruit's color is between red and yellow.

media.credit: USDAgov · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: USDAgov

questions.fun_fact: The orange is probably a very old mix of two other citrus fruits, the pomelo and the mandarin, first grown in southern China.

quality.notes: Cherry (cherry red) and lemon (lemon yellow) are also color names, but orange is clearly the one meant, so this is only a small point. The distractors are weak: lemons aren't sweet, and "gave its name to a color" points straight to orange. It's a pleasant riddle but not surprising.

revision.reason: Changed the color clue to a rainbow color, which fits only the orange.

previous.question: I have shiny green leaves and sweet-smelling white flowers. My sweet, juicy fruit gave its name to a color. What am I?

questions.description: Oscar night, when even drawn characters sit up straight and hope to hear their names.
questions.question: Which cartoon pair won seven Oscars, more than any other cartoon duo?
hints: They started out in short cartoons shown in cinemas.
They have been chasing each other since 1940.
The cat is gray and blue, and the little brown mouse nearly always wins.

media.credit: Prayitno · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Prayitno

questions.fun_fact: In their very first cartoon in 1940, Tom was called Jasper.

quality.notes: Seven Oscars is correct. "More than any other cartoon duo" is broadly true but hard to check in every detail. Hint 2 (chasing each other since 1940) already almost gives it away. q-2579 (Tom/Jerry analogy) shares only the topic.

revision.reason: Rewrote the description so it no longer mentions fighting, and replaced hint 1, which fit only Tom and Jerry, with a vaguer one.

previous.description: Some families fight over the remote; this pair fights over absolutely everything.
hints: They almost never speak.
They have been chasing each other since 1940.
The cat is gray and blue, and the little brown mouse nearly always wins.

questions.description: A boy who has written more sentences on a chalkboard than most writers have in their books.
questions.question: In the opening of The Simpsons, Bart writes lines on the chalkboard. What makes him stop and rush out of the classroom?
hints: It's a sound.
Everyone at school hears it many times a day.
It rings when lessons are over.

media.credit: Douglas P Perkins · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Douglas P Perkins

questions.fun_fact: Over the years, Bart has written hundreds of different sentences on that chalkboard.

quality.notes: The answer is easy to reason out (school, end of lesson → bell) even if you've never seen the show. The distractors are weak and none of them really fits a classroom. The difficulty is a little overrated.

questions.description: Twins who caused so much trouble in one building that they had to take the chaos somewhere new.
questions.question: Zack and Cody first lived in a fancy hotel in Boston. Where did they live in the follow-up series?
hints: It was owned by the same rich hotel family.
They went to school there too.
The new show was called “The Suite Life on Deck”.

media.credit: Basile Morin · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Basile Morin

questions.fun_fact: Zack and Cody were played by real twins, Dylan and Cole Sprouse.

quality.notes: This is narrow fan knowledge of a Disney Channel show from about 15 years ago; today's teens may not know it. Hint 3 names the show "on Deck", which comes close to the answer (hint 3 is allowed to).

questions.description: A street resident who has stayed six years old for more than 50 years.
questions.question: Which of these words does NOT describe Big Bird from Sesame Street?
hints: Big Bird is known for being gentle and friendly.
Another neighbor on the street is famous for this mood.
Oscar, who lives in a trash can, is the one with this mood.

media.credit: CaptJayRuffins · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: CaptJayRuffins

questions.fun_fact: Caroll Spinney played Big Bird for almost 50 years, from 1969 to 2018.

quality.notes: Big Bird is mainly a US character; many countries have their own Sesame Street lead characters (e.g. Germany's Samson, Mexico's Abelardo), so this doesn't travel well internationally. "Grouchy" obviously doesn't fit a kind character, so the question is easy to reason out. An odd-one-out about adjectives is dry.

questions.description: A flying office with very good legroom.
questions.question: Which world leader travels in the plane known as “Air Force One”?
hints: This person's plane is a huge blue-and-white jumbo jet.
This person works in Washington, D.C.
This person lives in the White House.

media.credit: Julian Herzog (Website) · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Julian Herzog (Website)

questions.fun_fact: “Air Force One” isn't the name of one plane: it is the call sign of any Air Force plane the president is flying in.

quality.notes: This is well-known knowledge, and "Air Force" already points to a military or national leader. A safe illustrative image (a generic jumbo jet) was possible, so decorative is the wrong role. It's a straightforward question.

questions.description: He held the most important meeting of his life without leaving the house.
questions.question: What is Grover Cleveland still the only US president to have done in the White House?
hints: It happened in June 1886.
The Marine Band, led by John Philip Sousa, played for the few guests.
The other person involved, 21-year-old Frances Folsom, became first lady that day.

media.credit: Harrison Keely · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Harrison Keely

questions.fun_fact: Frances Cleveland was just 21, which still makes her the youngest first lady ever.

quality.notes: This is US-centric presidential trivia. Players can reason towards the answer, since "only one ever" rules out yearly traditions like the egg roll and the tree. Hint 3 almost gives the answer away (allowed). The difficulty is probably above 8.

questions.description: Barcelona's most famous apartment building has a nickname that isn't on the doorbell.
questions.question: Gaudí's Casa Batlló in Barcelona has a wavy front with strange balconies and columns. What do locals nickname it?
hints: The nickname comes from what the columns and balconies look like.
The columns look a bit like parts of a body.
A skeleton is made of these.

media.credit: C messier · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: C messier

questions.fun_fact: The roof of Casa Batlló is covered in shiny scale-like tiles and is often said to be the back of a dragon.

quality.notes: Casa dels Ossos is a real nickname, but it is local Barcelona knowledge. A 13-year-old outside Spain would not know it, so difficulty 8 is too low. The question says “wavy front”, which points players to “House of Waves”; that is fair but may feel misleading. The description is weak: “a nickname that isn't on the doorbell” is not very funny. The Passeig de Gràcia image will likely show the bone-like facade, which helps a bit.

questions.description: Arches: ancient Rome's favorite way to show off.
questions.question: What is the wedge-shaped stone at the top center of this arch called?
hints: Without it, the arch cannot stand.
It is put in last, at the very highest point.
It locks all the other stones in place, like a key in a lock.

media.note: Close-up of the top of a stone arch where the central wedge-shaped stone is clearly visible; no labels.
media.credit: arjharris · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: arjharris

questions.fun_fact: While an arch is being built, its stones rest on a wooden frame, which can only be taken away once the keystone is in.

quality.notes: A sound vocabulary question, but it feels like a school test. The description is a short, plain remark with no real joke. Commons very likely has clear keystone photos.

questions.description: Japan gave the world many beautiful words, and one of them is sneaking into the wrong club.
questions.question: Which of these Japanese words is NOT the name of an art?
hints: Three of them are things people make to look beautiful.
One of them usually disappears within minutes of being made.
It is usually made with rice and fish.

media.credit: Basile Morin · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Basile Morin

questions.fun_fact: In traditional origami, you shape the paper using only folds: no cuts and no glue.

quality.notes: Some would say sushi-making is a culinary art, but the intended answer is clear. Kids know sushi is food, so it is easy. The Kyoto garden image may show pruned trees that look like bonsai, but that harms nothing.

questions.description: Look into the eyes of the person next to you: the odds are on this question's side.
questions.question: What is the most common eye color in the world?
hints: It is not a rare color at all: most people on Earth have it.
Most people in Africa and Asia have it.
It is also the color of chocolate.

media.credit: Jennifer Woodard Maderazo · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jennifer Woodard Maderazo

questions.fun_fact: Blue eyes have no blue color in them at all; they look blue because of the way light scatters.

quality.notes: A plain fact question. Hint 1 just repeats the question (“most people have it”), so it adds nothing. The question is filed under art, which is an odd fit. The fun fact about blue eyes is nice.

questions.description: Every billionaire superhero needs a helper, and some helpers don't even have a body.
questions.question: Tony Stark's AI helper runs his Iron Man suits, talks with a calm British voice and later becomes the hero Vision. What is it called?
hints: It first appears in the 2008 Iron Man film.
Later films replace it with a new helper that has an Irish voice.
Its name starts with the letter J.

media.credit: Alenoach · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Alenoach

questions.fun_fact: Marvel says JARVIS stands for “Just A Rather Very Intelligent System”.

quality.notes: The “Just A Rather Very Intelligent System” acronym comes from production and promotional material and is hardly said in the films, so “in the films” is shaky. JARVIS also only partly “becomes” Vision. Hint 2 repeats the Vision clue from the question. FRIDAY is an excellent distractor. Other Tony Stark questions (q-1509, q-3381) ask different facts.

revision.reason: Credited the acronym to Marvel in the fun fact and replaced hint 2, which only repeated the Vision clue from the question, with a new clue.

hints: It first appears in the 2008 Iron Man film.
Its voice actor, Paul Bettany, later played Vision in person.
Its name starts with the letter J.
previous.fun_fact: In the films, JARVIS stands for “Just A Rather Very Intelligent System”.

questions.description: Picking out every traffic light in nine blurry pictures: the strangest exam of your life.
questions.question: Websites often make you tick a box or find all the buses in a set of pictures. Who are these tests meant to keep out?
wrong_answers: Children too young to sign up
hints: The test is easy for people but hard for one kind of visitor.
These visitors can sign up thousands of times a minute.
They are often called “bots”.

media.credit: CSR2Forever · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: CSR2Forever

questions.fun_fact: These tests are called CAPTCHAs, and when you solve them you sometimes help computers learn to read words or spot objects.

quality.notes: Young kids may not have met CAPTCHAs, so this is slightly harder than 4. The answer is a bit more technical-sounding than the distractors. An illustrative image would be safe here, so decorative is the wrong choice.

questions.description: Machines have beaten humans at many tables, and they never even ask for a snack break.
questions.question: In 2017, an AI called Libratus beat four top professionals at a game where it couldn't see what its opponents held. Which game?
hints: In three of these games, every piece is on the board for both players to see.
In this one, your opponent keeps something hidden in their hand.
It is played with cards and chips.

media.credit: Indrajit Das · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Indrajit Das

questions.fun_fact: In 2019, an AI called Pluribus beat five top professionals at once in six-player poker.

quality.notes: Players can reason their way to the answer, which is good. The facts are right: Chinook (checkers), Deep Blue (chess), AlphaGo (Go), Libratus and Pluribus (poker). It asks a different fact from the poker hand question q-3833.

revision.reason: Rewrote the question around Libratus so the hidden-information clue points to poker in the real world, not just among the four options.

previous.question: AI has beaten top human players at all four of these games. In which one can the AI not see everything going on in the game?

questions.description: Eight researchers wrote one paper, and now your phone can write poems.

hints: Today it is behind almost every large language model.

revision.reason: Replaced the English-only hint 3, changed the wrong answers so they differ in meaning and still work after translation, and rewrote the description, which wrongly said there is only one landing.

questions.description: Advice that sounds like a librarian holding a baseball bat.

questions.description: Four wishes, no genie required.

quality.notes: Rockwell's Four Freedoms paintings are mostly known in the US, so this needs one country's knowledge. A dry date question. The Rockwell painting image might show a Saturday Evening Post cover with a 1943 date, which is not the answer but adds a misleading year.

questions.description: Your parents were right: those little green trees on your plate are doing you a favor.

quality.notes: True, but broccoli is only a modest source of calcium, so the premise is a bit stretched. A fairly standard school-health question. Hint 3 (Ca) is close to giving it away, which is allowed.

questions.description: The kitchen gadget that made every family argue about counter space.

quality.notes: "Deep fryer" has a slight claim because of the name and how the appliance is marketed, but the wording "really a small version of" makes oven clearly the answer. The fun fact repeats the idea in hint 1.

questions.description: The shiniest thing a soccer team will ever hug, and they all want a turn.
questions.question: It's made of gold, shows two figures holding up the Earth, and every team from Colombia to Japan dreams of lifting it. What is it?
hints: Teams from every continent try to win it.
The winning captain holds it high over their head after the final.
It's named after the biggest soccer tournament on the planet.

media.credit: John Shorten · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: John Shorten

questions.fun_fact: Only the champions hold the real trophy for a short time; FIFA keeps it, and the winners take home a gold-plated copy.
questions.concept: Trofeo de la Copa del Mundo

quality.notes: Distractors: the Champions League and European Championship trophies are easy to rule out with the clue “every team from Colombia to Japan”, and young kids probably don't know the other trophies at all. Unambiguous: the Champions League is for clubs, so “team” is a little loose, but the two figures holding up the Earth point only to the World Cup trophy. Fun: a fairly plain recognition question. Kids may know the trophy less well than a 2 suggests, so I'd rate it about 3.

review.feedback: This overlaps the approved q-0848 ("¿Quién se lleva este trofeo dorado?" → the World Cup champion team). That question shows the same golden trophy and ties it to the World Cup, so whichever one players see first answers the other. Drop this question or turn it into one about a different World Cup fact.

questions.description: A man who made a whole country hold its breath, and then made it cheer.
questions.question: Argentina's Emiliano “Dibu” Martínez stopped three penalties against Colombia in 2021, then won a top World Cup award in 2022. Which one?
hints: The award is for the best player in one special position.
Martínez saved a penalty in the shootout of the 2022 final against France.
Think about what a goalkeeper wears on his hands.

media.author: Master Sgt. Lance Cheung of U.S. Air Force

questions.fun_fact: Before becoming Argentina's hero, Martínez spent about ten years at Arsenal in England, mostly as a back-up goalkeeper or on loan to other clubs.

quality.notes: Distractors: “The Best Young Player Award” has a different form from the three “Golden …” options. The “stopped three penalties” clue already tells you he is a goalkeeper, so you can work out “Golden Glove” easily. The question's Colombia angle (the 2021 Copa América semi-final) is a regional detail but doesn't decide the answer. All facts check out, including about ten years at Arsenal (2010–2020).

questions.description: A hat so famous that the news gave its wearers a nickname.

media.author: Marsupium

questions.fun_fact: The UN peacekeepers won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1988.

quality.notes: Distractors: Olympic security guards and NATO fighter pilots are weak options. Anyone who links blue with the UN gets the answer quickly, and hint 2 makes it obvious. Fun: a fairly dry question about a term. The decorative world map is fine, since an illustrative photo would show the UN helmets.

questions.description: Athletics has more strange gear than a garden shed, and every piece gets its own event.

The 1986 redesign was for safety after Hohn's 104.80 m throw. 'Beyond the field' simplifies this a little. A plain identify question, so fun is moderate.

review.feedback: No candidate shows a javelin: the sheet has grass playing fields, a grass running track, a school sports court and a bullfight. A new search isn't allowed, so this essential image slot can't be filled. It needs a real photo of a javelin stuck in grass, for example from a search like "javelin stuck in ground". No suitable picture found for this question.

previous.feedback: None of the candidates shows toy play money: #1 shows real-looking euro notes on a clothesline, #2 is historical card money from a museum, and #3–6 are unrelated (a Buddhist procession and Soviet stamps). Find such a photo (for example "Monopoly money" or "toy money board game") before this question can go in. No suitable picture found for this question.

questions.description: Before paper money, a Swedish shopping trip could give you a very sore back.

review.feedback: This overlaps approved q-3103, which shows the donkey and says outright that it is the symbol of the US Democratic Party. quality.notes: The ¢ sign is mostly North American, and families elsewhere rarely see it, so the question leans on one region (International angle). Commons should have a clean cent-sign image, so the essential media is feasible. The typewriter fun fact is broadly true but a bit simplified. Recognising a symbol feels quite dry.

previous.feedback: The description ("for the tiniest prices") states the answer's defining trait. Looking only at the four options, it rules out the euro, copyright and degrees Celsius. Hint 1 ("very cheap items") and hint 2 ("one hundredth of something") give the cent away the same way. The description should play on shopping without saying how small the value is, and hints 1–2 should point elsewhere, for example at the region or the symbol's shape.

revision.reason: Rewrote the description and hints 1–2 so they no longer give away the small value; they now play on shopping and point at the symbol's shape and coins.
